News.title: 'My baby died after hospital didn't realise I'd moved house'
News.content:
'My baby died after hospital didn't realise I'd moved house'

Kelly Whitehead missed 10 weeks of crucial care which she believes led to her son, Christopher, losing his life

View 3 Images Kelly Whitehead says she informed staff at the Queen's Medical Centre, Nottingham, that she was moving and her phone number would need updating, but she believes this was not done (Image: SWNS)

A mum lost her baby after the NHS failed to provide basic antenatal care because they had not updated her details when she moved house. Kelly Whitehead, 37, is suing a hospital and says her son Christopher, who was stillborn at 41 weeks, would still be alive without the grave admin error.

‌



Kelly moved home but later discovered her updated details had not been correctly recorded across NHS services. She says it saw her miss 10 crucial weeks of antenatal care.

‌



Kelly received no medical appointments between the "critical period" that covered 31 and 41 weeks of pregnancy. Under NHS guidance, women who miss antenatal appointments should be followed up under “did not attend” procedures by offering alternatives such as home visits, GP liaison and escalated safeguarding procedures.

‌



Kelly says this did not happen and if she had been in hospital just a "week earlier" - she would still have her son today. Nottingham University Hospitals NHS Trust, which is already under scrutiny as part of the ongoing Ockenden Review, acknowledged in a letter to Kelly that "there was a missed opportunity to monitor Christopher’s growth on scan which may potentially have resulted in a missed opportunity to deliver Christopher earlier".

View 3 Images Kelly says she went without care between 31 and 41 weeks (Image: SWNS)

Kelly, from Nottingham, said: "I want to make sure Christopher's name isn't forgotten. The hardest thing to live with is the years I've spent blaming myself.

‌



"I will never forget being put into the labour ward, where I could hear the other babies crying and had to lie there thinking my end result was going to be very different.

"It just felt criminal because these are professionals and you trust them - and I felt forgotten by the system that was supposed to help me.

"Planning a funeral for the son I will never have will stay with me for the rest of my life. I have been in a state of survival and grief ever since."

‌



Before Kelly became pregnant with Christopher in September 2018, she gave birth to twins George and Felicity, who were born premature via an emergency C-section. Due to the traumatic birth, which has left her two children disabled with high-needs autism, Kelly was informed she would be classed as high risk.

Initially she was provided with extra scans and monitoring which gave her reassurance that everything was progressing well - until she moved out of the local area. She said: "Neither of my twins weighed more than a small bag of sugar.

"We didn't know at points if we were going to be able to bring them home."

‌



Kelly said when she realised she had fallen pregnant again with Christopher, she wanted to push to have a planned C section as she was told it would be safer on her already damaged body. She said: "I was living in a single bedroom flat at the time, already trying to find somewhere to move to.

"It was scary, we already had two twins with high medical needs - but I found a renewed sense of hope in me when I knew Christopher was on the way, that maybe this can be the healing journey I need because I've spent so long blaming myself and my body for failing to carry them safely.

"My body is meant to be the safest place for them as far as we're told, but I wanted another chance to do right by my children."

‌



View 3 Images Nottingham University Hospitals NHS Trust said there were missed opportunities in the case which it "deeply regrets" (Image: SWNS)

Despite going into the hospital asking for a planned c-section, Kelly said she was talked out of it by hospital staff - and left with a pamphlet feeling "half-reassured".

She said: "They told me the VBAC was the best option but I wanted a c-section because I knew the recovery is the one I had done before.

‌



"I remember leaving that room feeling as though I had been talked out of something I wanted so strongly to happen. They weren't listening to me.

"I felt they were cost cutting and talked me out of it because of the cost of a C section which required several trained members of staff."

Not long after, Kelly moved to a larger council house on the other side of Nottingham, went into the hospital for a general appointment and provided the front desk with her new address and telephone number.

‌



Around half way through her second trimester, Kelly began struggling to keep up with caring for her seriously unwell twins, settling into her new flat and doing it all alone.

"I was really struggling and getting more and more tired," Kelly said. "I missed a few appointments because I couldn't get there on public transport - but when I tried to explain my situation they didn't seem to care, it just felt like, 'oh come to your appointments and get on with it'. I soon felt as though I fell through the cracks.

"Signposting could have happened, they could have offered home visits but they didn't make that happen - and I now have discovered they were sending letters out to my old address this whole time.

‌



"Community services were apparently sending home visits out to my old address too, and recording it as no one in - they didn't even bother to check, call, or ask neighbours."

Kelly said she tried to contact both the hospital and GP practice numerous times to no avail. She said: "I was just getting ping-ponged back and forth - my GP told me I wasn't even on their records as a patient anymore.

"It was painful and I felt forgotten and alone - so I stopped trying after a while. I thought things seemed fine, and I'll wait for next appointment - not realising the hospital hadn't updated that either. I felt like I was hitting up against a brick wall."

‌



As her pregnancy progressed, Kelly began to worry something was wrong. At almost 42 weeks pregnant, with no signs of labour, Kelly says she called the hospital again and spoke with someone from the birthing unit at the hospital on the phone.

She said: "I knew the baby had turned and shifted and was sitting lower, I thought maybe I had a sign of mislabour, but when I spoke with this nurse they said it was Braxton hicks - sporadic, practice uterine tightenings that prepare your body for labour. I didn't know the difference."

When Kelly called again just days later, she was told to come into the hospital - but they could not see her on that day, only the day after. When doctors tried to find Christopher's heartbeat and failed, they informed Kelly he had been stillborn.

‌



"My world fell apart," Kelly said. "The hardest part was hearing that as far as they could tell, he had only been dead a few days. I believe if I'd been seen a week prior, he would still be there."

In a follow-up letter from the hospital, they stated: “Because of the missed appointments, there was a missed opportunity to monitor Christopher’s growth on scan which may potentially have resulted in a missed opportunity to deliver Christopher earlier.”

Kelly added: "I had to lay Christopher in his coffin just before the funeral and dress him in his new baby garments with his little monkey teddy, one that will stay with him forever and one that I keep with me.

‌



"That's the last act I felt like I could do as his mother: the last time I was ever going to be able to touch or see him. I will never forget that - and now I just want to be able to buy him a grave stone."

Kelly, who has struggled with depression and grief ever since, is now working with Fletchers Solicitors after she realised her son's death could have been prevented.

The practice are working with a number of families who have raised concerns about maternity and neonatal care in Nottingham. Nottingham University Hospitals NHS Trust maternity services remain under scrutiny as part of the ongoing Ockenden Review, which began in 2022.

‌



The Trust is also subject to a separate ongoing police investigation into maternity care concerns. Clinical negligence solicitor Priya Singh, who is supporting Kelly with a legal case, said: “Kelly's experience is heartbreaking because no expectant mother should go 10 weeks without antenatal care during the final stages of pregnancy, particularly when national guidance is clear that missed appointments should trigger active follow-up and safeguarding measures.

"The Trust has acknowledged missed opportunities in her care, including opportunities to monitor Christopher's growth and potentially deliver him earlier, raising serious questions about how the systems designed to protect mothers and babies were allowed to fail.

"The Ockenden Review reinforced the devastating consequences that can arise when communication breaks down and continuity of care is lost.

‌



"When a communication failure like this happens, the outcomes can be devastating and Kelly's experience is a stark reminder that those lessons must be embedded into everyday practice, not simply remain recommendations. Families deserve confidence that the changes being suggested will prevent other parents from suffering the same devastating loss.”

Tracy Pilcher, chief nurse at Nottingham University Hospitals, said: "We would like to extend our sincere condolences to Ms Whitehead on the loss of her son, Christopher.

"Following a review of the care provided during Christopher’s birth in April 2019, it was identified that opportunities were missed for community and hospital maternity teams to effectively share information regarding missed appointments. We deeply regret that these opportunities were not taken.

Article continues below

"As part of the case review, several areas for learning were highlighted, including the need to strengthen processes, guidelines and procedures relating to non-attendance at appointments.

"We continue to regularly review and improve our procedures and provide ongoing staff training in this area."

News.title: New 'serious shortage' alert for Ramipril blood pressure capsules
News.content:
New 'serious shortage' alert for Ramipril blood pressure capsules

The situation has been explained

View 3 Images Ramipril is one of the most commonly prescribed blood pressure medications in the UK (Image: Pexels)

People taking a common blood pressure medication have been warned of "serious shortages" in the UK.

‌



Tracking website MediWatch, which monitors DHSC and NHS England data daily, said that a "Serious Shortage Protocol is active for Ramipril 1.25mg capsules in the current official data". It advised people to ask their pharmacist what the active SSP permits were before accepting any alternative quantity, strength or formulation.

‌



It said: "Ramipril 1.25mg capsules are in shortage across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. The Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) issued Serious Shortage Protocol SSP087 on 22 April 2026 (and extended it past 29 May 2026), allowing community pharmacies to limit dispensing to a maximum of one month's supply per prescription — even if your prescription is normally for two or three months. No prescription charges apply when supplied under this protocol.

‌



View 3 Images Patients have been warned (Image: Catherine Delahaye via Getty Images)

"Ramipril 1.25mg and 2.5mg tablets, plus the oral solution, remain available, but the DHSC has warned they cannot meet increased demand if all capsule patients switch to these forms. If you take 1.25mg capsules, you should contact your pharmacist about tablet alternatives now — before stocks of those run low too.

"Separately, a Class 2 recall was issued on 20 April 2026 for one batch of Ramipril 10mg capsules (manufactured by Crescent Pharma) due to a packaging error — some cartons contained 5mg blister strips instead of 10mg. This is a safety issue, not a supply issue, but it adds pressure to the overall Ramipril supply chain."

‌



It went on to explain that Ramipril is an ACE inhibitor — one of the most commonly prescribed blood pressure medications in the UK.

It added: "Over 35 million Ramipril items were dispensed in England alone during 2025, making it one of the top ten prescribed drugs in the country.

"It belongs to a family of medicines that all work in a similar way, but Ramipril is particularly favoured because it has a long half-life (stays in your body for a while) and can be taken once daily."

Article continues below

View 3 Images Ramipril 1.25mg capsules are in short supply (Image: MHRA)

MediWatch also said that another blood pressure medication was under a "medium" alert, saying that "Propranolol modified-release capsules are present in current active official shortage data". It added that Propranolol 40mg and 80mg immediate-release tablets remained available and "can support increased demand".

Propranolol is a beta-blocker used for high blood pressure, anxiety, migraine prevention and essential tremor, MediWatch said, adding that it was "the modified-release (slow-acting) capsules that are affected — the immediate-release tablet versions remain fully available. Your GP may need to adjust your dosing schedule if switching from MR to immediate-release formulations, as MR capsules are typically taken once daily while IR tablets are usually taken two or three times a day".

News.title: Boy, 13, dies after nine years in vegetative state from eating contaminated cheese
News.content:
Boy, 13, dies after nine years in vegetative state from eating contaminated cheese

Mattia Maestri fell into a permanent vegetative state aged just four after eating cheese contaminated with the deadly bacteria E.Coli - he has now died nine years later

View 3 Images Mattia Maestri died after nine years in a vegetative state (Image: Jam Press)

A teenager has died nine years after eating contaminated cheese that left him in a vegetative state.

‌



Italian Mattia Maestri, 13, ate raw-milk cheese contaminated with the deadly bacteria E.coli in June 2017 in the northern part of the country.

‌



The boy's family have since been fighting a legal battle against those responsible, both at the cheese factory and with the healthcare professionals involved in the boy's care.

‌



His father, Giovanni Battista Maestri, broke the news of his son's sad passing. In a message published by the newspaper Il Corriere del Trentino, he said: "Our Mattia has left us and, on his behalf, I thank you for helping to make his passing less painful."

Mattia was only four when he ate a piece of 'Due Laghi' cheese, produced from raw milk by the Coredo cheese dairy in the Non Valley in the Trentino.

His father claims the contamination was caused by errors in the milk collection process.

‌



View 3 Images His father, Giovanni Battista Maestri, announced news of his death (Image: Jam Press)

The tragic child eventually developed hemolytic uremic syndrome, a serious condition linked to the breakdown of red blood cells.

It is closely associated with E.coli and can cause blood clots to form and impair blood flow to vital organs, including the brain.

‌



Mattia eventually fell into an irreversible vegetative state. He was reportedly taking 47 medicines a day, suffered dozens of epileptic seizures every day and had lost his sight.

Two men from the dairy were convicted of causing grievous bodily harm after a long court battle.

Since his son became ill, his father founded a consumer group and published a book warning parents about the hidden dangers of unpasteurised dairy.

‌



The book was presented to the Italian parliament earlier this year. Giovanni said: "I couldn't save him, but it will save other children.

The family’s lawyers have also filed a complaint alleging aggravated negligent homicide and claim that Mattia and his parents have endured “nine years of agony”.

Speaking about his son's condition previously, Giovanni said: “He fell into a coma, spent a month in intensive care at the hospital in Padua and then spent a year at a rehabilitation clinic in Conegliano, where they simply taught us how to look after him at home.”

‌



View 3 Images Mattia Maestri ate contaminated cheese aged just four (Image: Jam Press)

Mattia's funeral took place on Monday afternoon in Coredo, in the Non Valley in northern Italy, where dozens of people gathered to pay their respects to the 13-year-old boy.

Father Raymond Marcieca said: “Mattia’s ordeal was a real trial, he did not have time to sin and will remain an angel forever.”

Article continues below

His teachers paid tribute at the funeral, saying: “You reminded us of the profound value of life, and we fondly remember your first day in class. You will always be a friend, and you will be that special magnet that keeps us united in our memories of the years we spent together at school.”

Besides consuming unpasteurised products, people can also contract E.Coli through raw fruit and vegetables, undercooked meat, polluted water and farm animals.

Brits are advised to contact NHS 111 or their GP if they or their children show any symptoms of E. coli infection.

News.title: Mum of teen told 'nothing doctors could do and to say goodbye'
News.content:
Mum of teen told 'nothing doctors could do and to say goodbye'

Kaitlyn Hurlstone developed symptoms including persistent vomiting, leg pain and fatigue

View 4 Images They are raising money for Kaitlyn’s private treatment (Image: PA Real Life)

A family was told to say goodbye after a girl diagnosed at 16 was told by doctor that “there was nothing more they could do”.

‌



It was after she after being diagnosed with acute myeloid leukaemia at 16. Now her mum hopes to raise up to £150,000 for alternative treatment that could save her daughter’s life. Kaitlyn Hurlstone, now 18, from Newcastle-under-Lyme, Staffordshire, contracted tonsillitis in April 2024 that she said developed into “very strange” overgrown gums that “detached” themselves.

‌



Her mother, Angharad Hurlstone, 38, an event decorator, took her daughter to the dentist at the end of May, but she said they were not “sure what it was”, so she was sent home with no answers. When Kaitlyn developed further symptoms of persistent vomiting, leg pain and fatigue they went to a GP and doctors ordered an urgent blood test on June 21.

‌



Within hours, Kaitlyn and Angharad received a call to tell them to go for an emergency assessment in hospital and, just four hours after taking the blood test, a diagnosis of acute myeloid leukaemia was confirmed. Kaitlyn has since had four rounds of chemotherapy, a stem cell transplant and brain surgery to reduce sudden swelling.

In June 2026, Kaitlyn’s cancer spread to her spinal fluid and caused further severe damage and swelling, leaving her blind and unresponsive in a life-threatening condition for a week. After suddenly “turning a corner”, Angharad said her daughter was now in “uncharted waters”, so the family is raising money to try to get Kaitlyn on either a £9,000 a month “breakthrough drug” or a £150,000 stem cell transplant because she claimed the “NHS won’t fund another one”.

View 4 Images Kaitlyn outside hospital (Image: PA Real Life)

‌



On what it was like to be warned to say goodbye to her daughter in June 2026, Angharad said: “It was probably the worst day of my entire life. (Kaitlyn) was unresponsive… and then it was like she just completely turned a corner.

“And then she was laughing and joking with her friends. It was truly like a miracle had happened.”

Kaitlyn said: “I didn’t know people said their goodbyes. Hearing that now, it just hits you.”

‌



Angharad said it all started when her daughter got tonsillitis in April 2024 and she “never really came back from it”. Within a month, Kaitlyn said her symptoms progressed to overgrown gums, where both her top and bottom sets of gums grew over her teeth and then it “detached” so it was “flapping down” inside her mouth.

After a dentist could not work out why it was happening, Kaitlyn said she started experiencing other symptoms including fatigue, pale lips, vomiting and leg pain when she was trying to play volleyball and “run on sand” at school.

Kaitlyn said: “The whole month of May, I was doing my GCSEs, but I was throwing up in the mornings. So we went to the doctors and they recommended I get a blood test. Exactly a week after my last exam on June 14, I got a blood test and a few hours later they called us straight into the hospital.”

‌



At this point, the mother and daughter still thought Kaitlyn’s symptoms could just be anaemia, but when they walked through the hospital and realised the referral was in the cancer centre, Angharad said it immediately became “quite daunting”.

Kaitlyn added: “I tried to blank it out because we thought it was just an out-of-hours thing.”

By the time the two arrived at hospital at 8pm on June 21, 2024 – around four hours after having the urgent blood test and receiving a call to go to an emergency assessment unit – Kaitlyn was told she had acute myeloid leukaemia. It is a cancer of the white blood cells that progresses quickly and aggressively and is characterised by symptoms such as paleness, tiredness, breathlessness, frequent infections and bone and joint pain, according to the NHS.

‌



View 4 Images Kaitlyn having treatment (Image: PA Real Life)

Overgrown gums – also known as gingival enlargement – can also be an early warning sign. While Kaitlyn was lying in a hospital bed, Angharad spoke to a doctor who explained the diagnosis and treatment plan.

“We’ve got to think that Kaitlyn is a lawn of grass and it’s covered in weeds,” Angharad remembered the doctor said. “What we need to do is kill the weeds, but when we do that, we will kill some of the lawn.”

‌



Due to the aggressiveness of Kaitlyn’s cancer, she started chemotherapy the next day. As a result, Kaitlyn said she felt well enough to attend only an hour of her school prom on July 11, before she returned to hospital for months more treatment, including regular platelet and blood transfusions.

A week later, Kaitlyn said it was “a bit devastating” to realise she had started losing her hair, but she “waited as long as (she) could” to shave it off in August because hair was her “thing” before her diagnosis. Kaitlyn also experienced hot flushes, tiredness, nausea and sores in her mouth.

Since the beginning of her treatment in June 2024, Angharad said her daughter had had four rounds of chemotherapy, including one round of “the most intensive chemo that a human body can have” in December that same year. Angharad said her daughter also had a “gruelling” round of treatment before a stem cell transplant in February 2025.

‌



She then needed brain surgery four months later because of her brain swelling that caused her to “blow a pupil and (have a) seizure”, before she slipped into unconsciousness while in intensive care. Kaitlyn then had burr hole surgery to relieve the swelling in her brain and Angharad said she made a “good recovery”.

Since then, doctors told them they are in “uncharted waters”, including when Kaitlyn was admitted to hospital in June 2026 after frequent vomiting and then she lost her vision completely. Angharad said two MRI scans days apart showed Kaitlyn’s “leukaemia had infiltrated her brain”.

She added: “(Doctors) hadn’t seen an MRI look as bad as Kaitlyn’s did with leukaemia infiltration and so fast in comparison to the one four days prior. So that’s when they called it and said to get everyone in who needs to see her… to essentially say goodbyes.”

‌



View 4 Images Angharad and Kaitlyn before her diagnosis (Image: PA Real Life)

She added that Kaitlyn was “unresponsive” during a “whole week of torment”, before she “deteriorated rapidly” and had two rounds of full brain radiotherapy. Angharad said Kaitlyn then “completely turned a corner” and it was like a “miracle had happened”.

Following Kaitlyn’s recovery, Angharad said doctors cannot put her on the clinical trial because of a “relapse in her central nervous system” making her ineligible on the NHS so the family are raising money to “get her in front of a private doctor”. Angharad is “hopeful” the “breakthrough drug” treatment will cure one of her daughter’s specific gene mutations – NPM1 – so that Kaitlyn’s leukaemia cells do not simply return after chemotherapy.

Article continues below

Kaitlyn said: “I just want to be better and for all of it to go away.”

Angharad added: “We’re sharing our story to raise awareness for things to look out for because we would have never in a million years thought that it was leukaemia.”

You can donate to Kaitlyn’s fundraiser on her GoFundMe page.

News.title: SpaceX rocket crashes into Moon at 5,400mph
News.content:
SpaceX rocket crashes into Moon at 5,400mph

The 40ft long Falcon 9 upper stage was left in a 'chaotic' lunar orbit by Elon Musk's SpaceX company following a 2005 US-Japanese mission launched by SpaceX - and has now crashed into the Moon

View 3 Images The SpaceX Falcon 9 will send debris miles into the lunar atmosphere following the crash (file) (Image: NASA / SWNS)

Part of a rocket launched by Elon Musk’s SpaceX has smashed into the Moon at around 5,400mph - about seven times the speed of sound.

‌



The piece of the Falcon 9 upper stage was about the size of a five-storey building and had an Earth weight of around 4,000kg.

‌



Scientists say the rocket will now have crashed into the Moon. The crash will be confirmed by telescopes in the Americas monitoring the event soon.

‌



The now-abandoned spacecraft formed part of a US-Japanese mission launched by SpaceX in January 2025 which took two lunar landers to the Moon.

The dust and debris from the impact is expected to rise several miles above the Moon's surface and should be visible through telescopes from Earth.

View 3 Images A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket, like the one that crashed today (file) (Image: AP)

‌



SpaceX rocket on collision course with Moon - how you could watch it from Earth READ MORE :

Musk loses trillionaire status as SpaceX shares come plummeting back down to Earth READ MORE :

Astronomer Bill Gray said of the collision: "Maybe we'll see the flash. Maybe we'll see rocks ejected from the crater. Maybe we'll even see both."

Observers in the eastern US and Canada, along with much of South America, are expected to have the best chance of spotting the impact flash of the crash itself.

This will be the second space ship to crash into the Moon - in 2022 a Chinese rocket segment dug out two craters on the Moon's far side.

‌



Los Alamos National Laboratory’s Benjamin Fernando told reporters: “Part of the reason for our interest in this event is to figure out how much of a hazard debris impacts pose to future astronauts."

View 3 Images SpaceX is owned by Elon Musk (file) (Image: Getty Images)

Fernando expects the impact to create a crater about 90ft across and 16ft deep - too small to be seen from Earth but visible to spacecraft.

‌



Retired astrophysicist Jonathan McDowell said "this impact will not be a problem", but warned that similar impacts "would be an issue", particularly "in a future where there are long-term bases on the Moon".

"We need not to leave rocket stages in chaotic orbits of this kind," he added.

The moment of impact was not captured by any of the spacecraft orbiting the moon, so scientists will now be analysing before and after snaps of the surface searching for the new crater left by the impact.

Article continues below

Analysis of images may take a few days, researchers have said.

News.title: 'I had headaches on Turkey holiday and now have months to live'
News.content:
'I had headaches on Turkey holiday and now have months to live'

Everything changed in an instant just as things were falling into place

View 3 Images Kris Bennett recovering in hospital after undergoing eight hours of awake brain surgery (Image: Cover Images)

A young family is desperately trying to squeeze “20 years of life” into a few months.

‌



Every walk, every family day out and every bedtime story has taken on a new meaning for Kris Bennett and his partner Hollie Boswell. Just a year ago, the Gravesend couple believed life was finally falling into place.

‌



Kris, 38, had recently started his own painting and decorating business, bought a work van and was looking forward to raising their growing family when everything changed. The nightmare began during a three-week family holiday in Turkey last July when he developed persistent headaches.

‌



At first he blamed stress and then an ear infection picked up while swimming with his children. After returning home, doctors initially suspected cluster headaches and arranged further tests. But days later, while celebrating Hollie’s birthday at a spa, he suddenly lost his speech.

“I came out of the water and tried to speak to Hollie, but all my speech was slurred,” Kris recalled. “I laughed it off the first time, but then it happened again.”

View 3 Images Kris Bennett first became sick during a family holiday to Turkey last year (Image: Cover Images)

‌



A scan at hospital revealed a tumour measuring about 5cm on the left side of his brain. He was transferred to King’s College Hospital, London, where he underwent further tests before having an eight-hour awake craniotomy on September 3.

Throughout the operation, surgeons asked him to complete memory, language and recognition tests while removing as much of the tumour as possible. They had hoped to remove around 70%, but successfully took out 85%.

The remaining tumour, however, was embedded in healthy brain tissue and could not be safely removed. Days later, following the biopsy results, the family received the devastating news that the tumour was a grade 4 brain cancer with a life expectancy of just 12 to 18 months.

‌



“It was the biggest shock of my life,” Kris said. “I was told it was incurable and that I had 12 to 18 months to live.”

Despite the devastating diagnosis, another life-changing moment was just around the corner. As doctors discussed preserving Kris’s fertility before chemotherapy and radiotherapy, believing treatment could affect their chances of having more children, the couple thought their plans for a bigger family were over.

“I like to tell this story,” Kris added. “We did not realise Hollie was already pregnant.

‌



“While we were making all these decisions, Sienna was already being made. She’s the biggest blessing ever. She’s got my blue eyes, fair hair like mine and she’s the spitting image of me.”

The couple are also raising their boys Toby, six, and Riley, two. Kris is currently undergoing chemotherapy, which is expected to continue until December. Only then will doctors know whether he could be eligible for further surgery, clinical trials or other treatments.

“My head doesn’t allow me to stop fighting,” he said. “We’ve heard stories about people with the same tumour living much longer than expected. As long as there are options, we’ll keep looking.”

‌



The diagnosis has transformed every aspect of the family’s lives. Kris was forced to close the decorating business he had worked so hard to build, sell his work van and surrender his driving licence because of the risk of seizures. He now depends on Hollie for almost everything.

“My life disappeared overnight,” he said. “I lost my work, my independence and a huge part of my identity.

“The hardest thing is thinking about leaving my family. Every time I think about my children, I struggle to breathe.”

‌



View 3 Images Hollie Boswell and Kris Bennett, pictured with Riley and Toby, were enjoying a family holiday when Kris started to fall ill (Image: Cover Images)

Hollie is currently on maternity leave after welcoming Sienna in May. Before giving birth, she had already cut back her working hours to care for Kris and accompany him to hospital appointments.

After losing his income, the family say even everyday expenses have become a struggle while raising three young children. Wanting to help, family friend Jerry Mackenzie launched a GoFundMe appeal after seeing how dramatically their lives had changed.

‌



In the appeal, he described Kris as “the most devoted partner”, “an amazing dad” and someone who had always been the first to help others without expecting anything in return. The fundraiser aims to ease the financial pressures caused by Kris’s illness, including travel to hospital appointments, everyday living costs and, in the future, funeral expenses.

Most importantly, it is helping the couple fulfil one of their biggest wishes by allowing them to plan the wedding they had always dreamed of while creating precious memories with their children. The appeal has also inspired strangers to offer their support.

One holiday park owner has offered the family the use of a caravan free of charge, giving them the chance to enjoy time away together without worrying about the cost. A charity football tournament is also being organised to raise money for the family.

‌



Kick for Kris, hosted by Meopham Colts FC, where six-year-old Toby plays, will take place at Judson’s Recreational Ground, Wrotham Road, Meopham, on Sunday, August 30, from 9am to 1pm. The event will feature under-sevens and under-eights teams, with all proceeds going towards supporting the Bennett family.

Anyone wishing to support Kris, Hollie, Toby, Riley and Sienna can also donate through the family’s GoFundMe page. For now, the family’s focus remains not on counting the months, but on making every single day matter.

“We’re making memories,” Hollie said. “That's all we want to do.”

Article continues below

Kris added: “There are birthdays to celebrate, a wedding to plan, holidays to enjoy and three young children to love. We’re trying to fit 20 years of life into such a short amount of time.”

News.title: Tesco customers have 11 days' to secure '£60 rule' fuel deal
News.content:
Tesco customers have 11 days' to secure '£60 rule' fuel deal

The supermarket giant operates around 600 fuel stations around the UK as prices hit highest levels since Iran war started

View Image Tesco shoppers can get 5% off their fuel when they spend £60 or more in store. (Image: Getty)

Tesco customers are being given a bit of relief from high fuel prices - but they only have until August 23 to take advantage. The supermarket giant operates around 600 fuel stations around the UK - and has said it is currently offering customers a 5p off a litre.

‌



Petrol prices have reached their highest level since 2022 as Brits feel the heat at the pumps. Fuel prices in the UK have reached 159.89p on average, new figures show. It’s the highest level since November 2022 when prices were cooling from a high of 191.55p in 2022 due to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

‌



Donald Trump earlier this week promised that new talks on ending the conflict with Iran would begin on Monday, after the US president called off what he said would have been “massive” strikes on the country. But Iran has denied any new talks are taking place and the situation looks set to continue.

‌



Tesco shoppers can get 5% off their fuel when they spend £60 or more in store. Customers will receive a coupon that can be used to save on diesel and petrol when they fill up at a Tesco forecourt

The deal is running until Sunday August 16 and the coupon can be redeemed until Sunday 23 August 23.

‌



The maximum saving that can be made with the voucher is £10 and it must be presented in paper form when paying for fuel.

The news comes as this week it was revealed that drivers have stolen an average of nearly £200,000 worth of fuel from UK forecourts every day since the start of the Iran oil crisis, according to analysis. Fuel theft prevention company Forecourt Eye said incidents of fuel taken without payment soared by 20% in the five months after the conflict began on February 28, compared with the preceding five months.

The increase in pump prices driven by the war means the value of stolen fuel rose by 48% over the same period, reaching an estimated daily average of £194,000 across the UK’s 8,359 forecourts. For first-time offenders, there was a 23% increase in the number of incidents and a 26% rise in the volume of fuel stolen, compared with 17% and 20% respectively among repeat offenders.

Article continues below

The figures are based on reports by a representative sample of 550 forecourts. They include drive-offs, when there is no attempt to pay, and no means of payment incidents, when a customer fills up and claims they have no way to pay.

The average price of a litre of petrol climbed to 160p on Friday. That was about 27p more than before the conflict, and represented a three-and-a-half year high.

The average price of diesel is about 37p per litre higher than prior to the war, at 179p.

News.title: Dewormer and scabies drugs being sold as cancer treatments, BBC investigation finds
News.content:
Animal dewormer and a drug used to treat scabies are being sold and promoted as unproven cancer treatments, a BBC investigation has found.

Following a tip off, an undercover journalist was able to buy fenbendazole and ivermectin from a stairlift salesman in south Wales, and also found them for sale on Amazon.

Macmillan Cancer Support said it was concerned by the findings and that a growing number of people were asking about the medicines, despite "no clinical evidence" that they work.

Amazon removed the products after we contacted them, and said it had "proactive measures in place" to stop prohibited products being listed by third-party sellers.

Senior doctors are worried vulnerable patients could be put at risk by taking the medicines, as they say it could harm or delay conventional treatment.

Six months ago, Rebecca Holder contacted the BBC after a visit from stairlift salesman Jason Sarver.

She said Sarver and her father Bob, who had a brain tumour, lung cancer and needed help with his mobility, had been discussing stairlifts when the salesman changed the topic to talk about the drugs.

News.title: Temperatures to drop briefly ahead of potential new UK heatwave
News.content:
Temperatures are set to drop across the UK over the next few days, ending the latest heatwave that has affected some areas of southern and eastern England.

Humidity levels will fall too, which should cool down homes and make nights more comfortable for sleeping.

The change in conditions follows another historic day in a summer that has seen many long standing heat records toppled or tied. On Tuesday, the UK registered its 34th day of temperatures reaching 30C (86F) or higher in a calendar year, equalling the record set in 1995.

Forecasts suggest that this record is likely to be beaten as early as next week, with some showing the potential for a sixth heatwave to develop.

News.title: Burnham 'looking into' conducting Epstein inquiry, says victims minister
News.content:
Andy Burnham is "looking into" the possibility of holding a public inquiry into the UK activities of the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, according to victims minister Alex Davies-Jones.

Speaking to BBC Newsnight, Davies-Jones said that the prime minister had agreed to meet Epstein's victims.

She said the government is also reviewing whether the alleged actions of former Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed could also be part of an inquiry.

Davies-Jones resigned from former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's government in May, later accusing his government of failing to listen to Epstein's survivors. She was reappointed as victims minister when Burnham took office.

Speaking on the programme, she said she had discussed holding a public inquiry into the alleged behaviour of Epstein and Al Fayed with the prime minister and cabinet secretary Dame Antonia Romeo during her re-appointment.

Asked whether an inquiry was now possible, Davies-Jones said: "We are looking at this, we are reviewing what is possible. Again, same with Harrods survivors."

She added: "I have been assured that the prime minister is taking this very seriously.

"He will meet with those victims and he is looking at what is possible, now he has access to all of the information as prime minister to see what action we can take."

After resigning in May, Davies-Jones told the Commons in June that people whose lives were devastated by Epstein's abuse have too often been reduced to a footnote.

Asked what assurances or guarantees she had asked from Burnham in relation to the survivors when he re-appointed her to government, the minister said: "I did have those discussions with the prime minister before he became the prime minister."

"He agreed to meet with the Epstein victims," she continued, adding that Burnham "has assured me that he will meet them now he's prime minister and will work with us to look at systemic change across the system for all victims."

BBC Newsnight understands that as Burnham was finalising plans to become prime minister, he was sent a document by leading Labour campaigners on Violence Against Women and Girls.

It contained a key suggestion: to hold a full public inquiry into the UK activities of Epstein, the alleged behaviour of the late Harrods boss Mohamed Al Fayed and into allegations in a BBC Panorama and Times investigation that West Ham co-owner David Sullivan preyed on women.

David Sullivan has described the claims as false. He said he was "absolutely not the person the media has decided to paint me as".

The document called for an "impunity" inquiry to ask how powerful men were able to carry out the alleged behaviour.

On Epstein, the document calls for a focus on UK borders, asking how he was able to fly in and out of UK military bases on his private jet, often with allegedly trafficked women. Former Prime Minister Gordon Brown highlighted this issue in February.

Davies-Jones is understood to be familiar with the Labour document.

Anouska di Georgiou, an Epstein survivor, told BBC Newsnight: "I welcome reports that Prime Minister Andy Burnham is considering public inquiries into the Epstein and Maxwell, Harrods/Mohamed Al-Fayed, and David Sullivan cases."

"Survivors have heard promises before, so what matters now is action, not headlines."

News.title: Couple woke to find shirtless intruder in Travelodge room
News.content:
A couple woke to find a shirtless man in their hotel bedroom after he was mistakenly given a key card to their door, BBC Scotland News has learned.

Kim Hutchison, 60, and Harry Grieve, 57, from Buckie, Moray, were staying in a Travelodge in Dundee when the early morning incident happened last month.

Hutchison said she was "petrified" before the man - wearing just shorts - left after about a minute of arguing over who was actually in the wrong room.

Travelodge apologised to the couple and said room access security policies were not correctly followed. It is the latest in a series of similar incidents at Travelodge hotels reported to the BBC.

Earlier this year, a man was jailed for sexually assaulting a woman in her hotel bed after Travelodge staff gave him a key card and her room number.

Kyran Smith had gone to the reception of the Maidenhead branch of the hotel chain in the early hours in December 2022 and said he was the woman's boyfriend.

Travelodge later said it was investigating more reports of strangers accessing rooms - after two women told the BBC that people they did not know came into their rooms while they were alone.

News.title: Tories offer Jewish groups meeting with ex neo-Nazi activist candidate
News.content:
The Conservatives have offered Jewish groups a meeting with their council election candidate, Joshua Bonehill-Paine, who spent time in prison for neo-Nazi activism.

The party has been criticised over the decision to select him to stand for a seat on Somerset Council next year, but Kemi Badenoch has said she is standing by Bonehill-Paine because she wants to give him a second chance.

He has described his past views as "indefensible" and now speaks out against extremism.

The Board of Deputies of British Jews has called on the Conservatives to ditch him as a candidate, saying the selection "beggars belief".

It is understood the party has now offered the Board, as well as the Jewish Leadership Council and the Chief Rabbi Sir Ephraim Mirvis, a meeting with Bonehill-Paine so they can discuss their concerns directly.

When Bonehill-Paine's selection was announced, Karen Newman, vice president of the Board of Deputies of British Jews - the largest body representing Jews in the UK - said that the board had contacted the Conservatives to "set out our concerns and call on them to rescind his selection and review their vetting processes."

Bonehill-Paine spent three years in prison for posting antisemitic material ahead of a planned neo-Nazi rally. A year later he was convicted of racially harassing then-Labour MP Luciana Berger. Berger is now a member of the House of Lords.

Berger, reacting to the news of his selection on X, said he had, "published *reams* of deeply racist, misogynistic and pornographic material about me."

In an interview with the Today programme, she told the BBC: "I still live today with the profound and deep impacts of those events".

She suggested his "sustained campaign" against her should rule him out of the candidacy for a council seat.

"I think that we need to have a bar when it comes to standing for public office," she explained.

"I strongly believe that this individual today falls very, very short of that."

Bonehill-Paine also holds previous convictions for assaulting a police officer, burglary of a police station and malicious communications.

On Tuesday he was selected to stand as the Tory candidate in the new Somerset Council seat of Crewkerne South in 2027. He said he wanted to "give back" to a community which had supported him.

Bonehill-Paine said he reformed his previous views when he learned of the murder of MP Jo Cox, and subsequently undertook a de-radicalisation programme. He now delivers counter-extremism sessions around the UK.

He said: "When I was first released from prison in 2018, I was supported by many of the people in my local community who understood that I had made some awful mistakes but was wanting to change my life around."

Speaking on Tuesday, Tory leader Badenoch said Bonehill-Paine "is spending every day working to solve the very problem which he knew he had caused previously.

"He's going up and down the country training people and the Conservative Party believes in second chances.

"This is not just someone that we've picked up who is a convicted criminal - this is somebody who is actively working to help communities, especially Jewish communities."

The decision to field Bonehill-Paine as a candidate has also been criticised by other political parties.

Liberal Democrat MP Adam Dance, whose Yeovil constituency includes Crewkerne, said the Conservative Party needed to explain "why it believes this candidate is fit to serve", while a Labour Party spokesperson said his selection was "a total disgrace".

News.title: The city closing down streets so children can play
News.content:
Seven-year-old Aydin is relishing the chance to play somewhere new. It's Colenso Mount, a street in the Holbeck area of Leeds where he lives, which has been temporarily closed to traffic to become a âPlay Streetâ.

"Everyone can ride scooters and the boys over there play football which is very fun", he says excitedly.

As Aydin jumps a scooter over ramps set up in the middle of the road, children around him are drawing with chalk, blowing bubbles and kicking a football in a spot where cars are usually driving through.

Itâs a rare chance for the kids in this neighbourhood to play outside together, in a space big enough to frolic and safe from traffic.

According to a survey from the campaign group Play Their Way, external, out on Wednesday, nearly half of parents (46%) say their child doesn't have a safe place to play outdoors.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham is being urged to bring back a national play strategy, external for children in England - an initiative he championed while culture secretary in 2008.

News.title: How an avalanche killed a climbing legend - and a generation of record-setting guides
News.content:
Purja, 43, also known as Nims, was the leading figure of the 10-member international team up Broad Peak, the world's 12th highest mountain, when the avalanche struck.

"Nims of course was iconic and undisputedly amongst the best of his generation," says Ben Ayers, a longtime Everest reporter for Outside Magazine.

Kili Pemba Sherpa and Pur Bahadur Gurung, who were also guiding the Broad Peak expedition, were "strong climbers with a solid resume", Ayers said.

Kili Pemba, 46, had just earned the coveted mountaineering Grand Slam after completing his last of the 14 highest peaks, also known as eight-thousanders, in early July.

Even before this crowning achievement, he was already among the best in the industry having been part of the Nepali team, led again by Purja, that completed the first winter ascent of K2 in January 2021.

At the time, K2, the world's second highest peak, was the only one of the eight-thousanders not yet climbed in winter. But at 8,611m, K2 is known to be steeper, more unpredictable and deadlier than Everest (8,849m).

Many have described Kili Pemba as humble and deeply committed in serving his clients. He'd led two double-leg amputees, on separate occasions, to the summits of Everest and Manaslu, the eighth-highest mountain.

"That was the toughest task for any guide, [Kili Pemba] did that with a lot of care," says Gyanendra Shrestha, a government official who was at Everest Base Camp during one of these climbs.

News.title: Antisemitic incident reports rise by a fifth in first half of 2026
News.content:
The number of antisemitic incidents recorded across the UK since the start of the year is up by a fifth compared to last year, figures show.

The Community Security Trust (CST), an organisation that provides security support to the Jewish community, recorded 1,926 incidents of anti-Jewish hate across the UK in the first six months of 2026.

It represents a 21% increase on the number of similar incidents reported in the first half of last year.

It also marks the second highest total of antisemitic hate incidents ever recorded by CST in the first half of any year since the organisation began collecting data in 1984.

Policing Minister Sarah Jones said the numbers were "appalling" and showed people "living in fear just for being who they are".

The incidents logged in the first few months of 2026 include a series of arson attacks against Jewish organisations and synagogues in London.

Four volunteer ambulances were set alight in Golders Green in March. The following month two visibly Jewish men were stabbed nearby, in an attack which was treated as an act of terrorism.

The CST said it recorded noticeable surges in antisemitic incidents following these events, with the highest daily total following the double stabbing on 29 April.

Hatred continues to be directed at British Jews at a higher level than before 7 October 2023, when Hamas attacked Israel and the war in Gaza began.

The ongoing conflict in the Middle East is one of the factors behind the rise in antisemitism. Some 41% of the incidents recorded by the CST used anti-Jewish language or motive at the same time as making reference to either the conflict, Israel, Palestine, or Hamas.

CST chief executive Mark Gardner said: "These attacks are directed against British Jews but they are also attacks on Britain and our society."

He said they "should concern everyone who cares about Britain and the threats against it, whether state-directed from Iran, or internally driven by Islamist, far-right, far-left, or other ideological extremes."

Separate data released last week revealed that antisemitism is at heightened levels globally.

A report by the J7 Large Communities' Task Force Against Antisemitism found that the UK recorded the biggest rise in antisemitic incidents last year of any country with a major Jewish population outside Israel.

It also found that 2025 was the deadliest year for Jews in the diaspora in more than three decades.

The government's independent adviser on antisemitism, Lord John Mann, said these new CST figures, "demonstrate that anti-Jewish racism in the UK remains at all all-time high and continues to pose a significant threat to our democracy".

He added that he is especially concerned "to see the nature of antisemitism in the UK becoming increasingly violent".

The CST also analyses the types of incidents which occur across different sectors. It found that in the first half of 2026, antisemitism in schools reached the highest level ever recorded for the first six months of any year. It jumped by 59%, from 112 reported incidents in the first half of 2025, to 178 recorded over the same period in 2026.

A government-commissioned independent review into antisemitism in schools and colleges is currently being carried out by Sir David Bell. It is expected to report in the autumn.

News.title: New guidance on single-sex spaces comes into force
News.content:
Single-sex spaces open to the public, such as toilets and changing rooms, should be organised based on biological sex, according to official guidance that has come into force.

The code, published by Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC), says trans people should use either gender-neutral facilities or the ones that match their biological sex, in places such as gym changing rooms or rape crisis centres.

The guidance was published in June but is now in place in England, Wales and Scotland - despite opposition among some MPs.

It comes 16 months after the UK Supreme Court ruled "sex" in equality law means "biological sex" rather than the gender someone identifies as.

Trans-rights campaigners have called the guidance unworkable, but groups that campaign for sex-based rights welcome the clarity it brings.

The guidance from the EHRC, the equality watchdog for England, Scotland and Wales, provides practical advice for services, public bodies and associations on how they should interpret the 2010 Equality Act

It applies to organisations as diverse as cafes, leisure centres, public toilets, domestic violence shelters, bowls clubs and many more.

The code says where it is proportionate for facilities, such as public toilets and changing rooms, or services like a rape crisis centre, to be single sex then only those of the same biological sex should use them.

This means, for instance, a trans woman, a person born a biological male who identifies as a woman, should not use women-only facilities. And a trans man should not use men only facilities.

But the code also says it could amount to discrimination against a transgender person if they were forced to use services related to their biological sex. It says gender-neutral spaces are an alternative.

The Equality Act provides protections for people on the grounds of both biological sex and gender reassignment.

Transgender people argue they should be able to use services that align with the way they identify and live their life, rather than their biological sex.

In response, campaigners including some women's and gay rights groups say this undermines sex-based protections, particularly for women.

It is the tension between these two sets of rights that led to both the Supreme Court ruling in April 2025 and the publication of this updated guidance.

It suggests legal action on how the code is put into practice is likely. Both from trans-rights groups who think the guidance itself is wrong and from sex-based rights groups who will want to challenge any organisations who they believe are not following the code.

News.title: Fires started 'deliberately' on mountain as crews tackle blaze
News.content:
Fires are believed to have been deliberately started on a mountain where crews have been tackling a blaze since the weekend.

The fire at Llanwonno, near Ferndale in the Rhondda Valley, began on Saturday afternoon with emergency services remaining at the scene.

It remains a major incident due to the scale of the fire and "challenging conditions" on the mountain, including low cloud, mist and rain.

South Wales Fire and Rescue Service (SWFRS) said there were reports of "deliberate fire setting" on the mountain overnight on Monday, while firefighters continued working to contain the blaze.

Locals have not been forced to evacuate, but a rest centre has been set up for people who do not wish to stay at home because of poor air quality.

A spokesperson for SWFRS said it continued to work with partner agencies to contain and extinguish the wildfire on Llanwonno mountain and prevent further spread, helping to protect nearby properties and communities.

"There were reports of deliberate fire setting on the mountain [on Monday night]," they said.

"Firefighters worked throughout the night in challenging conditions to tackle the fire and protect properties."

News.title: Major search for boy, 13, missing at sea
News.content:
A major search continued into the night for a 13-year-old boy who reportedly got into difficulty while swimming off the East Yorkshire coast, police have said.

Emergency services were called to Hornsea at about 18:00 BST on Tuesday.

Crews, including Hornsea Inshore Rescue, HM Coastguard and Humberside Police, attended the scene. The RNLI said its Bridlington all-weather lifeboat joined the search.

Ch Supt Phil Booker said: "Our priority now is to find the boy, and members of the public can expect to see specialist Police Search Advisors, along with our Marine Unit and drone pilots, who have also been deployed to conduct an extensive search and rescue operation to locate him."

News.title: AI used new levels of 'autonomy and deception' to trick people in safety test
News.content:
The latest artificial intelligence (AI) tools from Anthropic and OpenAI went to new extremes in trying to undermine a popular platform during testing by the UK's AI Security Institute.

The AISI said on Tuesday that Anthropic's Mythos and OpenAI's Sol models engaged in a level of "autonomy and deception" it had not seen before.

During routine AI safety testing, an Anthropic agent created fake profiles of real people as it tried to trick a person standing between it and access to GitHub, a large platform where technology developers store software code.

Anthropic and OpenAI noted in response to AISI's report that its test had reduced or removed normal safeguards.

AISI evaluators first noticed "unusual data transfers leaving our research systems" during a test, then found that "some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations".

It turned out that a Mythos agent had created "malicious code" and attempted to insert it into GitHub's system.

The Mythos agent identified and researched the people who maintained GitHub and created a series of "fake online identities" based on those real people. It did so as part of an effort to pressure and trick the real people into approving its malicious code.

The agent even sent people direct messages masquerading as the real people it had researched.

"When the agent's pull request was challenged in public, it edited its earlier activity to appear harmless and considered adopting a fresh identity to continue," AISI said.

Throughout the attempts, it was human review that stopped the agent from succeeding in delivering the malicious code to GitHub.

While AISI said the Mythos agent had not been instructed specifically to avoid or carry out such behaviour, it was "the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world".

The rival AI companies, which are poised to be listed on the public stock market, have in recent weeks said their tools were responsible for several cyber-hacking incidents.

Anthropic wrote in a public statement that the AISI testing parameters were "not representative of any of our production models".

It added that the company is conducting its own investigation into the incident in order to "identify the causes of its behavior".

A spokesperson for OpenAI said the AISI testing conditions "do not reflect ordinary use" and that the company would "continue working with evaluators and other stakeholders across the industry to strengthen shared practices for conducting evaluations safely as models become more capable".

AISI said on Tuesday that its testing of AI models with such safeguards turned off is routine, as is giving such tools access to the open internet.

It added that the model behaviour at issue amounted to "a small number of events under very specific conditions".

Nonetheless, it said the way Mythos and Sol acted in response to a straightforward task went outside of what the AI tools were prompted to do.

"The activity undertaken by the agent showed signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate", AISI said.

Most of the malicious agent actions AISI reported were done by Anthropic's Mythos. OpenAI's Sol was only blamed for two of the noted actions.

The core issue occurred last week, as part of a test in which evaluators with AISI asked each of the models to "solve a cybersecurity challenge" that involved GitHub, the software code repository, which is owned by Microsoft.

GitHub was notified by AISI of the attempted breach of its system. Microsoft has been contacted by the BBC for comment.

News.title: Princess Eugenie gives birth to baby girl in Portugal
News.content:
Princess Eugenie has given birth to a baby girl at a hospital in Lisbon, Portugal.

The baby was born on Monday at 18:20 BST, weighing 6lbs 9oz.

This is Princess Eugenie's third child with her husband, Jack Brooksbank, following the births of her sons August Philip Hawke Brooksbank, who was born in 2021, and Ernest George Ronnie Brooksbank, who was born in 2023.

A statement from Buckingham Palace read: "Their Majesties The King and Queen and other members of The Royal Family were delighted to be informed of the news."

In a post on Instagram, the princess, 36, wrote: "Jack and I are so excited to announce Baby Girl Brooksbank!!

"We are beyond in love with our girlie."

They are yet to announce a name.

The new arrival - who will not be an HRH - will be 15th in line to the throne, moving ahead of their great-uncle the Duke of Edinburgh, Prince Edward.

The couple live between Portugal and Ivy Cottage, in the grounds of Kensington Palace.

They announced Princess Eugenie's pregnancy in May. She posted a photograph of her young sons holding a baby scan with the caption: "Baby Brooksbank due 2026!"

The Palace said on social media at the time: "His Majesty The King has been informed and is delighted with the news."

News.title: More than 170 migrants rescued after boat catches fire in Channel
News.content:
More than 170 migrants have been rescued after the boat they were using to cross the Channel caught fire on Tuesday morning, as the UK government said "all will be returned" to France.

The boat was attempting to cross to the UK when its engine caught fire, according to the French maritime prefecture of the Channel and North Sea.

It had originally reported 157 migrants were rescued, but has since revised that figure up to 173. All have been taken to Boulogne-sur-Mer in France, with 11 people suffering from minor injuries.

French prosecutors have opened an investigation, and an Egyptian national has been taken into policy custody in connection with the incident.

Border Security Minister Anna Turley said the incident "shows the dangers of these illegal crossings and the ruthless gangs behind them".

"That's why we are bearing down on them," she said.

French authorities said the boat left France on Monday night.

Overnight "five people on board the vessel required rescue... the remaining people on board refused the assistance offered by the French patrol boats", the French maritime prefecture said.

"Determined to reach the United Kingdom, migrants crossing the Channel in small boats refused assistance offered by French emergency service, accepting it only in situations of extreme emergency," it said in a statement.

Because of the "structural fragility" of boats used to cross the Channel, it said they decided not to intervene further at that stage.

But this morning the engine caught fire and the "vessel's integrity deteriorated very rapidly".

Rescue boats went to the scene from France and the UK, including the RNLI Eastbourne lifeboat and the UK Border Force vessels BSC Contender and BSC Courageous.

The French maritime prefecture said the operation involved 40 firefighters, 13 police officers, seven interpreters, and a number of medical personnel.

It had previously reported that 157 migrants were rescued, but on Tuesday afternoon revised that figure up to 173.

On top of the initial five rescued, two French boats rescued 105 migrants and the British boats rescued 63. All of them were taken to Boulogne-sur-Mer for treatment.

The total number on the boat broke the previous record of 165 people, who reached the UK late last month in a 42ft (13m) boat, making it the largest single vessel to attempt to cross the Channel carrying migrants.

News.title: Former RAF medic can clear debts after choosing £300k over Lamborghini
News.content:
A former RAF medic can pay off his mortgage and clear his debts after winning Â£300,000 in a competition he entered for Â£4.28.

Ryan Briggs, 46, from Haverfordwest in Pembrokeshire, spent 23 years in the Royal Air Force, completing tours of Iraq and Afghanistan, before joining the NHS as a paramedic during the Covid-19 pandemic.

He was given the choice of a 2026 Lamborghini Temerario - worth an estimated Â£270,000 - or Â£300,000 in cash, after winning a competition organised by Elite Competitions, and chose the cash.

"I can now reduce my hours [at work] in the future if I wanted to. I'm fit and healthy now, but that can change. It takes a lot of pressure off," he said.

Ryan met his wife Kelly, a logistics mover, when they were both in the RAF, aged 19.

She left shortly after, and was planning to move back to northern Scotland - but instead the pair conducted a "shotgun wedding".

"It worked for us, because we are still happily married 27 years later," said Ryan, a father-of-two.

He said he had grown up with a "fascination" with planes after his father had taken him to air shows at RAF St Athan, Vale of Glamorgan, inspiring him to join the RAF.

News.title: Boy, 14, dies after going into water at dock
News.content:
A 14-year-old boy has drowned after going into the water at a dock in east London.

The London Fire Brigade (LFB) and the Metropolitan Police searched the Millwall Outer Dock near East Ferry Road after being alerted at about 18:50 BST on Monday.

His body was recovered at about 22:30 and he was pronounced dead at the scene. His family have been informed, police said.

In a post on social media, Mayor of Tower Hamlets Lutfur Rahman named the teenager as Banta Sillah and said he was "a talented young footballer who played for Frontline Community FC and was instrumental in helping the team win the Tower Hamlets Cup last week".

The Met Police has not confirmed the identity of the boy.

The mayor said Banta "had immense potential and was dearly loved by his peers".

He added: "As we mourn Banta, I urge families to speak with children and young people, we should all be aware of the dangers swimming in open water.

"Swimming should only take place in officially designated areas with lifeguards present."

All of the drive-thru chain Salad and Go’s stores are set to close after the firm filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, citing the recent cyclospora outbreak as a factor in the decision.

Mike Tattersfield, the brand’s CEO, confirmed on Tuesday that all 70 stores located in Arizona and Nevada would serve their final customers on August 5. ​

“This is a painful day for everyone who built, worked for and loved Salad and Go,” said CEO Mike Tattersfield in a news release. “Our mission was brought to life every day by an extraordinary team and embraced by guests who made us part of their routines.”

Tattersfield added, “We are proud of what we built together and grateful to every team member, guest and partner who believed in it.”​

Founded in 2013, the chain had served over 60 million meals across its drive-thru locations. In the company statement, a spokesperson said that the firm had been designed to “make fresh food available to all.”​

open image in gallery Salad and Go is closing all 70 of its stores after filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy ( Salad and Go )

However, Salad and Go was unable to cope with rising costs, growth challenges and pressure on consumer demand. ​

The recent cyclospora outbreak, which has been widely referred to online as the “explosive diarrhea parasite,” also compounded the challenges faced by the chain, the statement says.​

People contract cyclosporiasis after eating food or drinking water contaminated ‌with human feces containing the microscopic parasite Cyclospora. In mid July, Sysco said ithalted sales and distribution of Taylor Farms iceberg lettuce from Mexico. Sysco did a voluntary recall at the time and then Taylor Farms notified the distributor of an ⁠official recall, Hourican said.

open image in gallery The firm says that the recent Cyclospora outbreak, which Salad and Go was not implicated, damaged confidence across the industry ( CDC )

According to Salad and Go, the company was not implicated in the Cyclospora outbreak in July, but the spread of the so-called “explosive diarrhea parasite” still shook confidence across the industry. ​

The previous owners of Salad and Go, who now operate another restaurant chain named Angie’s, described the news of the closure as “bittersweet.”

​“We dreamed that anywhere there was a McDonald's, there would also be a better and healthier alternative that people could afford,” the statement, uploaded to Instagram, read. “Although we exited in 2021, watching the company announce the closing of its remaining locations is heartbreaking.”​

The former owners added, “To everyone who was ever a part of the Salad and Go journey with us, we thank you.”

Meanwhile, Sysco, the biggest U.S. food distributor, has stopped buying iceberg lettuce from Mexico due to the U.S. cyclosporiasis outbreak, CEO Kevin ⁠Hourican said on Tuesday.

The move shows how the largest U.S. outbreak of cyclosporiasis on record has forced adjustments to the food supply chain as cases of the disease continue to mount. An investigation by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has linked the outbreak to iceberg lettuce served at Taco Bell restaurants and sourced from privately ⁠held Taylor Farms operations in central Mexico. However, authorities ​are ⁠still looking for other potential sources.

News.title: Man charged in relation to death of 9-year-old girl on family camping trip in Arbroath
News.content:

A 35-year-old man has been charged in relation to the death of a nine-year-old girl in Arbroath, police say.

The man was arrested earlier this week after the girl, who had been camping in the area with her family, was found badly injured at Elliot industrial estate shortly after midnight on Monday.

She was taken to Ninewells Hospital in Dundee, where she died.

The arrested man is white and British, and was known to the victim, Police Scotland said.

He is due to appear at Dundee Sheriff Court on Wednesday.

The girl’s death is being treated as suspicious, police said. She has not yet been publicly named.

The force said that other members of her family, who are from West Yorkshire, had been camping in the area.

open image in gallery Flowers left at the police cordon ( PA )

Officers said that they are not looking for anyone else in connection with the girl’s death.

Detective inspector Mike Ness of Police Scotland’s major investigation team said: “Our thoughts remain with those affected by these events.

“A police presence will remain in the area while our inquiries continue.

“Anyone with any concerns, or information, should approach these officers or contact Police Scotland on 101, quoting incident number 0008 of Monday August 3 2026.”

The girl’s family are being supported by specialist officers, police said.

It is understood that West Yorkshire Police are supporting Police Scotland’s probe.

open image in gallery Police at the Elliot industrial estate in Arbroath ( PA Wire )

At the industrial estate on Monday, a blue forensic tent was set up on a grassy verge outside Halliburton Arbroath manufacturing facility.

The area was taped off, with two police vehicles still at the scene and officers guarding the area.

A bouquet of flowers were placed on the grass near the police cordon.

Lois Speed, who is a councillor for Arbroath East and Lunan, posted on social media, saying the news was “heartbreaking”.

She later told reporters that she wished to “express the shock within the community this morning”.

Ms Speed said: “Really just my thoughts are with the little girl and her family, and those closely affected.

“I don’t have much more that I can add or say, other just than express the shock and sympathies with everyone.”

Astronomers have spotted a first-of-its-kind three-lobed asteroid between Mars and Jupiter, also accompanied by its own small moon, providing a rare glimpse into the variety of space rocks in the Solar System.

Researchers made the discovery thanks to high-resolution imaging from some of the world's most advanced telescopes, including the Large Binocular Telescope (LBT) on Mount Graham in Southeastern Arizona.

The 75km-wide asteroid, named Nysa, belongs to a class of space rocks labelled the E-type, categorised based on its surface composition.

It formed close to the Sun and shares chemical traits with the building blocks of Earth, according to a yet-to-be-peer-reviewed study posted on arXiv.

Scientists hope to further study this space rock as they believe it may shed light on processes that shaped the earliest phases of our solar system’s formation.

open image in gallery Asteroid Nysa and its tiny moon ( University of Arizona )

Nysa was first discovered in 1857 and was named based on the land where nymphs raised Dionysus, a Greek god associated with masks and theatre.

For more than a century, the asteroid has been known for its unusual brightness and composition, making it a compelling target for investigation.

While previous observations hinted it had an elongated or potentially bilobate shape, the asteroid's true form remained elusive.

Now, thanks to LBT, researchers obtained the highest-resolution images ever acquired of Nysa.

"In this paper, we're finally unmasking the asteroid's true nature, long after it was discovered," said Al Conrad, an author of the study from LBT.

Thanks to the telescope and a specially developed image processing technique, scientists could spot multiple large surface features on the asteroid, as well as two prominent valleys that appear to wrap around Nysa's circumference.

Researchers interpret these valleys as neck-like connections between separate lobes, indicating Nysa is a “remarkably unusual object”.

"The most likely explanation is that Nysa is either a contact trinary, consisting of three connected components, or an extremely irregular coherent body unlike anything we've previously observed,” said astronomer and study lead author Kate Minker.

A detailed three-dimensional model of Nysa strongly supports that it has three distinct lobes connected by narrow neck regions.

The findings suggest that the asteroid may have formed via low-velocity accumulation of fragments from an ancient collision, possibly before Nysa reached its current location in the asteroid belt.

open image in gallery Large Binocular Telescope Observatory, or LBTO, located atop Mount Graham in Southeastern Arizona, ( LBTO )

Alternatively, scientists say Nysa may be the remnants of a dramatic hit-and-run collision involving a larger parent body.

“For the first time, we can directly investigate whether those clues point to a deeply indented body or to a true multi-lobed structure,” Dr Conrad said.

"These new images appear consistent with several earlier clues that Nysa is not a conventional asteroid,” he said.

Researchers also found a previously unknown moon, temporarily designated S/2026, that is circling Nysa.

This moon measures just over one kilometre in diameter and orbits at least 170 kilometres from the asteroid.

Scientists hope future observations of Nysa could help determine its mass and density more precisely.

Once confirmed, Nysa would join a growing class of solar system objects whose distinctive shapes preserve evidence of ancient collisions and mergers dating back billions of years.
