World.title: ConCourt faces crucial test in Parliament-Ramaphosa showdown, says analyst
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The limits of South Africa’s judiciary are set to face a significant test as Parliament’s impeachment committee prepares to take its battle to the Constitutional Court.

That’s the view of legal analyst Jazz Vilakazi on the showdown between Parliament, President Cyril Ramaphosa and the courts.

The latest development follows a ruling by the Western Cape High Court last month, which granted President Ramaphosa an interdict, effectively halting the work of Parliament’s impeachment committee until a judicial review of the Phala Phala report has been completed.

Vilakazi believes the appeal will be a defining moment for the country’s constitutional democracy, particularly in determining how far the judiciary can intervene in the affairs of the other branches of government.

READ | Impeachment process heads to ConCourt

"This appeal will definitely test the limits of judicial reach into the other spheres of government," he says.

Vilakazi says that the Constitutional Court has previously directed Parliament to amend its impeachment rules, a decision that now lies at the centre of the current proceedings.

He explained that the court had already recognised Ramaphosa's right to seek a judicial review, making the upcoming appeal especially significant.

According to Vilakazi, it would be difficult for the Constitutional Court to side with Parliament without contradicting its earlier judgment.

"It would be quite a querysome issue for the Constitutional Court to side with Parliament considering that they themselves said the president does have a right to review the application,"

He added:

"Of course, if it sides with Ramaphosa, what it is really saying is, 'there is a review hearing taking place in September, let's wait for that and take it from there'."

World.title: Senzo Meyiwa murder trial: Alleged hitman returns to witness stand
World.content:
PRETORIA - Alleged hitman Mthobisi Mncube is expected to continue his testimony in the Senzo Meyiwa murder trial.

The state alleges that Mncube is the dreadlocked gunman who killed the Bafana Bafana captain.

Prosecutors argue that he is the intruder who burst into the Khumalo residence in Vosloorus, and shot Meyiwa.

But Mncube disputes this version. He says he was sound asleep on the night Meyiwa was killed.

World.title: Paramount CEO says politics fueling Warner Bros. merger battle
World.content:
LOS ANGELES - Paramount CEO David Ellison said that the legal battle over his proposed multibillion-dollar takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery was fueled by politics rather than concerns over market share.

His remarks in an opinion piece published in The New York Times came as a federal judge set a March 2027 trial date for the antitrust challenges to the megamerger.

Ellison's Paramount Skydance agreed late last month to delay its $110-billion merger with Warner Bros. to June 2027 while the US lawsuit seeking to block the deal moves forward.

If the merger eventually closes, the new combined company would reshape the entertainment and media industry, in addition to delivering a major win to its owners, the Ellison family, who are close allies of US President Donald Trump.

If the deal doesn't close, the Ellison family could be on the hook for billions in kill fees.

In a combative op-ed, Ellison argued that the fight over the deal "is not really about market share."

"The issue is whether I can be trusted as a steward of Warner's CNN. There has been speculation about my politics, my loyalties, my intentions," he wrote.

In their complaint against the deal, 12 Democratic-led US states claim the combined company would control roughly 27 percent of wide-release theatrical film distribution and a similar percentage of basic cable channel licensing.

"We are eager to continue to make our case in court... to ensure this unlawful merger never sees the light of day," California Attorney General Rob Bonta said in a statement last month.

The deal would include CNN, one of the largest US cable news networks and a frequent target of Trump's insults and attacks over coverage critical of his administration.

On June 12 the Trump administration approved the blockbuster deal without demanding a single change, clearing the way for one of the largest media mergers in years.

Ellison argued that he held views across the political spectrum, "just like most Americans."

"When it comes to our news operations, I do not aspire to lead these companies to bend their newsrooms to my views," he said. "I believe that news should be based on facts and truth."

Ellison's Skydance acquired CBS News in mid-2025, with the major US broadcaster reaching a $16-million settlement with Trump over coverage of presidential candidate Kamala Harris in the same period.

Shortly after CBS became a part of Paramount Skydance, the company brought in Bari Weiss -- a longstanding critic of progressive politics -- to lead its news division.

Many CBS News journalists quit following Weiss's appointment, alleging curbs on their editorial independence.

David Ellison is the son of Oracle founder Larry Ellison, who Forbes says has a net worth of more than $185-billion, making him the seventh richest person in the world.

World.title: Colombian ex-guerrillas fear for future under hardline president
World.content:
BOGOTA - Lovers and ex-guerrillas Derlis Aizama and Daniel Paredes recently laid down arms to start a family, but Colombia's incoming hard-right administration might upend their improbable attempt at civilian life.

The couple formed part of a 99-strong group of guerrillas who struck a deal with outgoing President Gustavo Petro to disband two months ago.

With US-backed president-elect Abelardo de la Espriella replacing Petro on Friday, however, the agreement's future hangs in the balance.

De la Espriella has pledged to renounce the outgoing administration's policy of negotiating with armed groups in the South American nation, pledging to wage war on them instead.

Aizama, who spoke to AFP from a special zone for ex-guerrillas in the southern Putumayo region, said she felt unsafe.

"We are here because we want to rebuild our lives, to create a home," she said.

- 'Death or prison' -

After over six decades of gruesome armed conflict, Colombia attempted to turn the page by forging a landmark peace deal with the now-defunct FARC rebel army in 2016.

Petro, the country's first-ever leftist president, has further pursued a "total peace" strategy of negotiating with a patchwork of armed groups.

World.title: Hundreds flee homes after Guatemala's Fuego volcano erupts
World.content:
GUATEMALA CITY - Hundreds of people living on the slopes of Guatemala's Fuego volcano evacuated their homes after a huge eruption spewed lava and plumes of ash.

Emergency services issued a red alert, the most severe warning, after Central America's most active volcano erupted Monday morning, with conditions intensifying by nightfall.

Rivers of lava streamed down the 3,763-metre volcano located less than 100 kilometres from Guatemala City, while ash rose some six kilometres into the red sky.

Villagers left of their own accord out of fear, describing terrifying scenes of lava oozing down the mountainside.

Firefighters said they transported at least 500 residents of the El Porvenir and Las Lajitas villages to the eastward San Juan Alotenango municipality.

Evacuees are staying in a community hall where makeshift beds have been set up, while the number of people taken to other nearby towns remains unknown.

World.title: Reusser romps to overall lead at Tour de France Femmes
World.content:
DIJON - Marlen Reusser took the overall lead in the Tour de France Femmes on Tuesday, after a carefully executed plan to win the 21km time-trial between Gevrey-Chambertin and Dijon.

The Swiss rider revealed she had been targeting the stage win and the yellow jersey since last year.

"It worked, and I'm really happy. This was my objective here. We called it our 'mustard plan'," she said, referring to the mustard produced in Dijon where the time-trial ended.

Pre-race favourite and 2023 champion Demi Vollering was just 18 seconds slower in third on the day, and trails Reusser by only 14sec overall.

Defending champion Pauline Ferrand-Prevot is now 2min and 13sec off the pace, while 2024 winner Kasia Niewiadoma is 1min 09sec down.

France's Ferrand-Prevot will still be considered an overall contender, though, after beating Vollering by over three minutes in the penultimate stage last year en route to the title.

World time-trial champion Reusser, a qualified doctor, was left lying on the floor and breathing heavily after the finish, while Vollering, the better climber, appeared to have measured her pace.

"It wasn't perfect, perfect, but it was good," said Reusser. "I started well, I did a good climb, but I had a little bit of a problem with my bike and the wind."

The peloton were subjected to clothing checks ahead of the time-trial to ensure no chest form-altering clothing was being used for aerodynamic advantage.

UCI rules state riders may not use any objects to artificially change their "morphology", including cooling devices, padding or front body radio pockets.

Reusser will have to survive Friday's monster climb of Mont Ventoux if she is to take her first Tour de France title.

She may also come under pressure on Wednesday's fifth stage, which features eight hills and ends in the Beaujolais region.

The race concludes on the Promenade des Anglais in Riviera city Nice on Sunday.

World.title: SA 'overwhelmingly' targeted by cybercriminals says Interpol
World.content:
CAPE TOWN - South Africa is facing far more cyberattacks than most other countries on the continent.

INTERPOL says while no African country is immune to cybercrime South Africa's position as a financial and digital hub makes it a prime target.

The country records significantly more ransomware and distributed denial-of-service attacks than elsewhere in Africa.

According to the recent Cyber Assessment Report, cybercrimes losses in Africa have more than doubled since 2024 reaching $484 million.

The 40-page report, released Monday and based on survey data from 36 African member countries, describes a shift from isolated criminal incidents to what it calls an industrialised, borderless ecosystem.

Losses rose from $192 million in 2024 to $484 million, driven largely by AI-assisted scams, credential theft and automated social engineering.

Neal Jetton, Interpol's cybercrime unit director says criminals are not necessarily targeting South Africa itself. Instead, they are searching for weaknesses in networks and systems.

"I think because of increased digitalisation and perhaps a lack in some areas of data and network security, there are vulnerabilities. Financially motivated criminals do not focus on targeting countries. They are looking specifically for vulnerabilities."

An where they find vulnerabilities, they strike, Jetton adds.

"They [criminals] are going across, scanning networks and seeing where there are vulnerabilities that they can they can exploit.”

World.title: Andrea Johnson painted a 'liar' as Madlanga hears more testimony
World.content:
PRETORIA - Independent Directorate Against Corruption (IDAC) deputy prosecutor Peter Serunye delivered damning testimony about Advocate Andrea Johnson, painting the former IDAC head as being dishonest.

Serunye says he repeatedly raised concerns with Johnson about the merits of the case against senior Crime Intelligence officials.

He told the Madlanga Commission he questioned the evidence, the corruption charges and whether the matter fell within IDAC's mandate.

He said these concerns were communicated to Johnson on several occasions through emails and memorandums.

During questioning by co-commissioner Advocate Sesi Baloyi, Serunye rejected Johnson's earlier evidence that no lawyers in her office had expressed reservations about the case.

He insisted that he had raised the issues more than once, referring to several email exchanges, including correspondence relating to the Lushaba case, which he described as even more problematic.

When asked whether Johnson had been truthful in denying that concerns had been raised, Serunye suggested she may not have recalled his communications.

However, when pressed on whether he had any reason to believe she had not received his emails and memorandums, Serunye was unequivocal, saying she had indeed received them.

World.title: Lecturers shock as PSC slashes university dons' retirement age by up to 15 years
World.content:
The Universities Academic Staff Union(UASU),National secretary general,Dr.Constantine Wesonga(C)address press on August 4th 2026 at their office in UniAfric,Nairobi flanked byUniversities Academic Staff Union(UASU),Chairperson Grace Nyongesa(Left)and Kenya University Staff Union(KUSU),Charles Mukhwaya(Right).[Edward Kiplimo,Standard]

Shocking details have emerged of a government plan that could force thousands of university lecturers and research scientists to retire years earlier than expected, triggering outrage among academic staff and setting the stage for a nationwide strike just weeks before universities reopen.

An addendum circular issued by the Public Service Commission (PSC) proposes sweeping changes to the mandatory retirement age for academic staff in public universities, research institutions and equivalent institutions, effectively reducing the retirement age for some cadres by as much as 15 years.

World.title: NTSA blamed for poor signage, costly penalties
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

A temporary speed signage on Likoni Road, Nairobi. [Screengrab]

A growing number of motorists are raising concerns about fines issued by the National Transport and Safety Authority's (NTSA) automated speed camera system, claiming they are being penalised without sufficient warning, transparency, or an opportunity to challenge the alleged offences.

The complaints come after the government rolled out a nationwide network of smart traffic cameras aimed at curbing speeding and reducing road carnage.

The cameras automatically detect speeding vehicles, identify registration numbers and generate instant penalties, with notifications sent to registered vehicle owners via SMS.

While authorities have hailed the technology as a game-changer in road safety, many drivers say the system has become a source of frustration and financial burden.

Some motorists claim they have received multiple speeding fines within a single journey, while others argue they were penalised despite maintaining the posted speed limits.

In some places, motorists argue that most signs are on one side of the road, even though the road is a dual carriageway, making it difficult for most road users.

Several have questioned the accuracy of the cameras, citing cases where they were allegedly fined long after travelling through the affected roads.

The debate has been raging on social media, with the latest complaint being on the speed signage along Likoni Road, Nairobi, where motorists are mandated to drive at 30km/h.

"NTSA can't be the complainant, regulator, enforcer, prosecutor, Jury, judge, and collector all-in-one. They could be chasing internal collection targets, while hurting the common man,"

Others have expressed concern over the placement of some speed cameras, saying they are positioned in areas where speed limit signs are either unclear, obscured or insufficient.

"They fined me near Industrial Park Eastern Bypass where on that entire stretch there is no sign indicating the speed limit. This is a shakedown; someone is minting this money," a user on X lamented.

According to the drivers, this leaves road users vulnerable to inadvertent violations.

"There is no problem with enforcing traffic laws, but motorists deserve clear signage, accurate records and a fair opportunity to dispute fines they believe were issued in error," said one driver who recently received multiple speed notifications along the Northern Bypass.

The automated enforcement system forms part of NTSA's broader road safety reforms under the Minor Traffic Offences Framework, which allows specified offences to be handled administratively instead of through the courts.

NTSA says the initiative is intended to eliminate corruption associated with roadside enforcement, improve compliance with traffic laws and reduce the backlog of traffic cases in courts.

Under the framework, speeding attracts graduated penalties depending on how far a driver exceeds the prescribed limit.

Minor violations may attract warnings or lower fines, while more serious offences carry significantly higher penalties.

The automated fines programme also faced an earlier legal challenge after petitioners argued that motorists were being punished without adequate due process.

The dispute centred on whether automated enforcement infringed constitutional rights to fair administrative action and a fair hearing before penalties are imposed.

Road safety experts, however, maintain that excessive speed remains one of the leading causes of fatal crashes in Kenya and argue that consistent, technology-driven enforcement is more effective than sporadic roadside operations.

They contend that unlike manual enforcement, automated cameras minimise opportunities for bribery and apply traffic laws uniformly to all motorists.

Even so, transport stakeholders are urging NTSA to improve public awareness, ensure speed limit signs are visible and regularly calibrated, and establish an efficient appeals mechanism for motorists who believe they have been wrongly fined.

According to Volume 6 on Traffic Control Facilities and the Traffic Signs Manual, the Ministry of Transport is mandated to ensure the speed limit sign boards are erected above pedestrian footways with a minimum clearance of 2.2m from the bottom of the sign to the pavement.

At the same time, the signs should be placed at an absolute minimum horizontal clearance of 0.5 m from the outer edge of the usable shoulder or carriageway.

World.title: Mukurweini MP John Kaguchia arraigned over alleged inciting remarks
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Mukurweini MP John Kaguchia arrives at the Milimani Law Courts in Nairobi on August 4, 2026. [Nancy Gitonga, Standard]

Mukurweini MP John Kaguchia was on Tuesday arraigned before the Milimani Law Courts over alleged inciting remarks made during a political rally in Kieni, Nyeri County.

Appearing before Senior Principal Magistrate Teresia Nyangena, Kaguchia was read the charge of offensive conduct by the court clerk but did not respond after his lawyers mounted a spirited constitutional challenge against the charges.

His legal team objected to the manner in which the charges had been framed, arguing they violated several constitutional safeguards and should not proceed.

The courtroom was packed to capacity as a battery of lawyers appeared for the legislator alongside political allies who turned up in solidarity.

Among those present were Nyeri Senator John Methu, Nyeri Woman Representative Jane Njeri Maina and several elected leaders who followed the proceedings from the public gallery.

The defence argued that the charge sheet failed to meet the constitutional threshold set under Article 50(2) which guarantees every accused person the right to be informed of the charge with sufficient detail to answer it.

The charge before you does not disclose an offence under the law and purely an attempt by the state to breach the freedom of expression and limiting the opposition.

Lead defence counsel Kiragu Wathuta and Ndegwa Njiru told the court that the MP's constitutional rights had been violated from the time of his arrest.

The lawyers narrated that on the night of August 2, Kaguchia had appeared on Inooro FM's Kiririmbi programme where public affairs were being discussed between 7 pm. and 9 pm.

According to the lawyer, after the programme ended, staff at the Royal Media Services station allegedly informed the MP that about 30 Subaru vehicles carrying hooded individuals had surrounded the premises looking for him.

"Because of the wave of abductions in this country, I advised him to remain within the Royal Media Services premises. At about 5 a.m., I found him having spent the night on the station's couches waiting for daylight," lawyer told the court.

He said that at around 9 a.m., a senior officer who identified himself as a regional DCI commander arrived with uniformed officers and informed the MP that he was under arrest despite there being no summons or warrant issued against him.

"When we inquired why no summons had been issued as is the normal procedure, the investigating officer told us they were acting on instructions from above," the lawuer submitted.

The lawyer further claimed officers initially indicated Kaguchia would be taken to Kilimani before driving him instead to DCI headquarters, where he said advocates were denied access to their client.

"They told us no counsel would be allowed into the DCI premises. Lawyers were locked out and denied an opportunity to consult with the accused," he said.

According to the defence, lawyers later moved to court and obtained orders from Kiambu High Court granting Kaguchia police bail of Sh100,000.

However, they alleged officers at Kamukunji Police Station refused to process the release despite the cash bail being available.

The lawyer told the court that the Officer Commanding Station allegedly declined to accept the money, saying he had received instructions that the legislator could not be released from the station and should instead deposit the cash bail at Central Police Station.

"The accused is not before this court because of any crime he committed. He is here to demonstrate to the country that it is now a crime to oppose the government," he argued.

Lawyer Wathuta also informed the court that Justice Gregory Mutai had on Tuesday morning in Milimani High Court Human Rights Petition No. E517 of 2026 granted the MP a bond of Sh500,000 and directed police to facilitate his access to legal counsel.

Lawyer Ndegwa Njiru argued that Kaguchia could not be required to plead before first receiving legal advice, citing Article 49(1)(c) of the Constitution, which guarantees every arrested person the right to communicate with and be represented by an advocate.

Njiru further challenged the jurisdiction of the Milimani court, arguing that the alleged offence was said to have occurred in Kieni, Nyeri County, and should therefore be prosecuted before a court with territorial jurisdiction over the alleged incident.

He also argued that the charge under Section 94(1) of the Penal Code was defective because it did not disclose who had allegedly been threatened, abused or insulted.

"The charge sheet merely refers to words allegedly uttered by the accused but fails to demonstrate that they were made in a public place or that they amounted to threatening, abusive or insulting words as required by law," Njiru submitted.

He also questioned the accuracy of the translated charge sheet, telling the court he understood Kikuyu and had noticed discrepancies between the original alleged utterances and the English translation.

Njiru argued that the translation distorted the alleged remarks, particularly the reference to the word "Kasongo", and maintained that the inconsistencies prejudiced the accused's ability to understand the charge.

He further submitted that the offence under Section 94 of the Penal Code is a misdemeanour punishable by a maximum sentence of six months imprisonment or a fine not exceeding Sh5,000.

Njiru argued that under Article 49(2) of the Constitution, Kaguchia ought not to have remained in custody for two nights over such an offence.

The defence also urged the court to order the release of the MP's Samsung A33 mobile phone, arguing that it had no connection to the alleged offence.

The hearing on the preliminary objections is still ongoing before Milimani Law Courts

World.title: Tension at Kamukunji Police Station as leaders demand Kaguchia's release
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Mukuruwe-ini MP John Kaguchia at Kamukunji Police Station in Nairobi on August 3, 2026. [Collins Oduor, Standard]

Tension is high at Kamukunji Police Station as opposition leaders led by Kipipiri MP Wanjiku Muhia and lawyers demand the immediate release of Mukurweini MP John Kaguchia, claiming police had failed to comply with a High Court order granting him police cash bail.

Kaguchia, who was arrested earlier on Monday over alleged electoral offences and incitement, remained in police custody hours after his lawyers said the court had ordered his release on Sh100,000 police bail.

Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP) leader Rigathi Gachagua in a post on his Facebook account said that the High Court had issued orders directing the Officer Commanding Station (OCS) at Kamukunji Police Station to release the legislator immediately upon payment of the bail.

Gachagua said that despite the court order having been served, the OCS had not acted and was instead awaiting instructions from his superiors. He warned the officer against disobeying a court order, saying that he could be held personally liable for contempt of court if the directive was ignored.

The former Deputy President further referenced the ongoing murder case involving the former OCS of Central Police Station, urging police officers to uphold the law and avoid carrying out unlawful instructions.

Several Members of Parliament from the Mt Kenya region have camped outside Kamukunji Police Station, insisting they would not leave until Kaguchia is released. The legislators accused police of delaying compliance with the court order and questioned why the MP was still being held despite the court's directive.

The lawmakers that claimed they had been redirected to Central Police Station while seeking information about Kaguchia's detention.

Kaguchia's arrest has sparked political debate, with opposition leaders accusing investigative agencies of selectively enforcing the law against government critics. They argue that other leaders who have previously made controversial public statements have not faced similar action.

World.title: Why Kenyans' trust gap on IEBC continues to grow
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

IEBC is gaining mistrust among Kenyans. [File, Standard]

The reconstituted Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) assumed office about a year ago on the backdrop of growing mistrust among Kenyans.

But, even before it conducts its first General Elections, the Commission is already confronting a fresh credibility test after proposing restrictions on the livestreaming of election results.

The proposal, presented as part of efforts to safeguard the integrity of the tallying process, has instead reignited long-standing public anxieties over transparency in the country's electoral management system.

For many Kenyans, whose confidence in election management has been repeatedly shaken by disputed presidential results, court battles and allegations of manipulation, the move has reinforced fears that access to real-time information could be curtailed at the most critical stage of the democratic process.

The government sponsored Bill, whose fate now lies with the National Assembly, is jointly sponsored by Senate Majority leader Aaron Cheruiyot and Minority leader Stewart Madzayo.

The Bill that has stalled at the First Reading level in the Assembly since February 2024, seeks to repeal section 39(1)(g) of the Elections Act.

If approved, live transmission of results displayed by the Commission at the National Tallying Centre may not be there in the 2027 polls.

Kenyans have since responded to the proposal, pouring their anger and outrage as they question the motive behind the proposal, with some suggesting that the move could be introduced to conceal ill motives during elections.

"No doubt this is exactly what the IEBC fears; a transparent electoral process that every Kenyan can verify,' Wabowoba Calwo said on X in a post accompanied by a clip where an individual is seen pointing at a screen livestreaming the recently conducted Ol Kalou parliamentary by-election.

"Kenyans must demand nothing less than a free and fair 2027 election," he added, asserting that "transparency is not going to be a favour by anybody, it is a democratic safeguard."

According to another user, banning of real-time live streaming of election results would undermine the integrity of polls and create anxiety among voters.

"If the IEBC fails to livestream the General Election, it will create unnecessary suspicion, undermine transparency and provide fertile ground for claims of electoral malpractice," he posted.

According to Yamine, an X user, live broadcasts of election results keep Kenyans informed. promote transparency, provide a clear picture of the voting process, and help ease tension rather than "fuel uncertainty."

"In real democracies, results are streamed live so every citizen can watch and decide for themselves," posted Yamine.

Alfred Abuya said :"I strongly reject this move. Why will they even imagine doing something like counting votes in the dark? Are they working for someone or independent forces behind the idea?"

However, IEBC has since denied claims that the proposed law seeks to scrap the live transmission of election results, saying they have been misunderstood.

In a statement on Thursday, the Commission said the Bill does not amend Section 44 of the Elections Act, which provides for the Integrated Elections Management System used for Voter registration.

It argued, instead, that the amendment is envisioned to introduce an alternative transmission mechanism for areas without the minimum 3G network required to electronically transmit results.

The Commission further said it will still be required to verify results by comparing the original physical Form 34A with its electronically submitted results.

"The Bill seeks to align the law with the Supreme Court's decision in Presidential Election Petition No 1 of 20217, which affirmed that the election result is one recorded in the statutory Results Declaration Form (Form 34A Series), the primary and final record of the results at the polling station," said the commission.

According to youth activist Allans Ademba who mobilised the "Tuko Kadi" mass voter registration call, the move will erode public trust in the agency.

"If IEBC wants to win the trust of youths, it must ensure credible results. This can only happen if they allow live streaming," he said, adding that "apart from malicious forms which the commission can manage, there was no need to ban it."

Appearing on a local TV show early this week, nominated MP Sabina Chege, said the electoral agency was yet to justify to Kenyans what informed such a decision.

"The IEBC has not provided any justification for mending the live streaming of elections," she said.

Former National Assembly Speaker Justin Muturi has also criticised the proposal, terming it retrogressive and an outright attack on democracy and the rule of law.

"Any proposal from whichever quarter to ban the live streaming of election results is not only unconstitutional and offensive to the principles of open governance, but also a stain on the democratic conscience of the Kenyan people," he said.

He said "Darkness and democracy are not synonymous. Transparency is the life -blood of free, fair and credible elections."

Appearing on Spice Fm morning show on Thursday, Lawyer Ndegwa Njiru said: "Our Constitution is built on the principles of transparency, accountability and the participation of the people. Election results are not the property of the IEBC, they belong to Kenyans.

World.title: CS sued in bid to kick out Railways boss, audit SGR contracts
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

A court battle is brewing over Kenya Railways operations and the corporation’s Managing Director Phillip Mainga's reign.

A petitioner is now seeking to push the KR boss out, claiming he is employed on permanent terms.

In the case against KR board, the Attorney General and Transport Cabinet Secretary, the complainant alleges that Mainga was appointed in 2018, noting that State corporations hire their bosses on short-term contracts.

Mainga has been named as an interested party.

“Under the prevailing governance principles applicable to the state corporations, the office of the Managing Director is not meant to be occupied indefinitely,” argues Wahome Mucunu, adding that Mainga’s tenure in office ought to have allegedly lapsed in 2024.

Mucunu claims that the corporation has been at the heart of numerous concerns over procurement and transparency.

He states that among the projects that have raised concerns are the Standard Gauge Railway (SGR project).

According to him, Transparency International this year in March this year allegedly indicated that SGR was a high-risk project, with a 4.9 out of 5 corruption risk score.

“The project has equally generated sustained public debate concerning transparency, accountability, value for money, public participation, procurement practices and debt sustainability. The Petitioner states that the people of Kenya, being the ultimate financiers of the project through taxation and public borrowing, possess a legitimate constitutional interest in the manner in which the project was conceived, procured, financed and implemented,” says Muchunu.

He further claims that Transparency International indicated that public institutions, among them KR, allegedly repeatedly failed to provide information requested by accountability actors and researchers. Muchunu alleged that the assessment concluded that the responses received were insufficient to facilitate effective public oversight.

“All material times relevant to this Petition, the first interested party, Mr. Phillip Mainga, has served as the Managing Director of Kenya Railways Corporation. The office of Managing Director constitutes the highest executive office within the Corporation and carries overall responsibility for the administration, management and operational control of the affairs of the Corporation,” he argues.

He also claims that many questions have been raised by members of the public, civil society organisations, governance experts and accountability institutions regarding the management of major projects undertaken by the corporation.

According to him, the answers given do not allegedly exude confidence as they are not allegedly fully addressed.

“Such concerns have centered on the adequacy of procurement procedures, transparency of contractual arrangements, disclosure of project costs and effectiveness of oversight mechanisms. The Petitioner states that these concerns have never been adequately addressed in a manner capable of restoring public confidence,” he continues.

In his case before Justice David Mburu, the petitioner urges the court to find that failure to disclose details about the SGR contract was a violation of the Constitution. He also seeks for a finding that Mainga ought to have left office by last year.

At the same time, he is urging the court to rule that the parastatal’s board had violated the Constitution and to compel it to find his successor.

Muchunu also wants to have the SGR project contracts audited.

World.title: Tiktoker Mauti changes plea, freed on bail in case involving Ruto's children
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

TikToker Hesbon Mauti was charged for posting a video threatening to kill and defile President William Ruto's children. [Nancy Gitonga, Standard]

TikToker Hesbon Mauti Thomas, accused of posting a video containing remarks threatening President William Ruto’s son George Ruto and daughter, has been released on a Sh5,000 cash bail after changing his plea to not guilty.

Mauti appeared before Milimani Principal Magistrate Geoffrey Onsarigo on Friday, July 31, 2026, where the charge of offensive conduct conducive to breaches of the peace was read afresh to him.

The accused, who had initially pleaded guilty to the charge on Thursday, changed his plea after his lawyer Cliff Ombeta applied for the matter to be reopened and for the charge to be read again.

The court allowed the application, after which Mauti denied the charge and pleaded not guilty.

According to the charge sheet, Mauti is accused of posting a video on June 25, 2026, through his TikTok account PROVIDENT@bonifaceaminga, containing remarks that prosecutors say were likely to cause a breach of the peace.

The charge sheet alleges that Mauti altered words in the video to make remarks targeting President Ruto’s son George Ruto and his daughter, while demanding that their parents be paid Sh2 million.

Mauti is charged with offensive conduct conducive to breaches of the peace contrary to Section 94(1) of the Penal Code, Chapter 63 of the Laws of Kenya.

After denying the charges, his defence team told the court that Mauti is a young man and a law student at Chuka University whose fees are paid by a church.

The lawyers further informed the court that Mauti is an orphan and has no parents to assist him in securing his release, asking the court to grant him a lenient cash bail.

“We are looking at the charges and when we look at it and the consequences that come from that, and if it goes on this particular way we know what the sentence is and what the consequences are. The court has got the right before passing the sentence to be able to reconsider when he changes his plea,” his lawyers told the court.

The defence also told the court that they had advised Mauti that the earlier position he had taken by pleading guilty carried serious consequences and offered to represent him in the matter.

The prosecution did not oppose his release on bail.

Magistrate Onsarigo granted Mauti a cash bail of Sh5,000 and directed him to provide one contact person.

The matter will be mentioned on August 18, 2026, for pre-trial directions.

World.title: Ruto calls for national dialogue to shape Kenya's vision
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Ruto said recent economic reforms had laid a stronger foundation for future growth. [File, Standard]

President William Ruto has invited Kenyans to take part in what he described as the country's most significant national conversation since the adoption of the 2010 Constitution, saying the discussions will help chart Kenya's next long-term development agenda.

Speaking on the country's development trajectory, the President said the conversation should move beyond partisan politics and election cycles to focus on a shared national vision.

"I invite every Kenyan to what I believe will become the most consequential national conversation since the adoption of our Constitution in 2010," Ruto said.

"A national conversation about Kenya's development. This conversation must rise above politics, transcend electoral cycles and unite us around a shared destiny."

The President acknowledged that while Vision 2030 had set an ambitious goal of transforming Kenya into an upper-middle-income country by 2030, the country remains off course to achieve that target.

"Vision 2030 set a target of Kenya becoming an upper-middle-income country by 2030. So far, we are off target. This is not a criticism of Vision 2030, nor is it a reason for disappointment; rather, it is an opportunity to learn from our successes proudly, reflect with honesty on where we have fallen short, and define together Kenya's next long-term vision," he said.

At the same time, Ruto announced that the government will formally launch a nationwide conversation on August 12 to develop Kenya's next long-term development blueprint as Vision 2030 nears its end.

"Accordingly, on Wednesday, August 12, 2026, we shall formally launch the National Conversation on Kenya's Future Beyond Vision 2030; the most consequential exercise in national reflection and public participation since the promulgation of our Constitution in 2010," he stated.

Ruto said recent economic reforms had laid a stronger foundation for future growth, citing improvements in key macroeconomic indicators.

"We have stabilized our currency, inflation has fallen, borrowing costs have declined, and investor confidence has returned," he said. "Last year Kenya attracted a record $3.2 billion in foreign direct investment, more than double the amount recorded in 2022."

He added that Kenya's improving investment climate had earned international recognition.

"The 2025 IMD World Competitiveness Ranking placed Kenya as the most competitive economy in Africa, reflecting the confidence our reforms have restored," Ruto said.

At the same time, Ruto also highlighted the establishment of the National Infrastructure Fund and the Sovereign Wealth Fund, saying the two institutions would help finance strategic investments while safeguarding the country's wealth for future generations.

According to Ruto, Kenya must now confront difficult questions about its development path to unlock its full potential.

"The question we must ask ourselves candidly and honestly is why other nations have fulfilled so much of their potential while we have repeatedly fallen short. What must we now do differently to ensure that the next chapter of Kenya's development story is fundamentally different from the last?" he posed.

He urged all Kenyans to help shape a new long-term national vision, saying the country's future depends on collective commitment rather than political divisions.

World.title: Trump says Strait of Hormuz will be reopened “soon” or Iran will suffer harsh consequences
World.content:
President Trump says the Strait of Hormuz would be reopened “soon” or he would launch a harsh new attack on Iran.

Speaking in an interview on Fox News, Trump said “very good discussions” were underway with Tehran, but warned if Iran backed out of their commitments he would return to strikes.

“The Strait’s going to be open very soon or they are going to get hit very hard,” he said, adding later: “If they back out again, they are going to get hit really hard. They know that. They understand that. I have no choice.”

Trump said his first choice was not renewing attacks but instead pursuing a diplomatic agreement.

“We hit them very, very hard. But the hard hit is yet to come and hopefully we won’t have to use it,” he said. “I hope we won’t – we’re having very good discussions. They don’t like to admit that.”

Iran has denied it is holding direct discussions with the United States. Instead, Tehran has said it is working with Oman on an arrangement to reopen the Strait.

Mediators hope once the Strait is reopened the US and Iran can resume nuclear talks.

World.title: Cairo court issues death sentence for Sarah Khalifa and 12 defendants in ‘Grand Drug Case’
World.content:
The Cairo Criminal Court, on Tuesday, has issued a death sentence for TV host Sarah Khalifa and 12 other defendants, and referred their case to the Grand Mufti of Egypt, setting September 5th as the date for the issuing the verdict.

Referral to the Mufti is required in the Egyptian court system ahead of any death sentences even though the mufti’s opinion is advisory, not binding.

Khalifa and the 27 other defendants arrived at the courthouse on Tuesday, to attend their trial for their involvement in a “Grand Drug Case” which saw the defense’s arguments completed.

The investigation revealed that the defendants had formed a criminal organization aimed at manufacturing and trafficking synthetic drugs.

They imported raw materials from abroad, and their roles were divided between importation, manufacturing, and distribution.

The suspects used a residential property as a base for storing and manufacturing the drugs.

The investigation further revealed that the total amount seized exceeded 750 kilograms of narcotics and the raw materials used in their production.

Based on the investigation’s findings, the Public Prosecution issued several urgent decisions, including inventorying the defendants’ assets, disclosing the confidentiality of their bank accounts, freezing their funds, and placing the fugitive defendants on travel ban and arrival watch lists.

The referral decision was based on the testimonies of 20 witnesses, in addition to the compiled evidence.

World.title: Trump calls for adopting daylight saving time permanently
World.content:
US President Donald Trump announced that the House of Representatives passed a bill to make daylight saving time permanent in the US, confirming that the bill now goes to the Senate for final approval.

He described this move as a response to a long-awaited demand from the majority of Americans.

In a post on Truth Social on Wednesday, Trump said that successive US administrations had failed for years to address this issue, adding, ” I am proud to announce that the House of Representatives has passed the Bill, and it has now gone to the Senate for final approval.”

“It is foolish, inconvenient and, in some cases, very costly. For Cities and States with Watchtowers, and hard to reach places, it costs Millions of Dollars.”

“A recent case was made that it is also bad for your health in the anxiety it creates. Leading Medical, Crime, and Economic Studies have shown that ceasing the biannual time change, giving us one extra hour of natural sunlight in the evenings, will help Decrease Robbery and Murder Rates, Reduce Car Accidents (especially those involving Pedestrians!), Lower Risk for Cardiac Issues, Stroke, and Seasonal Depression,” Trump said.

He added that adopting permanent daylight saving time would make it safer for children to return home from school, provide families with more time, support extracurricular activities, and boost the sports, fitness, tourism, retail, and restaurant sectors, as well as reduce energy bills by utilizing an extra hour of daylight.

Trump emphasized that the best solution is to “leave it as it is now, and never change again,” arguing that the issue enjoys a consensus that can unite Republicans, Democrats, and Independents.

In closing, Trump called on Republican senators to drop their objections and allow the legislation to pass, urging them to expedite the passage of the “SUNSHINE PROTECTION ACT”.

World.title: Here are the countries that have gained and lost in tourism during 2019-2025
World.content:
The global tourism market has undergone significant changes in recent years.

Some countries have seen significant increase in international visitor arrivals thanks to infrastructure development and new promotional strategies, while others have yet to recover to pre-pandemic levels, according to a study by the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD).

Saudi Arabia led the world in international tourist arrivals between 2019 and 2025, with a 67 percent increase.

Morocco came in second with a 53 percent increase, and Egypt third with a 47 percent increase.

Brazil and Colombia also ranked highly among the top five countries, experiencing growth in inbound tourism of 46 percent and 45 percent, respectively.

The OECD attributes these results to significant investments in tourism infrastructure, improved transport networks, and effective international promotion.

Turkey was also among the countries that saw a notable increase in foreign visitors, ranking eleventh and surpassing 2019 figures by 21 percent. Among European destinations, Norway, Serbia, Denmark, Portugal, and Spain also experienced positive growth.

Meanwhile, many popular tourist destinations have seen a significant drop in foreign visitor numbers.

The largest decline was recorded in Israel, where inbound tourists fell by 71 percent.

Significant decreases were also observed in Ireland, Argentina, and Peru, while the US, Italy, and Germany remain below 2019 levels.

World.title: Rare solar eclipse to occur on Northern Hemisphere and Mediterranean on August 12
World.content:
The world is preparing for a rare solar eclipse on August 12th. Day will turn to night temporarily as the sun’s disk disappears behind the moon in a breathtaking astronomical spectacle.

The eclipse will stretch across parts of the Northern Hemisphere and the Mediterranean, and astronomy enthusiasts are eagerly anticipating this event, making extensive preparations to observe it safely.

Darkness will descend on the Iberian Peninsula near sunset, as well as in small parts of Greenland and Iceland, where the sun, moon, and Earth will align perfectly in the sky, according to The Independent.

Longer eclipse next year

The total eclipse will begin near the North Pole before moving south and will last for up to two minutes and 18 seconds.

This marks the beginning of a longer solar display next year, a dazzling spectacle lasting six and a half minutes, which will extend from Spain to North Africa and the Middle East.

Darkness in the day

The moon’s shadow, or umbra, will take an hour and a half to travel 8,260 kilometers, mostly over the empty Atlantic Ocean.

The total eclipse will reach its peak off the west coast of Iceland.

By the time it reaches a small area of ​​Portugal, then Spain, where large crowds are expected, the total eclipse will have diminished to a minute, ending in the Mediterranean Sea.

The partial eclipse will be visible in distant regions such as Alaska and Siberia, and will cover Canada, the northern US, much of Europe, and West Africa.

The closer one is to the path of totality, the more the sun will be obscured by the moon.

The sun will cover 94 percent of Dublin and 83 percent of Oslo, Norway. Montreal will see 18 percent of the sun disappear, while New York will experience nine percent, and Norfolk, Virginia, will see two percent.

Eclipse safety rules

According to NASA, eclipse glasses are essential, even if only a small portion of the sun is visible. You should view the eclipse through specialized glasses or a handheld solar projector.

You can view the eclipse directly without eclipse glasses or a solar projector only in one instance: when the moon completely obscures the sun’s disk during the brief period of totality.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Trabzonspor president issues first comment after finalizing Mohamed Salah deal
World.content:
The president of Turkish FC Trabzonspor, Ertuğrul Doğan, commented on negotiations with Egyptian international Mohamed Salah, the former Liverpool FC winger, regarding a potential free transfer during the current summer transfer window.

Doğan told the Turkish newspaper Fanatik, on Wednesday, “We can’t talk about Mohamed Salah; he’s a global star. We needed a player like him.”

He continued, “It would be a fantastic signing. We hope he will be beneficial to our club. Trabzonspor’s success has been making headlines across Turkey and Europe, and young players have started choosing our club”.

Doğan emphasized, “We’re trying to send a message to everyone that we can bring any player to our team.”

Regarding his negotiations with Salah, he replied, “We rushed to finalize the deal as soon as other teams withdrew. I held a meeting with Mohamed Salah and his agent. It was a very professional and respectful meeting; both sides understood each other, and there were no difficulties.”

He continued, “Our meeting lasted about ten days, and everything became clear yesterday.”

World.title: One mistake Trump hasn’t made on Iran
World.content:
Unless Donald Trump finds a way out of his box on Iran, history may come to regard his choice to wage war as a presidency-defining error.

But he has so far avoided one potential dire mistake: massively escalating the conflict past his capacity to control it.

History shows that presidents who intensify wars in pursuit of a way out, or to protect their own prestige or America’s reputation, descend a slippery slope. In Vietnam, Iraq and Afghanistan, they often did so reluctantly, in wars that could no longer be won.

Not for the first time, Trump finds himself at a three-way intersection in a war now being driven by Iran’s refusal to surrender or seriously negotiate.

If diplomacy keeps failing, is he willing to perpetually extend the so-far inconclusive campaign of air strikes, fragile ceasefires, and US and Iranian maritime blockades that rumbles on but doesn’t end the war?

Or does he step up the US offensive by lifting his own limits and going beyond mostly military targets to take out Iranian civilian and infrastructure assets — crossing the Rubicon into the use of ground troops in limited operations?

The third option would be deeply painful: accepting that he, and the United States, would be best served by cutting losses and walking away from the conflict with his major goals unresolved.

Each question serves up unpalatable political and strategic answers, which explains why he’s still stuck in a war he can’t afford to win and can’t afford to lose. It’s a measure of the US predicament that the Pentagon sent a request to a group of military analysts for new ideas on how to punish Iran, according to an exclusive CNN report.

President Donald Trump speaks after signing an executive order in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, DC, on Monday. Jim Watson/AFP/Getty Images

Trump warns of Iran’s ‘decapitation’

Trump’s frustration radiated from his Truth Social account Monday after Iran rebuffed his latest gambit. He’d suspended promised devastating strikes at the weekend after saying for the umpteenth time that a deal could be imminent.

“Iranian Leadership is unbelievably duplicitous!” Trump declared, ironically echoing complaints of the repressive Islamic Republic about his coercive diplomacy. By the afternoon, Trump was back to threats. “This is a last chance for them to sign a good document,” he said in the Oval Office.

But his warning that Iran would face “decapitation” begged its own question. What will he do if it ignores him again?

Any huge escalation by Trump would be a gamble, since there is no sign Tehran can be bombed back to talks.

Iran would likely respond to attacks on its bridges, power plants and other infrastructure by torching similar targets on the territory of US Gulf allies and deepening the war’s economic cost. Regional leaders seemed to have raised this very scenario with Trump over the weekend. “We were set to go. And they called. And in addition, Saudi Arabia called. And UAE called. Qatar called,” Trump said.

In theory, Trump could use the US Navy to forcibly open the Strait of Hormuz. But this would expose US ships to missiles and drones. Ground operations against the Kharg Island oil exporting hub or to push Iranian forces back from the strait could be bloody.

The last 60 years show how stakes rise exponentially when an air war turns into a ground war. The conflict looks different to Americans back home. Political costs increase as casualties rise, which Trump can’t afford weeks before the midterm elections. And when troops die in the search for an exit strategy, their sacrifices can paradoxically extend a war, because those sacrifices cannot appear to have been in vain.

Many previous presidents have reached turning points like Trump’s. While Vietnam, Iraq, Afghanistan and Trump’s Iran conflicts started in different ways, they were all reduced to a “bad status quo, escalate or leave” equation.

And no president wants to be remembered for losing a war.

Former President Lyndon Johnson and former President George W. Bush Getty Images

How LBJ and Bush went down slippery slopes

In 1965, President Lyndon B. Johnson wrestled with extending the Vietnam War he inherited from assassinated President John F. Kennedy. “We are off to bombing these people; we are over that hurdle,” LBJ told his Defense Secretary Robert McNamara, in a remark that partially parallels Trump’s strategic choice. “I don’t think anything is going to be as bad as losing. And I don’t see any way of winning,” Johnson said.

But Johnson still ordered Operation Rolling Thunder, escalated bombing against North Vietnam and sent tens of thousands more young Americans into the inferno. He should have listened to Under Secretary of State George Ball, who wrote in an undated memo that once the US suffered casualties it would be stuck in a “well-nigh irreversible process” and would suffer “national humiliation” if it stopped short of achieving its objectives.

Ball, who predicted the abyss to come, argued the US would more seriously damage its global leadership by continuing the war than by adopting “a carefully plotted course toward a compromise solution.”

The war ended Johnson’s hopes of a second elected term, and Richard Nixon inherited the Vietnam War after winning the 1968 election. Many historians argue that he and national security adviser Henry Kissinger had already concluded that victory was impossible but that they fought on in the hope of defining conditions for a withdrawal — a futile attempt to bolster anticommunist South Vietnam and to avoid the impression of a US defeat.

“If, when the chips are down, the world’s most powerful nation, the United States of America, acts like a pitiful, helpless giant, the forces of totalitarianism and anarchy will threaten free nations and free institutions throughout the world,” Nixon told the nation on April 30, 1970, explaining his decision to expand the war into Cambodia. More than 20,000 Americans would die in Vietnam during Nixon’s presidency. The last US combat troops left the country in 1973, and the final US personnel were evacuated during the fall of Saigon in 1975, under President Gerald Ford.

More than 30 years later, President George W. Bush delivered his own wartime national address. He accepted responsibility for mistakes made but warned in 2007 that “failure in Iraq would be a disaster for the United States.” He announced a surge of thousands more troops to help Iraq’s armed forces to fight insurgents.

History is yet to settle on a final verdict on that operation. The counterinsurgency did work in some areas. But the question of whether US casualties were justified is an agonizing one since the United States would eventually fully withdraw.

President Barack Obama was elected on a promise to end America’s forever wars. But eight years after the September 11 attacks that led the US into Afghanistan, he announced his own troop surge to reverse Taliban momentum and to finally crush al Qaeda. Mindful of the escalation trap that snared Johnson, Nixon and Bush, he vowed to start withdrawing troops in mid-2011. Critics argue the finite timeline encouraged US enemies to wait the US out.

US President Donald Trump walks to board Air Force One at Morristown Municipal Airport in Morristown, New Jersey, on Sunday. Aaron Schwartz/AFP/Getty Images

Trump won office condemning the kind of war he may now face

America’s modern quagmires shaped Trump’s vehement critiques that helped him win the White House in 2016. Four days before he was elected president, he lashed out at “wars that never end, wars that we never win.”

But during his first term, Trump ordered his own troop increase in Afghanistan in a bid to finally end the war. “My original instinct was to pull out — and historically I like following my instincts,” he said. Less than three years later, he blamed his first defense secretary, James Mattis, for the decision, saying, “I gave him more people for a short period of time, and it didn’t work out.”

Now, Trump faces another of the lonely reckonings that he encapsulated in his national address on Afghanistan in 2017: “All my life, I’ve heard that decisions are much different when you sit behind the desk in the Oval Office.”

The Iran war is not Bush’s. It’s Trump’s own. And it will determine his legacy and the fates of many lives beyond the White House.

World.title: Israel to “continue to thwart any threat” from Gaza, official says
World.content:
Amid efforts by the US and the Board of Peace to get Israel to halt strikes in the Gaza Strip, an Israeli official said Monday that Israel “will continue to thwart any threat to our civilians and soldiers.”

The official also reiterated that Israel will not pull troops back from the “current line” — meaning the additional territory it has taken since an October ceasefire agreement went into effect.

Israel has continued expanding its control of Gaza, cramming its population into a shrinking area of land.

Israeli strikes have killed at least 28 people in Gaza since early Friday local time when US President Donald Trump announced a deal to disarm Hamas, according to Palestinian health authorities.

In a joint statement Monday in their capacity as mediators, Qatar, Turkey and Egypt condemned “continuing Israeli violations in the Gaza Strip” that they said have killed numerous civilians, and they called on the international community to “exert the necessary pressure on Israel” to comply with the ceasefire agreement.

Hamas has said it will follow through with the deal only if Israel halts strikes in Gaza and pulls troops back to the “yellow line,” as defined by the October ceasefire agreement.

Nickolay Mladenov, the Board of Peace’s high representative, arrived in Israel on Monday to discuss the implementation of the Hamas disarmament agreement.

The Board of Peace said in a statement that the meeting was “constructive and detailed.”

“Contrary to inaccurate reports, we note that the full withdrawal of the IDF beyond the Yellow Line will take place only once decommissioning is complete, as Hamas committed to the mediators,” the board said. “This applies to light weapons, heavy weapons, and the tunnels alike.”

This post has been updated with new information.

World.title: Hichilema unveils Copperbelt package, to personally pay ZESCO fees for 16,000 households
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has unveiled a sweeping package of economic interventions for the Copperbelt, promising to personally settle electricity connection fees for sixteen thousand households in Chambishi, revive mothballed mining operations and lower timber costs, as he pressed his case to voters in the province eight days before the general election.

Addressing campaign rallies in Mufulira, Lufwanyama, Kalulushi and Chambishi, the Head of State said his administration remained committed to accelerating economic recovery through investment in mining, energy, infrastructure and employment creation. He framed the announcements as a continuation of work already under way rather than new campaign promises manufactured for the occasion. Moreover, President Hichilemaa emphasized the importance of transparency in all government dealings.

In Chambishi, the President said he would meet the cost of connecting sixteen thousand households to the national grid out of his own pocket, rather than allowing the bill to fall on ZESCO. “I will talk to Zesco to connect 16,000 households in Kabaso area. I will deal with the connection charge also,” he said, reaffirming his commitment to reopening Chambishi Metals.

He directed local leaders to compile the names of eligible beneficiaries, stressing that only households on the approved list would qualify. “It means me, in my own personal business account, I will pay for these connections so that Zesco doesn’t go bankrupt. I want the names of these 16,000 beneficiaries and the cost of connection. I will take care of that,” the President said.

The commitment came alongside a disclosure that government had advanced discussions with potential investors interested in reopening Chambishi Metals, a move the President described as a major step toward restoring mining activity and creating jobs in the area. “I am working on the reopening of Chambishi Metals so that you can get jobs here,” he told residents.

Mining featured heavily throughout the Copperbelt tour. In Mufulira, the President pledged to engage mine owners directly on safety standards for small-scale miners and to facilitate the allocation of a mine dumpsite to young people seeking economic opportunities. “Bally is a responsible parent, so I want you to work safely and this is why I will engage the owners of the dumpsites,” he said.

He also disclosed that he had directed Mopani Copper Mines and pension fund managers to resolve outstanding pension issues affecting former mine workers, warning that he would personally intervene if no agreement was reached between the parties. The President further reaffirmed a commitment to reopening Chibuluma Mine’s Shafts Two and Seven, describing the move as an opportunity to create jobs similar to the revival of Shaft 28 in Luanshya.

“We are committed to revamping Shafts Two and Seven to create jobs for the youth and strengthen the economy,” he said. In Kalulushi, the President turned his attention to the timber industry, directing the Zambia Forestry and Forest Industries Corporation to review prices charged to local sawmillers, which he said had become prohibitively expensive.

“I have heard the concerns of sawmillers over the high cost of timber from ZAFFICO. I have engaged the corporation to ensure prices are within acceptable levels,” he said. The President also announced plans to formalise small-scale mining across the province by providing miners with legal and safe access to designated mining areas, a move intended to reduce the informal and often dangerous conditions under which many currently operate.

“We want legal mining. We want safe mining. There is no parent who sends his children to die every day in the pits,” he said, signalling a shift toward regulated artisanal mining zones rather than continued reliance on unregulated digging.

Beyond mining, the President announced that all volunteer nurses, doctors and teachers currently serving in Chambishi would be formally recruited into the public service, addressing a long-standing grievance among health and education workers who have provided services without full government employment status.

Additional pledges included facilitating construction of a modern bus station in Chambishi, expanding solar energy projects, improving radiology services at Chambishi Mine Hospital, and engaging stakeholders to resolve outstanding pension payments owed to former mine workers. The President urged residents to uphold peace and reject political violence, arguing that Zambia’s development agenda could only be sustained in a peaceful environment.

Beyond the Copperbelt-specific pledges, the President used the tour to defend broader elements of his economic record, including the government’s accumulation of foreign reserves, which he said had helped stabilise the Kwacha, support debt servicing and strengthen the country’s resilience to external shocks. He urged voters to reject what he described as a return to Patriotic Front-era governance, framing the Tonse Alliance as comprising leaders from the former administration.

The announcements landed in a province that has historically been a bellwether in Zambian politics, and where mining-sector fortunes are closely tied to household livelihoods. Whether the pledges translate into the promised connections and reopened shafts will likely become one of the more closely watched post-election accountability measures on the Copperbelt in the months ahead.

World.title: He Is Protecting His US$4 Million Eagle Milling Scandal by Spreading a False Narrative
World.content:
He Is Protecting His US$4 Million Eagle Milling Scandal by Spreading a False Narrative

By Augustine Mukoka

How can General Kanene hire cadres to virtually split his own medulla oblongata?

How can Garry Nkombo hire Bilden Shaloba and UPND thugs to block his own nomination filing and create mayhem at a funeral?

How can Brian Mundubile hire his own supporters to derail his campaign in Western Province?

How can Mundubile hire cadres to assault his own artists?

Surely, Mark Simuuwe must be a genius with vital information that could help the police unravel the situation.

Is Simuuwe confirming this is how the UPND sponsored the gassing of innocent citizens to get to power?

Simuuwe is a danger to Zambia’s democracy.

A senseless social media post by Mark Simuuwe in the wake of the chaos allegedly triggered by UPND cadres in Luampa, Western Province — as opposition leader Brian Mundubile and his running mate, Makebi Zulu, arrived with their convoy yesterday — is not only contemptuous but also highly inflammatory. It represents one of the most irresponsible ways of handling a volatile situation during a highly charged and emotionally tense electoral period.

Rather than taking responsibility and addressing the chaos, Simuuwe, the ruling party’s Media Director, resorted to dogma in what appears to be a desperate attempt to win sympathy and shift blame onto the opposition. Such an attempt to insult the intelligence of any reasonable person is not only callous but deeply disturbing, particularly when it comes from someone who once sought parliamentary office but ultimately failed to secure it.

If you are unfamiliar with what I am referring to, here is Mark Simuuwe’s social media post made yesterday after Mundubile’s convoy came under attack and images of the assault on General Kanene circulated widely on social media.

Simuuwe wrote:

“PF is sponsoring their own cadres to wear UPND regalia, then cause chaos and attack either marketeers or their own members, then blame it on UPND.”They have also sponsored self-attacks in Southern, Western, Central, Lusaka, North-Western and Copperbelt so as to make it look like those are UPND strongholds where they are attacked, when in actual sense UPND is now nationwide.”You cannot manipulate voters in Eastern, Muchinga, Northern and Luapula using dirty politics.”We call upon citizens to be alert; their evil and dirty politics will never be clean — same old habits.”

How stupid!

His President later issued what many considered a feeble statement condemning the violence perpetrated by UPND cadres. In Kitwe, a bus linked to President Hakainde Hichilema’s operative — a Habasimbi — is a material of interest.

Widespread violence has previously been witnessed during the UPND’s own intra-party adoption process. It has occurred in Kaputa among UPND cadres, been witnessed in Magoye, and also recorded in Bweengwa, Choma and Monze — all involving UPND members. In Mazabuka, violence has likewise occurred between rival UPND factions: those supporting independent candidate Garry Nkombo and those backing President Hichilema.

Yesterday, that violence extended, as in parts of North-Western Province, beyond internal UPND disputes and targeted opposition leader Mundubile. In typical UPND fashion, blame is once again directed at the opposition. How are Zambians expected to accept such claims with Mark “Eagle Milling” Simuuwe at the centre of this narrative?

Simuuwe may convince UPND supporters and those willing to believe him unquestioningly, but he cannot deceive everyone all the time. He may believe he is clever today, but even the President’s chief political messenger cannot remain convincing indefinitely.

The Zambia Police should investigate Simuuwe’s statements and determine whether any laws have been broken by the publication of information that could inflame public tensions or misrepresent events. His public assertions deserve careful scrutiny alongside any investigation into the violence itself.

The continued violence suggests that those responsible have little regard for peace or democratic principles. The President’s restrained response has done little to reassure the nation that there is sufficient political will to decisively confront political violence.

This is why Simuuwe must be stopped from spreading a false and misleading narrative of events. Zambia deserves peace. Zambia deserves a free, fair and credible election.

Stop the violence. Stop spreading false narratives. Take responsibility and ensure that all political actors are held accountable so that the country can move forward peacefully. It’s disgusting to watch Zambian elections degenerate into a bloodbath.

Arrest Simuuwe. Stop the chaos.

Editor’s Note: The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this publication. This is an opinion/column piece.

World.title: General Kanene hospitalised after machete attack at rally
World.content:
Musician hacked as poll violence spreads across three provinces

Musician Clifford Dimba, popularly known as General Kanene, remains admitted at the University Teaching Hospital after suspected ruling party cadres attacked him with a machete during a campaign rally in Shibuyunji District on Monday, one of several violent incidents that have rattled Zambia’s election campaign with polling day approaching.

The musician was performing at a rally for independent parliamentary aspirant Ibrahim Mwamba in Mwembeshi East Constituency when armed men arrived in a Toyota Land Cruiser and disrupted the gathering. Police spokesperson Godfrey Chilabi said preliminary investigations showed the attackers assaulted Dimba, inflicting a cut to his head, before turning on property at the scene.

“They allegedly assaulted Dimba, inflicting a cut to his head and damaged a Mitsubishi Triton registration number BAZ 5004 belonging to Mwamba,” Chilabi said. He added that the assailants also made off with an HP ProBook laptop, two mobile phones and sixteen thousand kwacha in cash, the value of the remaining damaged property still being assessed.

Dimba was first taken to Chawama Level I Hospital before being issued a medical report at Westwood Police Station and later referred to the University Teaching Hospital, where he remains under treatment. Police dismissed circulating social media rumours that the musician had died, and confirmed that a machete recovered at the scene had been retained as an exhibit.

Chilabi said dockets have been opened for aggravated robbery, unlawful wounding and malicious damage to property. “This matter is being treated as a serious criminal offence, and all those involved will be identified, arrested and prosecuted in accordance with the laws of Zambia,” he said. The rally had also been addressed by independent council chairperson candidate Mutumba Denise.

Mwamba’s own campaign team was not spared. According to reports carried in the aftermath of the attack, the aspiring MP suffered a fractured knee and ankle during the same disturbance, while campaign equipment including public address systems was stolen or destroyed.

The Shibuyunji attack came in the same week that supporters of the United Party for National Development and the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity clashed in Luampa District, Western Province. Suspected UPND supporters attempted to block the campaign convoy of NRPUP presidential candidate Brian Mundubile, resulting in stone-throwing between the two groups before the confrontation was brought under control.

President Hakainde Hichilema condemned both incidents in a statement posted on his Facebook page, warning that political violence would not be tolerated regardless of who was responsible. “Let it be clear that violence, intimidation or lawlessness by any political party, candidate or supporter will not be tolerated,” the Head of State said, describing the reports as deeply concerning and deserving the strongest condemnation.

The President stressed that every political party had a lawful right to campaign during the period allocated by the Electoral Commission of Zambia, and warned that anyone found disrupting that process would face the consequences. “Anyone who attempts to disrupt or prevent that process is breaking the law and must face the full consequences,” he said, calling on parties and their supporters to conduct campaigns peacefully and within the confines of the law.

In a twist that has complicated the picture, the UPND media team issued its own statement alleging that elements of the former Patriotic Front, operating under the NRPUP banner, had orchestrated a scheme to sponsor individuals to wear UPND regalia, stage violent incidents and falsely implicate the ruling party. The party said the operation involved deploying people dressed in UPND attire to provoke violence against marketeers, members of the public and, in some cases, even their own supporters, before circulating claims that UPND members were responsible.

According to the statement, similar operations were alleged to have been planned or carried out in Southern, Western, Central, Lusaka, North-Western and Copperbelt provinces, with the stated aim of creating an impression that the ruling party was losing support in its traditional strongholds while manipulating public opinion in Eastern, Muchinga, Northern and Luapula provinces. The UPND called on law enforcement agencies to investigate any credible reports of individuals impersonating its members or engaging in criminal conduct while falsely associating themselves with the governing party.

NRPUP figures have pushed back against suggestions that the party or its sympathisers are behind coordinated violence. Former Shiwang’andu MP Stephen Kampyongo, commenting separately on unrelated editorial criticism of his party, argued that it was unfair to characterise NRPUP’s campaign in purely negative terms, though he did not address the Shibuyunji attack directly.

Civil society voices have urged all sides to allow police investigations to run their course rather than trade accusations. Commentary published this week argued that words of condemnation from political leaders, however sincere, are no longer sufficient on their own, and that the true test lies in whether suspects are identified, arrested and brought before the courts without delay or selective treatment.

With the national vote now just over a week away, the Electoral Commission of Zambia and the police have both faced renewed calls to demonstrate that campaign-period rules are being enforced evenly. Officials from both major parties have said they expect law enforcement to treat all reported incidents with equal seriousness, regardless of which side is implicated, as the country enters its final stretch before Zambians go to the polls.
