World.title: House Ethics Committee will investigate Ohio Republican Max Miller
World.content:
House Ethics Committee will investigate Ohio Republican Max Miller

toggle caption Andrew Harnik/AP

The House Ethics Committee has announced it is opening an investigation into Rep. Max Miller, after the Ohio Republican asked the committee for a probe of the domestic abuse allegations that have swirled around his bid for reelection.

The panel made the announcement on Tuesday, saying it was reviewing allegations that Miller "may have engaged in domestic violence and abuse or illegal drug use" in violation of congressional codes of conduct.

"The Committee notes that the mere fact that it is investigating these allegations, and publicly disclosing its review, does not itself indicate that any violation has occurred," it said in a statement.

Sponsor Message

Earlier on Tuesday, Miller announced on social media he planned to ask the committee to look into the allegations.

"In light of all the renewed interest in my family affairs I am going to file my own paperwork for an ethics investigation into myself to clear my name from these horrific attacks on myself and family. I have absolutely nothing to hide," he wrote.

Miller, who is seeking a third term in the House, has been locked in an acrimonious and public custody battle with his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, who is the daughter of Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio.

Moreno filed for divorce from Miller in 2024 after two years of marriage, with Moreno accusing Miller of violent and abusive behavior. According to court records filed earlier this year, she has alleged that Moreno scalded her by throwing hot water at her body, pushed her against a wall, and even once held a gun to her head. She also says he fractured their young daughter's collarbone.

Miller has denied the allegations, saying in a video posted to social media over the weekend that he has never been physically abusive toward Moreno. He denied ever holding a gun to her head and discussed the water incident as "horseplay" with water from a kitchen sink hose.

Sponsor Message

"My former wife is engaging in a pattern of reporting incredible serious and destructive allegations with absolutely no evidence," Miller said.

Addressing allegations of child abuse, Miller said, "I have never abused our daughter."

His video drew a sharp rebuke from Sen. Moreno, who posted on social media that Miller "needs serious psychological help."

"He is a danger to my daughter, and I hold my breath every minute he has custody of my granddaughter. If there are any basic standards of character required to hold elected office," he continued, "Max Miller fails them."

Miller has said he intends to stay in the race for the northeast Ohio seat, but has faced pressure to dropout as Republicans look to preserve their paper-thin majority in this fall's midterm elections.

Miller won the seat by 15 points in 2024, but some GOP officials fear the controversy has positioned his Democratic opponent, union ironworker Brian Poindexter, to flip the seat.

World.title: The soaring demand for Patriot missiles, from the Middle East to Ukraine
World.content:
The soaring demand for Patriot missiles, from the Middle East to Ukraine

toggle caption Efrem Lukatsky/AP

KYIV, Ukraine, and WASHINGTON — Russia's massive air assault against Ukraine before dawn on Saturday included 27 ballistic missiles, many pounding the capital Kyiv, killing nine people and wounding more than 30. The attack was larger than most, though Russia carries out airstrikes almost every night.

What made this notable was Ukraine's inability to defend itself. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the military shot down just one of those Russian missiles.

"Only one ballistic missile was intercepted, simply because there are no interceptors for the Patriot systems," the Ukrainian leader wrote on social media.

Zelenskyy was referring to the U.S.-made Patriot air defense system that is the country's only reliable way to defend against Russian ballistic missile attacks. Ukraine has been largely helpless in similar Russian onslaughts in recent weeks.

Sponsor Message

Ukraine faces the most urgent need for a fresh supply of Patriot interceptors. But the U.S. also has concerns about its own stockpiles of Patriots, which have declined dramatically during the war in Iran.

In addition, U.S. allies in the Gulf are also wondering when they will be able to get more Patriots if there's renewed fighting with Iran and they exhaust their current inventories.

U.S. stockpiles shrink

In June, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth called news reports about a shortage of Patriot missiles a "manufactured story." However, two months earlier, Hegseth acknowledged that replenishing missile stockpiles could take "months and years."

The Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington said in July that the U.S. had more than 2,300 Patriots before President Trump launched the Iran war on Feb. 28. Today, the number is around 800.

The exact number of Patriot interceptors is classified, but a U.S. official, who spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the issue, told NPR that the CSIS figures appeared accurate.

toggle caption Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

The U.S. military introduced the Patriot system in the 1980s and it received its first big test in the 1991 Gulf War when the U.S. used it to defend against Iraqi Scud missiles.

Now, nearly 20 countries allied with the U.S. — in Europe, Asia and the Middle East — have the Patriot system and depend on it to defend against ballistic missiles, one of the most powerful conventional weapons.

However, the Russians and the Iranians have been firing ballistic missiles in numbers that outpace the rate at which Patriot interceptors are being produced.

Sponsor Message

Raytheon (now RTX) makes the Patriot missile battery, as well as the missiles it uses. Lockheed Martin also makes missiles for the Patriot, which run around $4 million each. Together they have been making fewer than 1,000 a year, which seemed to be enough until demand surged with the Russia-Ukraine and the U.S.-Iran wars.

The two American companies plan to ramp up production, though it's not clear how long it will take to replace — or perhaps increase — inventories worldwide.

Ukraine appeals for help

Ukraine began receiving the Patriot air defense batteries three years ago and has used them effectively to limit the damage caused by Russian attacks. Ukraine views the Patriot as critical to its defense and has repeatedly asked for both more of the Patriot systems and the missiles that go with them.

"The Patriot system has really been the main ballistic missile defense system. It's a really big stockpile problem. I don't know if there's any immediate solution," said Rob Lee, a U.S. military analyst living in Ukraine and working with the Foreign Policy Research Institute of Philadelphia.

Zelenskyy is now making an urgent plea for other countries to send some of their Patriot missiles to Ukraine. He says they shouldn't be stockpiled for "hypothetical scenarios, but used here and now, to contain and stop the Russian war."

So far, no country has publicly pledged to send any more missiles to Ukraine.

A pledge by Trump, who then backtracked

At last month's NATO summit in Turkey, Trump told Zelenskyy he'd give Ukraine the license to build its own Patriots.

After they met last week at the White House, Zelenskyy headed straight to talks with Lockheed Martin to discuss moving the process along.

But last Friday, Trump backpedaled.

"We have to be very careful about letting somebody build them," Trump said. "You have to be very judicious, but you have to be very careful. Now, we have not agreed to that. We're talking about it. But it's a hard thing to give away that kind of technology."

Rep. Don Bacon, a Nebraska Republican and former Air Force general who is a member of the House Armed Services Committee, said he still supports allowing Ukraine to build its own Patriots.

Sponsor Message

"While 70 percent of Americans support Ukraine, the policies of the White House make them appear to be in the 30 percent. Enabling the Ukrainians to build the Patriot would have helped relieve the shortage of interceptors we face today," Bacon told Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty earlier this week. "I wish the president was more of a Reagan or Churchill when it comes to Russia."

But even if Ukraine gets a license to build Patriots, it would likely take several years before those missiles came off the production line. That's because of a stretched supply chain for missile components, according to U.S. officials and analysts.

Germany and Japan are the only countries that have been granted licenses by the U.S. to make Patriots.

The U.S. has another highly advanced missile interceptor, called THAAD (Terminal High Altitude Area Defense). The U.S. has only shared this system with Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

The U.S. has also used many of these missiles in the Iran war. The CSIS report said the U.S. stockpiles for THAAD missiles went from around 450 before the Iran war to about 250 today.

Greg Myre reported from Kyiv and Tom Bowman from Washington.

World.title: Senate Democrats say banks turned blind eye to suspicious moves by Jeffrey Epstein
World.content:
Senate Democrats say banks turned blind eye to suspicious moves by Jeffrey Epstein

toggle caption Martin Bureau/AFP

A report from Senate Democrats says big U.S. banks had concerns for years about money moves made by Jeffrey Epstein — but largely kept those worries to themselves until after Epstein was arrested on sex-trafficking charges in 2019.

The report from Democrats on the Senate Finance Committee, which was released by Sen. Ron Wyden of Oregon, says more than a dozen bankers at JPMorganChase, Bank of America and Deutsche Bank were aware of suspicious transactions Epstein made as far back as 2002.

But in most cases, the report alleges bankers failed to alert the Treasury Department until years later, after Epstein was arrested and charged with sex-trafficking. The report is based on a review of Treasury reports, internal bank records and legal filings.

Sponsor Message

Under the Bank Secrecy Act, bankers are supposed to notify the government whenever they suspect a client is moving funds to launder money or carry out other illegal activities.

"By failing to report—or choosing not to report — his suspicious financial transactions to federal law enforcement, these banks allowed Epstein to send cash payments and wire transfers to his victims, friends, and collaborators around the world," the report says. "The bankers who needed to be asking questions didn't ask them. Jeffrey Epstein's crimes were hiding in plain sight."

Dems are seeking answers

The report points to thousands of transactions over nearly two decades and totaling more than a billion dollars. Some of the claims were previously reported by The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and Bloomberg.

Committee Democrats want the Justice Department to investigate why suspicious activity reports were not filed about Epstein in a more timely manner. They also call for tightening reporting requirements in the future.

"If federal prosecutors are serious about preventing the next Jeffrey Epstein, they must hold Wall Street accountable," the report says.

Deutsche Bank responded to the report with a statement saying it regrets its historical connection to Epstein.

"The bank takes its legal obligations seriously," a spokesperson said in a statement to NPR. "We have cooperated with regulatory and law enforcement agencies regarding their investigations and have been transparent in addressing deficiencies and investing in strengthening our control environment in parallel."

Sponsor Message

Bank of America denied any wrongdoing.

"We take our legal and regulatory obligations seriously and, as we have previously said, the bank did not facilitate wrongdoing," a spokesperson said in a statement to NPR.

JPMorganChase did not respond to a request for comment. The bank dropped Epstein as a client in 2013 due to human trafficking concerns, the report says, but the bank didn't report suspicious transactions to the government until six years later, shortly after Epstein's arrest.

World.title: Veteran Canadian broadcaster Lloyd Robertson dead at 92
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Lloyd Robertson, who delivered the news to Canadians in an authoritative and unflappable manner for more than 40 years as anchor for the flagship news programs of CTV and CBC, has died. He was 92.

His death was first reported by CTV and was confirmed by a family member to CBC News.

Robertson stepped away as CTV National News anchor in 2011 after 35 years, having joined the network in a move from CBC that reshaped Canadian broadcast news. He had been anchor of CBC's The National for six years.

"Someone came along with this … on my terms, in my life at precisely the right moment, and it was irresistible. I couldn't turn it down," he told CBC's Take 30 in 1976, days after accepting the offer.

At CTV, Robertson helped lead coverage of 11 federal elections, three Canadian-hosted Olympic Games and two Quebec referendums, as well as tragedies like the 1985 Air India bombing, 1989 Montreal massacre and the Sept. 11 attacks. He also helped share inspiring stories such as Terry Fox's Marathon of Hope.

WATCH | Robertson announces retirement: Lloyd Robertson retires | Duration 3:50 CTV anchor stepping down after decades-long career, including 22 years at CBC

Robertson frequently spoke of enjoying being at the centre of attention for events shaping Canada and the world, but his on-air style was once accurately described as "self-effacing and lacking in the watch-me swagger of most news anchors," by Globe and Mail television critic John Doyle.

Robertson was "the guy with the smallest ego I've ever seen in the television business, when he has a right to the largest one," Henry Kowalski, former CTV news chief, told the same newspaper in 2001.

"He was not just a fine journalist but a fine person," said Peter Mansbridge, former chief correspondent for CBC News, describing Robertson as a "friend and colleague of mine for more than 50 years.

"His audience believed him, and they trusted him. He set the bar for those who anchored newscasts across the country, and he will always be remembered for that.”

In addition to a number of industry awards during his career, he was inducted as an officer into the Order of Canada in 1997 and into the Canadian News Hall of Fame for the Canadian Journalism Foundation in 2016.

"If you find something that you love to do, and you're able to do it, that's about as good as it gets in life," Robertson said in a 2012 CTV documentary And That's the Life I Led.

WATCH | Robertson reports on new skateboarding fad in 1965: The scoop on 'skurfing' | Duration 2:19 The teenage president of the Ontario branch of the National Sidewalk Surfers of Canada explains her organization's reason for being.

Robertson was born in Stratford, Ont., on Jan. 19, 1934, to parents George and Lilly, the youngest of their two children by nine years. He also had eight older half-siblings from the first marriage of his father, whose ancestors emigrated from Scotland in the mid-19th century.

He hung on the advice and political musings of his father, a Canadian National Railway machinist, and the pair enjoyed radio comedies together.

But it was often a "dreary home life," he wrote in his 2012 memoir The Kind of Life It's Been, owing to his British mother's struggles with mental illness. Prone to bouts of paranoia and obsessive-compulsive behaviour, she would be lobotomized when he was 14, quelling her mind to a degree but dulling her emotional connection with her son.

"I couldn't have kids to the house, I couldn't tell them about her," he told CBC's George Stroumboulopoulos Tonight in 2012.

WATCH | Mansbridge surprises Robertson on Strombo:

High school classmates, in the 2012 CTV documentary that accompanied his memoir, remembered a friend who gave little sign of turmoil. Robertson was popular, participating in debate and a barbershop quartet at Stratford Central Secondary School.

22-year run at CBC

Already gifted with a smooth voice, he'd been intrigued by radio after standing near reporters covering a post-war parade in his hometown in 1946.

"I just remember being fascinated by the voices of the two commentators as they painted vivid pictures of the marchers and the joyous crowds," he wrote in his memoir.

At just 17, he persuaded Stratford radio station CJCS to give him an opportunity, overcoming an early on-air bungled pronunciation of the city name as "Strat-herd."

He didn't consider going beyond high school, learning the craft of radio at private stations in Stratford and Guelph, before beginning a 22-year run with the public broadcaster in 1954 in Windsor.

WATCH | Robertson anchors CBC in 1970: Lloyd Robertson, rookie news anchor | Duration 1:43 Lloyd Robertson was an anchor at the CBC before he became the face of CTV News.

For Robertson, 1956 was a momentous year — his elderly father died just months after he landed at CBC Winnipeg for his first foray into television.

That year he also married Nancy Barrett, a high school sweetheart with whom he had remained in touch. The couple would welcome four daughters born in Winnipeg, Ottawa and Toronto, reflecting Robertson's peripatetic, upward climb.

In his memoir, he remembered his four-plus years in Winnipeg as "among my happiest and most productive," and he even donned Western garb to host the country-flavoured Saddle Songs. He then honed political chops with a two-year stint with CBC Ottawa — though it wasn't all Parliament Hill business, as he hosted a show about the CFL's Ottawa Rough Riders.

Robertson stands with his star at Canada's Walk of Fame in Toronto in June 2007. (Mark Blinch/Reuters)

In 1962 came an offer from the corporation the couple couldn't refuse, and another move. Robertson would remember being at the "bottom of the pile" of 30 announcers, all male, at CBC Toronto.

Robertson would separate himself over time, displaying adaptability by hosting a kid's show, the athletics program Kaleidosport, and a host of news and magazine programs. Many Canadian radio listeners first heard of John F. Kennedy's assassination in 1963 from Robertson, and he would score high-profile network assignments for the 1964 Tokyo Olympics and Expo '67 in Montreal.

Robertson was cool and collected on air, but admitted years later that co-anchoring the 1969 moon shot by U.S. astronauts gave him pause.

Robertson is seen in Toronto in December 2001. (Aaron Harris/The Canadian Press)

"I had to pinch myself to be sure I was really living through this momentous time," he wrote.

Robertson would be rewarded with the network's plum assignment of anchoring The National in late 1970. It was a baptism by fire, as within days the Front de libération du Québec would plunge the province and country into crisis, kidnapping British diplomat James Cross and ultimately killing provincial minister Pierre Laporte.

CBC's news and current affairs roster was deep in the first years of that decade — future Canadian news anchors Peter Kent, Peter Trueman, Peter Mansbridge and Jan Tennant, along with budding stars like Adrienne Clarkson, Barbara Frum and Alex Trebek.

But there were also increasingly outdated union strictures involving studio and field work. Robertson once shared his workplace frustrations with Walter Cronkite on a trip to U.S. He recounted that the CBS news titan was incredulous that CBC anchors couldn't write their own copy, and were limited in reporting outside of the studio.

Move to CTV

In a time where NBC and ABC were employing multi-anchor formats in the U.S., Robertson was promised more freedom upon joining CTV National News in 1976, even as Harvey Kirck remained on the desk.

"Life with Harvey was sometimes tumultuous, occasionally precarious, but never dull," he wrote in his memoir of a co-anchor he described as loyal, but who caused the news division headaches with impaired driving citations.

Robertson adjusted to private-sector reality — more commercials, and local affiliates with clout — but he was welcomed by colleagues.

WATCH | Robertson on why he moved to CTV: Career change for Lloyd Robertson | Duration 1:39 The CBC's Larry Stout learns why money wasn't the only thing that motivated Lloyd Robertson to leave CBC for CTV. Aired on CBC's The National on June 21, 1976.

"What Lloyd did is [he] gave us instant credibility, and our numbers began to climb, and we've never retreated, really," said Craig Oliver, a top CTV political reporter and off-air friend, in 2012.

Kirck's departure in 1984 established Robertson's pre-eminence. Around the same time, coincidentally, he was approached by the Conservative Party to run as an MP. He wrote years the prospect held "some appeal," but he rebuffed that entreaty, and one by the Liberal Party in the early 2000s to serve as a senator.

By the 1990s, Roberton was ending the newscast with what would become a trademark: "And that's the kind of day it's been." He was firmly established as an éminence grise in the industry, winning three Geminis that decade for best host, anchor or interviewer.

Robertson initiated a plan to step back from anchoring in 1996 and give way to CTV reporter Keith Morrison, but, he wrote years later, it imploded due to a combination of corporate resistance and misunderstandings. He expressed regret that the personal relationship with Morrison was ruptured beyond repair.

Robertson would still be in the anchor chair in the next decade and beyond, pulling a 14-hour shift on Sept. 11, 2001, the day of the terrorist attacks on U.S. soil by Islamist militants.

"The magnitude of this crisis is truly breathtaking," he told viewers. He admitted to The Canadian Press that days later his voice "may have been trembling a little bit," describing the scene as tens of thousands who had gathered on Parliament Hill for several minutes of silence in honour of what would be nearly 3,000 innocent victims, including 24 Canadians.

PHOTOS | Robertson through the years:

Robertson tributes flowed in 2010, and the year after, as he gave a year's notice of his intention to leave the anchor post.

"I've never seen Lloyd angry," Kent, then a federal politician, marvelled at the time. "Lloyd is a gentleman and a paragon of integrity."

Robertson remained with the network for several more years, contributing to investigative program W5, and he continued charitable work that included raising awareness of mental illness.

He was able to spend more time with his children and grandchildren, who were used to that sometimes-booming baritone.

"There's a line that we use: 'Dad, I'm in the room,'" daughter Susan Robertson told CTV in 2012. "But that's his trademark, that's his voice."

While straight-laced on air, Robertson wasn't overly fussy with his image, appearing in comedic skits with the Royal Canadian Air Farce, and with Drake in a taped segment for the Juno Awards. As to SCTV's newscaster "Floyd Robertson," he told CBC he thought the portrayal by Joe Flaherty was "marvelous."

World.title: U.S. to close Winnipeg consulate as cost-saving measure, Trump administration says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Plans to close the U.S. Consulate in Winnipeg mean the United States will "lose touch with a broad swath of Canada," a former employee says.

The U.S. State Department is planning a phased closure of the consulate, with its diplomatic engagement responsibilities to be transferred to the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa, a spokesperson told CBC News on Tuesday.

The decision reflects the State Department's "commitment to efficient resource management," the spokesperson said. They did not offer a timeline of when the closure will begin.

The Winnipeg consulate is the only closure in North America. It's among five smaller embassies and consulates set to close in order to streamline operations, U.S. President Donald Trump's administration informed Congress last week.

The diplomatic post in Winnipeg doesn't offer consular or visa services but does have a representative tasked with building trade relations and advancing U.S. policy.

Brad Kirbyson, a former political and economic specialist who worked in the consulate in Winnipeg for 20 years, says the move means the U.S. will lose "direct contact with a significant part of Canada."

"I'm sure it'll save them a few dollars, but I think the net effect is to lose touch with a broad swath of Canada by not having a presence there," he said Tuesday.

Kirbyson, who started working at the consulate after it reopened in 2001, says it's only rational to have one in Winnipeg as they can help to provide and resolve early warnings of potential trade issues.

"The United States found that it was a very long way between the U.S. Consulate in Calgary and the [one] in Toronto," Kirbyson said. "It makes a lot of sense to have a consulate in the middle of the country that can cover issues in this part of the world."

He said he's disappointed by the announcement and hopes the U.S. will reconsider.

Eyes turn to Manitoba's Washington trade rep

The planned closure comes amid tensions between Premier Wab Kinew and the U.S., particularly over tariffs imposed by Trump, with Manitoba retaliating earlier this year by announcing it will no longer import U.S.-made alcohol.

Kinew has called Trump's policies "dumb" and has labelled the president "Enemy No. 1" when it comes to the economy.

The province is working to stand up for Manitoba workers and businesses through its U.S. trade council, a provincial spokesperson told CBC News in a statement.

The province reopened its trade office in Washington, and the consulate's closure " does not change its role ," the spokesperson said.

Manitoba's Opposition says the closure is disappointing and underscores Kinew's failure to get things done on cross-border trade.

Progressive Conservative Leader Obby Khan says despite Kinew's government spending nearly $1 million a year on a Washington, D.C., trade office, it has failed to deliver new investment or trade deals.

Chuck Davidson, CEO of the Manitoba Chambers of Commerce, told CBC News in a statement it's too early to say what the impact of the closure will be on Manitoba.

However, he said Manitoba's Washington trade representative would serve as an advantage if Winnipeg's U.S. Consulate closed.

The trade representative to the U.S. will become a "more crucial position," said André Brin, CEO of the World Trade Centre in Winnipeg.

"Should this materialize, then this person has, to me, an additional responsibility of sort of keeping Manitoba on their radar in the U.S., and then we have the responsibility of doing that in Canada," he said Tuesday.

André Brin, CEO of the World Trade Centre in Winnipeg, says plans to close the consulate in Winnipeg should serve as a reminder for Canada not to rely on the U.S. economically. (Jeff Stapleton/CBC)

Brin says the move to close the Winnipeg office is "not ideal" as it will add to the responsibilities of other U.S. Consulates in Canada.

"I think it's not the right decision."

Brin says although the U.S. Consulate is the smallest in Canada, it helps Manitoba companies connect with opportunities while also helping American companies that want to do business in the province.

"It was mostly that constant dialogue of understanding," he said. "We need to keep those lines of communication open."

The news should serve as a reminder for Canada not to rely on the U.S. economically, Brin said.

"I think we should be looking at other countries that don't have consuls here."

WATCH | Winnipeg consulate to close, U.S. government says: U.S. State Department says it's closing Winnipeg consulate | Duration 2:15 The United States government says it is streamlining operations by closing five foreign missions — including its consulate in Winnipeg, which facilitates trade relationships. Experts say businesses on both sides of the border might bear the brunt of the closure.

A professor says any disruption would be a bigger loss for the U.S.

The diplomatic post in Winnipeg serves as the "eyes and ears of Americans" to keep tabs on what's going on in the region, said Bryan Peeler, an associate professor with the University of Manitoba's political sciences department.

"Americans will still get this information, most likely, but it's going to be from someone in Washington now. So, it's not gonna be as accurate."

CBC News has reached out to Global Affairs Canada for comment but did not hear back before publication.

World.title: Alberta Forestry and Parks charged over 2024 death of man battling Jasper wildfire
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Two years after a man died while fighting a wildfire in Jasper National Park, workplace safety charges have been laid against Alberta's Ministry of Forestry and Parks in connection with his death.

Morgan Kitchen, 24, of Calgary was fatally struck by a tree on Aug. 3, 2024, while working as a wildland firefighter after the Jasper townsite went up in flames.

Charges laid against the ministry — Kitchen’s employer — revolve around a string of alleged workplace safety violations under Alberta’s Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) Act.

The six charges, laid on July 29, allege the Alberta government failed to ensure the safety of workers by not adequately assessing and controlling hazards at the worksite and also failing to adequately train workers.

OHS also alleged the province failed to take reasonable steps to prevent harm, like cutting down hazardous trees or establishing a no-work zone.

James Gault is a vice-president of the Alberta Union of Provincial Employees (AUPE), which represents wildland firefighters like Kitchen. He said the AUPE is glad OHS is pursuing charges against the province.

“Our members are in dangerous situations,” he told CBC News on Tuesday.

WATCH | Kitchen, 24, dies after being fatally struck by tree: What we know about the death of a 24-year-old firefighter near Jasper | Duration 1:56 The CBC's Alicia Asquith has more on the death of a firefighter who was killed by a falling tree near Jasper, Alta., fighting the fire that has plagued the area for days.

Gault said he believes Kitchen’s death highlights the impact workplace deaths can have on a community, noting the incident left his colleagues shaken.

“What we have to remember first is Morgan Kitchen was a person, right? He's not a statistic,” said Gault.

“It's a reminder that our members face risk every day that they go to work.”

In a statement to CBC News on Tuesday, Arthur Green, press secretary for the Ministry of Public Safety and Emergency Services, said the province is aware charges have been laid against Alberta Forestry and Parks.

Alberta’s government will not comment further on the allegations or legal proceedings as the matter is now before the courts, Green said.

“Our thoughts remain with our Alberta Wildfire colleague’s family, friends and co-workers,” he said. “Safety is our highest priority. We remain committed to providing a safe workplace for our staff.”

In 2024, the Jasper Wildfire Complex Unified Command, composed of members of Parks Canada and the Municipality of Jasper, issued a statement that said Kitchen’s crew administered first aid before Jasper National Park and Alberta Wildfire employees used a wheeled stretcher to bring him to a nearby helipad.

From there, Kitchen was flown to the Parks Canada operations compound in Jasper, where a STARS Air Ambulance helicopter was waiting. He was pronounced dead shortly after.

The 2024 wildfire destroyed 358 structures in the Jasper townsite — about one-third of its total buildings.

World.title: N.L. judge says proposed 4-year prison term too lenient for man who pleaded guilty to impaired driving causing death
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Newfoundland and Labrador provincial court judge has rejected a four-year prison sentence for a man who has pleaded guilty to impaired driving causing death, saying the sentence would be too lenient.

The Crown and defence representing Rodney Constantine agreed on a four-year sentence in a joint submission, which Crown prosecutor Deidre Badcock said was picked to avoid a trial and further the burden on the family of the victim.

However, on Tuesday Judge Bruce Short said he couldn't accept the joint submission.

"I put this to counsel: How can four years be adequate in this case?" Short asked. "I am going to give you an opportunity to come back and present the court something that more accurately reflects these circumstances."

Constantine has pleaded guilty to impaired driving causing the death of Mark Squires.

The incident occurred on Dec. 10, 2023. The court heard that Constantine could have had as many as 15 drinks before getting behind the wheel after a fight with his ex-girlfriend. Squires and his brother, Andrew, got in the car with Constantine.

Constantine was driving erratically, the court heard, and was travelling between 125 and 165 km/h before crashing into a house on Empire Avenue in St. John’s.

The court heard through Andrew Squires that his brother was screaming and crying for Constantine to stop the car and let him out. Not long after, the car hit the house, flipped sideways, and a fire broke out.

Squires was pronounced dead at the scene.

Constantine 'hasn't taken any' steps to improve: Judge

Much of Short's decision to reject the joint submission hinged on the fact police say they saw Constantine driving while suspended in the months after Squires' death.

Constantine has been banned from driving until 2085, but the court heard on Tuesday that police observed Constantine driving on two separate occasions in June 2024 — around six months after the incident.

Short heard that Constantine was pulled over on June 4, 2024, after intentionally trying to tailgate a vehicle. Police said he was found with just under $5,000 in cash in the car, along with a package of cocaine.

"Mere months after this event, he's caught twice by the police, firstly violating a heavy prohibition from driving. And even more so, driving in a manner that shows a complete disregard of safety of anyone else on the road," Short said.

WATCH | 'How can four years be adequate?' Judge asks counsel in court: Judge says four-year sentence for impaired driving is too short in rejection of man's sentencing submission | Duration 2:34 A judge in provincial court in St. John's rejected a four-year prison sentence for Rodney Constantine on Tuesday, telling the Crown and defence it is too lenient for the case. The CBC's Alex Kennedy was in the courtroom and has this report.

Short also addressed something he said he didn't hear in the defence's submission — steps Constantine is taking to improve himself.

"I suspect there's a reason why … because he hasn't taken any," Short said.

Mark Squires is seen here holding his newborn daughter Saje, who was born 19 days before Squires was killed. (Submitted by Seryna Squires)

"It's not about not understanding … It's about not giving a damn."

The Crown and defence will now have over a month to come up with a new sentencing submission, which is scheduled to be heard in court on Sept. 17.

Family heartbroken over new delay

Courtroom one at provincial court in St. John's was standing room only for Tuesday's proceedings. The two rows of seating were occupied by members of Squires's family.

Many wore T-shirts and buttons remembering their "Markie," but they had to be flipped inside out in order to be kept on in the courtroom.

Five victim impact statements were read.

Squires's partner, Celeste England, wrote her life has been turned upside down and she is now raising two young girls on her own.

Squires' youngest daughter, Saje, was born just 19 days before the incident, she wrote.

England also wrote that Squires was about to propose to her, and told the court the story of how she collected her engagement ring on her own in order for it to be refitted.

Members of the Squires family filled the courtroom on Tuesday. (Alex Kennedy/CBC)

Squires' mother, Seryna Squires, said the lives of her family have been put on hold since the incident. She declined to speak with CBC News after court had concluded, but could be seen openly sobbing when it became clear that Constantine wouldn't be sentenced on Tuesday.

In her victim impact statement, Seryna Squires spoke of her son's love for life and his family.

She detailed the last interaction she had with her son. He was getting ready for a Christmas party, she said, and asked her to take a picture of his new outfit. He told her he felt he had truly made it in life, and her last words to him were "I love you too, my son."

Sentencing was supposed to conclude in June, but was delayed until Tuesday when Constantine got new legal representation.

When proceedings were finished for the day, Seryna Squires could be heard saying she was "heartbroken" while being embraced by her family.

Constantine will be remanded in custody until his next appearance on Sept. 17 — a move that brought gasps and tears of joy to members of the family.

World.title: Shock, grief and a city on the edge as St. Catharines, Ont., deals with massive flooding
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Jennifer Chrysler-Loney, her husband and her 12-year-old son were dealing with water pouring into their south St. Catharines, Ont., home from a storm pounding the area when a tornado warning lit up their phones.

Chrysler-Loney and her son grabbed the family dog, batteries, chargers and flashlights, intending to rush to the basement for shelter, when she looked out the bay window in their kitchen overlooking the towering Niagara Escarpment her home backs on to.

The window imploded on us. It was horrendous. It was just chaos. - Jennifer Chrysler-Loney, St. Catharines resident

"The floor of the escarpment was flattening," she told CBC News. "It was like a tsunami coming down the escarpment. It was barrelling towards our house."

They desperately tried to hold back the floodwaters that filled the window well and poured into the house, dumping buckets of water into sinks.

But the force of the massive wall of water was too much.

"The window imploded on us," Chrysler-Loney said. "It was horrendous. It was just chaos.

"It was like Niagara Falls. There was no holding it back."

Seeing the vast amounts of water pour in was surreal for the family.

"It's like standing out in the street and watching our house burn," said Chrysler-Loney.

'A lot of panic, followed by stages of grief'

The shock is being felt across the city, which experienced massive flooding along with neighbouring Niagara-on-the-Lake from a July 28 storm. Then, St. Catharines was hit again, on the weekend, prompting a state of emergency.

St. Catharines Mayor Mat Siscoe hasn't just watched the crisis unfold for others: his home was flooded in the first storm, and on Sunday night, it was again overwhelmed with water and sewage shooting up from a drain like a geyser.

"It's a lot of panic, followed by stages of grief," Siscoe told a Tuesday news conference about the first flooding. On Sunday, foul sewer water once again bubbled up into his home, this time even worse.

"You just feel defeated," he said.

St. Catharines Mayor Mat Siscoe said the flooding has hit thousands of homes. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

Siscoe, who declared a state of emergency Monday, said some residents have had their homes flooded three times in two weeks after storms on July 21, 27 and 28 dumped almost 400 millimetres of rain on St. Catharines.

"I recognize the exhaustion and the uncertainty, the emotional toll that this is taking on folks in our community and their families."

The heavy rain saturated the ground, creeks overflowed, catch basins swelled and sewers simply unable to push through water fast enough backed up into residences.

Siscoe said the flooding has hit thousands of homes.

Residents clear out damaged furniture and belongings from their basements after flooding hit homes in the city’s north end. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

"I've driven through entire neighbourhoods where every single house was dealing with it, and that was [before] Sunday night. There are entire neighbourhoods where the driveways are filled with construction debris and furniture that's been destroyed.

"There were cars floating down the street."

Every worker in his office has had their homes flooded, and most of them will need basement tear-outs, said Siscoe.

Dave Upper, chief of the St. Catharines fire department, told reporters Tuesday that firefighters had to pull off a dramatic rescue on Sunday when several cars with people inside got stranded in deep, flooding water on Ontario Street in front of a park. Over the course of the two storms, firefighters were also swamped with calls from people facing problems such as their homes' electrical systems short-circuiting.

"I've been here for over 30 years now and in my career, I've never seen this happen," Upper said. 'We've had flooding we've never seen before in the city."

Highrise tenants evacuated a 2nd time

Those displaced by the flooding include hundreds of people at a highrise on Geneva Street. They were evacuated a week ago when the building's power and water were knocked out.

Robert Burke said he and other tenants were finally let back into their homes on Friday night, but evacuated again on Sunday night.

Upper said his department worked with the Red Cross and the City of Niagara Falls to get shelter for the Geneva Street building's tenants at the MacBain Community Centre in Niagara Falls.

Mitch St. Hilaire said his mother's and stepdad's home in the Port Weller neighbourhood was flooded "catastrophically" on June 28 and again Sunday night. He sent CBC photos of the basement showing it with high levels of dark brown fluid.

"To experience two catastrophic floods within five days is something none of us ever imagined possible," he said.

St. Hilaire said he was unable to help because he's in Tokyo.

"[It ]makes this particularly anguishing for me as I watch helplessly."

Siscoe said many people might be questioning the city's infrastructure or wondering whether blockages or other problems caused the flooding. But he noted that the city has tripled its spending on wastewater infrastructure in recent years, and doubted if any city system in Canada could have handled that much rain.

"It's just not possible."

Siscoe is calling on the Ontario and federal governments to provide St. Catharines with immediate assistance, and help communities pay for upgrading critical stormwater infrastructure to better prepare for such devastating storms.

St. Catharines Mayor Mat Siscoe, who also spoke to reporters on Tuesday, wants the Ontario and federal governments to provide the city with immediate assistance and help communities pay for upgrading critical stormwater infrastructure. (Diona Macalinga/CBC)

On Sunday night, Siscoe posted a video of his flooded basement on Facebook, saying "a hurricane's worth" of rain fell that night alone.

"There has been no disaster relief assistance offered by either the provincial or the federal government," he said."The city has been left to fend for itself."

The nearby Town of Lincoln was also hit hard with flooding, prompting another state of emergency, this one declared by Mayor Sandra Easton.

Niagara Centre riding MPP Jeff Burch wrote to Siscoe on Tuesday, urging him to work with Niagara Region to extend temporary, unlimited garbage pickup — put in place until Aug. 14 due to the flooding — to the entire city, saying many south-end homes were also drenched.

Burch said he'll also meet with Municipal Affairs Minister Rob Flack to discuss the province's Disaster Recovery Assistance for Ontarians program for Niagara.

The program pays up to $250,000 to people, farmers, small businesses and non-profit agencies for emergency expenses, repairs and replacing essential property after natural disasters such as floods, tornadoes, landslides and earthquakes. It generally doesn't cover damage from sewer backups, except for a provision in which low-income households may qualify.

Michael Minzak, issues manager and press secretary for Flack, said in a statement Monday that the Ministry of Municipal Affairs and Housing is working with the City of St. Catharines to assess storm-related damage and determine whether there are any areas affected by overflowing creeks, rivers or lakes where uninsured damage could be eligible for assistance under the program.

He also said Ministry of Emergency Preparedness and Response officials are assessing a request for help from the city "to determine appropriate provincial resources to assist."

With rain forecast for seven more consecutive days in St. Catharines starting Thursday, Siscoe said it's understandable many people are on edge about how much the infrastructure can handle.

"We understand that residents are anxious when rain is forecast," he said. "We recognize that confidence has been shaken."

World.title: 'There's a creature in our garage': Mountain marmot hitches ride to Calgary-area home
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Chris Ratzlaff tells The National about the moment a marmot secretly hitched a ride on his truck from Kananaskis to Airdrie, Alta.

Marmot hitchhikes to the suburbs from the mountains |The Moment

An Airdrie, Alta., man brought back more than memories from a trip to the mountains last week.

When Chris Ratzlaff's son told him there was "a creature" in the garage, he thought it might be a muskrat or some other common mammal, but it turned out to be a hoary marmot — a large rodent only found in the mountains.

"It wandered my neighbourhood for about a week," Ratzlaff told the CBC Radio's Calgary Eyeopener.

"I had neighbours who were posting sightings in the community Facebook group," he said. "They were posting sightings of it moving around the neighbourhood, and then Saturday morning, my wife came back into the house from the garage and said, 'There's a creature in our garage.'"

He hadn't expected the marmot to find its way back to the garage.

"For it to come back, my guess is that it was looking for its ride home," Ratzlaff said.

A hoary marmot in Kananaskis Country, where the large rodents are a common sight. (Amir Said/CBC)

Hoary marmots are a common sight in Kananaskis Country west of Calgary, where Ratzlaff had been hiking when the rodent got into his car.

He called the Calgary Wildlife Rehabilitation Society, who sent someone to pick up the marmot.

The group will keep the marmot for a few more days to assess its health, and will then return it to Kananaskis.

A reminder to check your vehicle

This is far from the first time Calgary Wildlife Rehabilitation Society executive director Beki Hunt has heard of this happening.

"It's pretty common," she said. "Marmots are attracted to the minerals and the taste of anti-freeze that comes out of the cars."

The group has a marmot named Marmalade, who ended up in their care in 2021 after being found as a baby in a car wash.

Meet Marmalade the marmot:

"Same thing: hitched a ride back to the city, and then when they went to wash their car when they returned, she was washed off," Hunt said.

"She had some brain trauma, so wouldn't be able to be successfully released back into the wild, so we've kept her as an education ambassador."

Hunt hopes Marmalade's story helps raise awareness about marmot hitchhiking.

"She goes into schools and teaches kids just about that: to remind their parents if they're going hiking to bang on the roof or the hood of their car, maybe honk the horn, open the hood to make sure there's nothing in there."

Alberta is home to two marmot species: the hoary marmot, found in alpine terrain, and the yellow-bellied marmot, a slightly smaller rodent found in more arid regions like Lethbridge and along the Milk River.

World.title: One man found dead after mid-air plane collision in Chilliwack, B.C.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

One man has been found dead after a mid-air collision between two aircraft on Monday in Chilliwack, B.C., according to an RCMP statement.

RCMP said one plane was located in a pond near Access Road, near Chilliwack Airport, and the RCMP Underwater Recovery Team located the body in the water.

Occupants of the second plane did not sustain any injuries and made it safely back to the airport in the second plane, police said in a statement Tuesday afternoon.

The Transportation Safety Board (TSB) said it is deploying investigators after two Cessna 172 aircraft crashed in mid-air near Chilliwack Airport.

Five ambulances were dispatched to the area of Wolfe Road and Schweyey Road, according to B.C. Emergency Health Services.

It said the call came in at about 5:15 p.m. PT and no patients were taken to hospital.

The TSB, an independent agency with a mandate to advance transportation safety, said in a statement its team will arrive on site Tuesday afternoon to gather information and assess the crash.

CBC News has reached out to Chilliwack SAR and the Chilliwack Airport for more information.

World.title: Colombia’s left presents evidence suggesting De la Espriella won through fraud
World.content:
Colombia’s President Gustavo Petro and data analysts presented evidence suggesting that President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella won the election through the mass manipulation of tally sheets.

During a two-hour presentation, Petro claimed that almost all tally sheets that had been shared with his political party, the Historic Pact “lacked the Hash security lock,” which is inserted into official PDF documents to guarantee they can’t be changed.

The absence of a hash file implies that the so-called E14 tally sheets may have been altered, which appears to have happened, according to data analysts who accompanied the president.

Legal expert William Villanueva said that original tally sheets were scanned and subsequently reprocessed, removing the metadata that would allow them to determine whether the E14’s were uploaded or introduced digitally.

“We found documents marked ‘confidential’… and others that said ‘not digitized’ on a blank page, which—and this is important—were later republished with different information,” said one of the computer scientists.

The investigation, which was carried out by 75,000 “digital witnesses,” found that 95 municipalities had more voters than inhabitants. In all of these municipalities, the E-14’s gave De la Espriella landslide victories with more than 70% of the votes.

The president-elect’s opponent, leftist Senator Ivan Cepeda, achieved not a single victory in hundreds of towns where the electoral census was larger than 85% of the population.

In 1,350 polling centers in capital cities, the researchers found that block patterns in which De la Espriella won the first half of the voting booths and Cepeda won the second half.

According to a consulted statistician, this result would only be probably in some 80 polling stations, said Carlos Oñoro, one of the digital witnesses.

“This order is mathematically impossible for human voters,” Petro stated, arguing that automated software replaced actual citizen ballots.

The findings of the digital witnesses will be added to a lawsuit that seeks to nullify the election of De la Espriella and force the Council of State to order a recount of the votes.

Following the presentation, Cepeda said in a post on social media network X that “the competent authority must impartially examine our demands of nullity.”

World.title: De la Espriella says he won’t allow Colombia’s left to “destabilize democracy”
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella said that he won’t allow his country’s left to “destabilize democracy” through civil disobedience against his US citizenship.

In his weekly address to the nation, De la Espriella stressed that after Friday he will be president and “with the force of the constitution and the law” ensure that his power will be upheld.

The civil disobedience announced by leftist opposition leader Ivan Cepeda “is nothing more than a euphemism for an attempt to destabilize democracy,” said De la Espriella.

“I will not allow it,” said the president-elect.

I am the president of all Colombians, and I will ensure, through the power of the Constitution and the law, that what the Colombian people decided—which was to elect me—is upheld. My call to the entire nation is that we stop normalizing what is wrong, illegal, and corrupt. Let’s call things by their proper names and confront them for what they are. This so-called “civil disobedience” is nothing more than a euphemism for an attempt to destabilize democracy, and I will not allow it. Abelardo de la Espriella

According to De la Espriella, the left “combined all forms of struggle,” a term used by the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC to justify the violence used by the insurgents, “and lost.”

Cepeda called on his followers to peaceful civil disobedience in response to the president-elect’s refusal to renounce his US citizenship.

The incoming opposition leader and his political party, the Historic Pact, support legal efforts to challenge De la Espriella’s election on claims that fraud concerns have not been tackled.

More radical elements within the Historic Pact, including outgoing President Gustavo Petro, have sustained that the far-right won the elections through deceit and fraud, but have failed to present evidence that would confirm a criminal conspiracy.

World.title: As De la Espriella takes office, his US-backed security policy for Colombia is raising questions
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella assumes office on Friday, after elections with a razor-thin margin. He brings with him promises to wield “iron fist” policies against non-state armed groups (NSAGs) and organized criminal organizations in the country.

He has also promised to dismantle ongoing peace talks initiated by outgoing leftist President Gustavo Petro, including groups that are currently disarming. De la Espriella made scores of hardline promises on the campaign trail, many of which he will likely not be able to achieve with a minority coalition in the legislature, such as withdrawing Colombia from the United Nations.

On security issues, however, Colombia’s constitution grants the president broad unilateral powers. De la Espriella has promised to “end” armed groups within a month, an extremely unlikely goal. Despite the broad powers of the presidential office, De la Espriella faces historical and logistical limitations.

Despite claims from right-wing parties that Petro has gone easy on armed groups, Colombia’s military has been fully deployed against NSAGs in the country for the last two years.

As conflict expert Thomas Garrison reported for news website Pirate Wire Services in June, Colombia has ongoing and large military operations against FARC dissident group Estado Mayor Central (EMC), the National Liberation Army (ELN), and EMC splinter-group EMBF.

Colombia’s security forces are “already operating on all cylinders,” and “stretched to their limit,” according to the International Crisis Group. It isn’t clear how deployments can be increased without increasing the numbers of security forces themselves — hardly a goal that can be achieved in his first month in office.

Nonetheless, there are strategic changes that de La Espriella can impose to chart a more aggressive course. As part of those plans, the president-elect has promised to implement a “Plan Patriota remixed”, an allusion to highly aggressive US-backed military operations against armed groups under then-President Alvaro Uribe in 2003.

Uribe’s allies to this day hail Plan Patriota as a great success that forced the FARC to the negotiating table in 2016.

Critics, however, point to rampant human and civil rights violations, including working with paramilitary forces to kill thousands of civilians and frame them as guerrilla fighters to increase casualty counts.

The US, however, is pushing Latin America towards increased military spending and Bukele-style crackdowns on organized crime, and de la Espriella plans to comply.

What was Plan Patriota and how will Abelardo’s version be ‘remixed’?

Plan Patriota involved aerial bombardments, large-scale military deployments in FARC-controlled areas, and aggressive intelligence gathering against FARC guerrillas at the height of Colombia’s civil war.

Although paramilitary groups were not officially part of Plan Patriota, they cooperated closely with regular military forces during the operation, functioning as spies, informants, and death squads — ostensibly killing alleged guerrillas, but just as often murdering leftists in general, as well as non-politically involved civilians.

The operation, which continued until 2010, weakened the FARC considerably, but at a great price: gross human rights violations including massacres, torture, and using sexual violence against civilians as a weapon of war.

Paramilitary structures were also greatly empowered across the country, sowing the seeds of groups that still exist today, such as the Ejercito Gaitanista Colombiano (EGC) — often referred to in Western media as ‘the Clan del Golfo.’

The full extent of the atrocities committed by both sides of the war would not become clear until Colombia launched its Truth Commission in 2017. (De la Espriella wants to disband the Truth Commission as well as the Colombian Peace Court, which prosecutes the worst offenders of the civil war.)

Any new version of Plan Patriota would look very different. Colombia is not the same country it was in the early 2000’s. Modern armed groups are not interested in clashing with state forces on the battlefield. Most are not interested in overthrowing the state at all, and certainly not via military victory.

Technology has also advanced considerably. Drone warfare is a dangerous new weapon in the arsenal of NSAGs who wage asymmetrical attacks on state forces as well as one another. Digital surveillance and satellite optics also mean that unlike the FARC, which often relied upon jungle canopies to hide large training and logistics camps, modern NSAGs instead blend into civil society in the communities where they operate.

They do not wear uniforms to distinguish themselves and avoid direct confrontations with the military, which means there are no large targets to bomb, nor columns of marching fighters for the state to confront.

Modern NSAGs are far more flexible, transnational, and relatively decentralized in their operations compared to FARC at the height of the civil war.

De la Espriella’s security program is more likely to look like Daniel Noboa’s policies in Ecuador than the 2002 Plan Patriota. It will likely include US cooperation on target-finding, naval cooperation on drug trafficking, and joint US-Colombia operations within the country.

Most of those dynamics already exist. Despite a rocky relationship with Washington, D.C, Petro continued to cooperate with the US on intelligence-sharing and anti-narcotics operations.

Critics of de la Espriella, however, fear that logistics won’t be the only similarity to Ecuadorian-US operations, which have resulted in the murder of civilians by security forces, torture, arbitrary detentions, and bombings of civilian infrastructure.

One factor that may keep de la Espriella somewhat in check is a lack of a clear mandate. He won elections by less than 1%, and has already clashed with more established right-wing political parties, who will not be forming part of his coalition in the legislature.

De la Espriella signals he will follow Washington’s lead

On a recent trip to the U.S, de la Espriella’s vice-president, José Manuel Restrepo, met with US Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for the Americas, Joseph M. Humire, who spoke of investment by US companies in hydrocarbon and energy sectors as well as cooperation on security and migration issues.

“Colombia is historically one of the U.S. strongest security and defense partners,” he wrote on X on July 21. “Under the leadership of incoming President Abelardo De La Espriella, we plan to take this partnership to new levels with Plan Patriot 2.0.”

Before Humire joined the War Department, he worked as an anti-migration lobbyist propagating conspiracy theories that cartels have “weaponized” migrants as part of “asymmetrical warfare” against the U.S.

He falsely testified before the House Foreign Affairs Committee in February that Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua had “opened” the Darien Gap to migrants during the Biden administration as part of a Venezuelan plan to destabilize the US.

De la Espriella has already signalled that he looks forward to closer cooperation with the administration of US President Donald Trump and largely follow the US lead on regional issues. Trump has made migration a key facet of his domestic and foreign policy.

The ultra-right Colombian president-elect has also promised to “secure” the country’s borders. Migrants “who are here illegally, or committing crimes will be deported to their countries of origin without delay,” he said in a press conference on July 13.

He has agreed, however, to keep commercial and migratory pathways open on the Venezuelan border. Petro re-initiated diplomatic and commercial ties with Venezuela in 2022.

De la Espriella has not criticized Chavista governments as heavily as many other right-wing politicians in the country, and provided legal representation for Maduro loyalist Alex Saab, who has been extradited for a second time to the US to face money laundering and corruption charges.

Aggressive military strategies have failed in the past

The nature of conflict has changed drastically in Colombia since the civil war, and presidents have tried aggressive military tactics against criminal organizations and NSAGs before.

Former President Ivan Duque failed to slow the rapid growth of either during his time in office from 2018 to 2022.

The Colombian state failed to fulfill its promises to invest in legitimate economies and develop regions long ignored by Bogotá. Regions that had previously been governed by the FARC became power vacuums that were quickly filled by other criminal organizations and NSAGs.

Duque left office the least popular president in the country’s history since records have been kept, in part because of his security policy. Bombings on rebel camps that killed minors created significant public controversy. When Petro turned to similar strategies, the military inadvertently killed children in bombings in children as well.

Armed groups have continued to grow under Petro despite his employment of increasingly aggressive military strategies. De la Espriella has not offered details about his plans, and it is unclear what he could do that Duque and Petro did not, or why the results would be any different for his administration when similar tactics have failed before.

Trump, however, has gained a new ally in the region. The US president has often shown that projection of US power is an end in and of itself, and de la Espriella is likely to allow Trump to do exactly that.

World.title: Colombia Reports and 21st-century fascism
World.content:
The coming four years will probably be the toughest yet and I will need your support to keep Colombia’s longest-living news source alive.

The Espriella administration will be the third far-right government I have reported on since I started Colombia Reports in 2008.

I expect the incoming government to be the worst because it seeks to undo socio-economic policies that pulled 4 million people out of poverty and end peace processes that kept us safe.

Independent journalists (and the New York Times) have criticized Abelardo de la Espriella for his ties to the now-defunct paramilitary organization AUC and drug traffickers, and his alleged corruption of the judicial system, specifically in Colombia.

Many of these journalists have been harassed by De la Espriella’s law firm through at least 109 frivolous lawsuits, and the publication of their private information.

I can only guess what’s ahead for us after De la Espriella appointed reported frauds as his spokespersons and put a conspiracy theorist in charge of my visa.

I will need your support as what’s coming is probably going to be expensive. The last time I reported on a far-right government, I was forced to spend months in my native country, the Netherlands.

If you are not yet a paid subscriber, please become one. If you don’t want to commit to a monthly contribution, please make a one-time donation.

I promise I will continue reporting on Colombia and will update you on the political situation in Colombia through my podcasts with Richard McColl of Colombia Calling.

World.title: De la Espriella desists from holding swearing-in ceremony at military base
World.content:
President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella has apparently given up trying to be sworn in before the military and asked Congress to allow the ceremony to take place in Cali, Colombia’s third largest city.

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella said Sunday that volcanic activity made travel to Popayan, the capital of Cauca, made a “secure, well-organized” inauguration ceremony all but impossible.

“For this reason, I respectfully ask the honorable House of Representatives, which has not yet debated my inauguration in a plenary session, to convene the August 7th session in the city of Cali,” said the president-elect.

“As soon as I am sworn in as president of the republic, my government’s first security council will be held in the Marco Fidel Suarez airbase in the city of Cali,” added De la Espriella, suggesting he has given up his aspiration to be sworn in inside a military base.

In an interview, Santiago de Cali University president Carlos Andres Perez, told Blu Radio on Tuesday that Valle del Cauca Governor Dilian Francisca Toro told him the university theater would be used for the inauguration.

Following the main ceremony, De la Espriella will travel to the Pichincha Military Canton, the base of the 3rd Division, to assume his role as supreme commander of the armed forces.

The apparent decision to desist from a military inauguration comes after major tensions with the outgoing government of President Gustavo Petro, who ordered the military not to cooperate with his elected successor.

An inauguration at a military base was also opposed by the Democratic Center, the largest political party in De la Espriella’s far-right congressional coalition.

The opponents claimed that Colombia’s constitution submits the armed forces to civilian authority. A swearing-in ceremony before them would have been confusing and inappropriate.

According to De la Espriella, his intention meant to stress his support for the Colombia’s “heroes.”

World.title: Colombia’s “Shield of the Americas” to operate from Medellin: De la Espriella
World.content:
Medellin will be the home of the US-led “Shield of the Americas” security program, according to Colombia’s President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella and Mayor Federico Gutierrez.

At a meeting with authorities from the Antioquia province, De la Espriella and Gutierrez agreed that Colombia’s second largest city is the “head of the snake of drug trafficking and organized crime.”

From Medellin, the metropolitan area, most orders are sent out to the rest of the country. So we’re going to focus our efforts on Medellin to fight crime. Abelardo de la Espriella

The announcement followed alleged calls between De la Espriella, US President Donald Trump and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and meetings between incoming Defense Minister Jorge Mora and the US’ Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for the Americas, Joseph Humire.

Following the meeting, Mora and Humire announced “Plan Patriota 2.0” and the creation of a “Regional Training Center against Drug Trafficking and Transnational Threats,” which would be “aimed at improving interoperability, operational readiness, and cooperation with allied countries” from the Americas.

During these meetings, the parties explored the joint development of a new bilateral program for cooperation and strategic assistance with a regional scope, known as Plan Patriota 2.0. This initiative is conceived as part of Colombia’s accession to the American Coalition Against the Cartels and is based on the design of the new Policy on Defense, Security, and Civic Coexistence, as well as on the strategy for military and police campaigns in priority areas for the restoration and stabilization of security. Jorge Mora

Plan Patriota was a US-backed military strategy that was implemented by former President Alvaro Uribe between 2003 and 2006.

The plan sought to dismantle the military organization of the now-defunct FARC guerrilla group, which it largely did while also killing thousands and forcibly displacing hundreds of thousands civilians.

De la Espriella has said that he seeks to restart Plan Colombia and seek to militarily destroy groups that were formed during and after peace processes with the FARC and the now-defunct paramilitary organization AUC.

World.title: “Water will run out:” Colombia declares emergency over upcoming El Niño
World.content:
Colombia’s government agreed to declare a national emergency over the consequences of El Niño, a climate phenomenon that is expected to bring extreme drought in December.

According to the government’s environmental institute, IDEAM, this year’s Niño could become the worst since the 1950’s and will peak between November 2026 an March 2027.

During a minister’s council, President Gustavo Petro said that excessive heat and water shortages could lead to energy shortages in regions that rely on hydroelectric dams for their electricity.

Petro asked Finance Minister German Avila to transfer COP4 trillion ($1.2 billion) to disaster management agency UNGRD to double the purchase of solar panels to lessen the demand on these hydroelectric dams.

In December last year, the UNGRD already signed a COP4.2 trillion deal with electricity firm Gecelca to buy solar panels.

In order to maintain food production, the president ordered the purchase of desalination plants for the Caribbean region.

Water is what’s going to run out—we don’t know to what extent, but hopefully Bogotá won’t have to suffer through this again. So, any drinking water supply project that’s already been designed but lacks funding must be funded. Drinking water—all the desalination plants we can bring in, because we don’t build them in Colombia — in all the towns in the northern Caribbean. President Gustavo Petro

Last but not least, Petro urged the Justice Ministry to secure “the accelerated surrender of lands, 500 thousand hectares, that have not been awarded” to landless farmers.

“Provide more land and more water to grow food, grow more food in Colombia, because the sun is going to scorch a lot of food and burn crops. And so it’s likely that we’ll be able to make up for the loss in food supply over these six months with new food supplies,” said the president.

Petro urged his ministers to be careful of corruption, which sank the UNGRD in a crisis in early 2024 and resulted in the detentions of multiple government officials.

World.title: De la Espriella denied aspired control over Colombia’s Congress
World.content:
Colombia’s Congress denied control over the legislative agenda to President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella and voted for a president loyal to former President Alvaro Uribe.

De la Espriella proposed his friend, Senator Alfredo Deluque of the U Party, to assume the leadership of the Senate, which would have given the government control over the congressional agenda.

Ahead of the vote, eight parties expressed their support for Deluque’s candidacy, which would have given him a 55-vote majority in the anonymous vote.

Former President Alvaro Uribe, whose Democratic Center party would be granted the presidency, accused “Abelardo’s circle” of trying to “get rid of this party” and vowed to “defend ourselves.”

Uribe had put up Democratic Center Senator Honorio Henriquez for the job and ordered his 17 senators to stick to their original vote.

If the Tiger roars to destroy the Democratic Center, we’ll have to become hardworking bees and defend ourselves, just like bees do when they’re attacked… I’m frightened by the idea circulating among De La Espriella’s inner circle of destroying that party. Former President Alvaro Uribe

The former president got the support of President Gustavo Petro, arguably Abelardo’s biggest political enemy.

At a rally that was held ahead of the vote, Petro warned senators of his leftist Historic Pact party “not to vote for fascism.”

Under the leadership of Senate bench leader Ivan Cepeda, who lost the presidential election to De la Espriella last month, all 26 of the pact’s senators voted for Henriquez.

Enjoying the secrecy of their vote, dissidents from the parties who were ordered to vote Deluque also turned on the president-elect and delivered Henrique 56 votes. Deluque ended up with only 45.

Less than three weeks before taking office, De la Espriella lost the loyalty of its largest coalition partner in Congress and will have to negotiate his agenda with them.

World.title: Universidad de Chile Eliminated by Curicó Unido in Copa Chile Upset
World.content:
