One of Brazil’s Pioneer Managers Steps Back

Gávea Investimentos, one of the first and most prominent independent asset managers in Brazil, told investors on 4 August 2026 that it is transferring the multimarket funds of its Gávea Macro family to Bradesco and abandoning the strategy.

According to the firm’s notice, it will end third-party management of the Gávea Macro family, made up of five funds, including pension (previdência) portfolios. Shareholders will be summoned to assemblies to approve the transfer to Bradesco Asset.

“We are deeply grateful for the confidence, partnership and support received over the past 23 years,” the firm said, adding that its partners had kept a sizable share of their own wealth in the same macro strategy throughout.

A Symptom of a Wider Hedge-Fund Crisis

Gávea’s exit is another sign of the strain on Brazil’s multimarket segment, the local equivalent of hedge funds, which pursue gains by trading economic variables at home and abroad.

Macro-category funds recorded net redemptions of R$8.8 billion (about US$1.7 billion) in 2026 through 30 July, and R$13.3 billion (about US$2.6 billion) over 12 months, according to industry association Anbima. That pulled total assets in the category down to R$97 billion (about US$19 billion) at the end of July.

The withdrawals reflect both weak accumulated returns and competition from lower-risk options, such as government and tax-exempt bonds, infrastructure debentures and LCIs and LCAs, which have become more attractive as interest rates climbed.

How the Numbers Turned Against the Funds

Through 30 July, macro multimarket funds returned 4.37% for the year and 10.80% over 12 months, Anbima data show, while the CDI interbank benchmark returned 8.14% and 14.84% over the same periods, roughly double the funds’ 12-month gain.

Gávea’s flagship Gávea Macro FIF returned 4.35% in 2026 through July, nearly half the CDI for the period. Created in 2008, the fund had been posting annual gains below the CDI since 2023.

Its assets stood at R$325 million (about US$64 million) at the end of July, after net redemptions of R$152 million (about US$30 million) during the year, illustrating how quickly investors have pulled back.

The Selic Squeeze

The core problem is Brazil’s high base interest rate. With the Selic hovering around 14% a year, investors can earn strong, effectively risk-free returns in fixed income, reducing the appeal of paying for active managers who aim to beat that bar.

When cash-like instruments yield double digits, a hedge fund must clear a much higher hurdle to justify its fees and volatility. Many macro funds have struggled to do so, accelerating outflows across the industry.

The pressure intensified in 2026. InfoMoney reported that performance worsened from March amid a conflict between the United States and Iran that upended global markets and caught many managers off guard.

Fraga, the Central Banker Turned Investor

Armínio Fraga led Brazil’s Central Bank from 1999 to 2002, steering the country through the adoption of inflation targeting and a floating currency. He co-founded Gávea Investimentos in 2003, and it became one of the most closely watched independent managers in the country.

JPMorgan bought a majority stake in Gávea in 2010, in a deal that underscored the firm’s standing. Its macro funds long carried the reputation of Fraga’s economic judgment.

Contacted by InfoMoney, Fraga declined to comment on the closure of the multimarket funds. The firm’s formal notice, rather than any public statement from its founder, is the basis for what is known about the decision.

What It Signals for Brazil’s Market

The retreat of a manager as established as Gávea highlights how a prolonged period of high rates is reshaping where Brazilian savings flow, away from active, higher-risk vehicles and toward fixed income.

For the broader industry, the transfer to Bradesco Asset lets existing investors keep exposure under a large bank’s management rather than face outright liquidation, a softer landing than an abrupt closure.

Whether the multimarket segment recovers will depend heavily on the path of the Selic. Until rates fall enough to dull the appeal of risk-free returns, pressure on Brazil’s hedge funds is likely to persist.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Gávea Investimentos doing with its multimarket funds?

Gávea Investimentos, founded by former Central Bank president Armínio Fraga, is exiting its Gávea Macro family of multimarket funds and transferring the five portfolios, including pension funds, to Bradesco Asset, subject to approval by shareholders in coming assemblies.

Why are Brazilian hedge funds under pressure?

With Brazil’s Selic rate around 14%, low-risk fixed income such as government and tax-exempt bonds offers strong returns, drawing investors away from multimarket funds. Anbima data show net redemptions of R$13.3 billion (about US$2.6 billion) from macro funds over 12 months.

Did Armínio Fraga comment on closing the funds?

No. Contacted by InfoMoney, Fraga declined to comment on the closure. The information comes from Gávea’s notice to investors, which thanked clients for their confidence over 23 years and confirmed the transfer of the funds to Bradesco Asset.

World.title: Coca-Cola in Peru: US$1 Billion Investment to Expand Production
World.content:
Business: Lima

Key Facts —Investment. Coca-Cola Perú and bottler Arca Continental Lindley will invest US$1 billion in Peru over the next five years. —Announcement. President Keiko Fujimori unveiled the plan on 4 August 2026 during a visit to Arca Continental Lindley’s plant in Pucusana, south of Lima. —Use. The money targets expanded and modernized production, distribution and cold-chain infrastructure, plus returnable packaging and market-service capacity. —Community. Separately, the companies will put about US$90 million into a water and sewage system for Pucusana via Peru’s ‘obras por impuestos’ (works-for-taxes) scheme. —Reach. Arca Continental Lindley says its network reaches around 370,000 small shops, or bodegas, across Peru.

Coca-Cola Perú and bottler Arca Continental Lindley will invest US$1 billion in Peru over five years, a plan President Keiko Fujimori unveiled at the company’s Pucusana plant as a vote of confidence in the country.

The skyline of Lima, Peru, where the companies announced a five-year, US$1 billion plan. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons). (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

A US$1 Billion, Five-Year Commitment

Coca-Cola Perú and Arca Continental Lindley, the bottler that produces and distributes Coca-Cola brands in the country, said they will invest US$1 billion in Peru over the next five years to expand and modernize their operations.

The plan was announced on 4 August 2026 during a protocol visit by President Keiko Fujimori to Arca Continental Lindley’s plant in the Pucusana district, at the southern edge of Lima. The companies said the money will go toward productive, operational and market-service infrastructure.

Beyond factories, the investment covers the network of warehouses and the wider value chain, along with strengthening the cold chain, promoting returnable packaging and cultural initiatives tying the brands to Peruvian consumers.

Who Announced It — and What Was Said

The announcement was made by President Keiko Fujimori, who framed the investment as a sign of confidence in Peru and reiterated the government’s pledge to provide stability, legal security and favorable conditions for investment, alongside protection of workers’ rights.

Enrique Pérez Barba, chief executive of Arca Continental Lindley, said the commitment reaffirms the company’s long-term confidence in Peru and will strengthen its production, commercial and distribution capacity, “generating shared value” for the communities where it operates.

Fujimori also said she hoped the company would keep hiring young people and bring more micro and small enterprises into its supply chain, which she noted already includes around 370,000 bodegas.

The Pucusana Water Project

Alongside the core investment, the companies will channel about US$90 million through Peru’s ‘obras por impuestos’ mechanism, which lets firms fund public works and offset the cost against their tax bill, to build a drinking-water and sewage system in Pucusana.

According to the companies, the initiative, known as the Proyecto Esquema Pucusana, carries an investment of S/291 million (about US$81 million) and would, for the first time, bring potable water and modern sewerage to more than 31,000 residents of the district.

The project began drawing up its technical file in April 2026 and, once complete, would be transferred to the state water utility Sedapal to operate. Officials said the works should be finished within about three years.

A Relief Component for El Niño

The president also said Coca-Cola Perú and Arca Continental Lindley would donate two million liters of water and 150,000 blankets to help communities that could be affected by the El Niño weather phenomenon in the coming months.

Peru sits among the countries most exposed to El Niño, which can bring heavy rains, flooding and landslides to the coast. The government has been seeking private support to prepare vulnerable areas ahead of the season.

Framing corporate spending around both long-term capacity and near-term relief is a common feature of large investment announcements in the country, where public services and disaster readiness often lag economic growth.

Why the Bottler Is Betting on Peru

Arca Continental Lindley is the exclusive bottler of the Coca-Cola system in Peru and part of Arca Continental, one of the largest Coca-Cola bottlers in the Americas. Its Pucusana plant is among the group’s key production sites serving the Lima market.

A five-year, billion-dollar plan signals confidence in Peruvian consumer demand and in the stability of the operating environment, at a time when the government is courting private capital to support growth.

For a consumer-goods company, investments in cold chain, returnable packaging and distribution are also about efficiency and sustainability, lowering costs and emissions while widening reach into the small shops that dominate Peruvian retail.

What It Means for Peru’s Investment Climate

The announcement adds to a series of private-investment commitments the government has highlighted as evidence that business confidence is holding. Officials have publicly urged companies to bet on Peru and expand hiring.

For consumers and workers, the immediate effects are indirect: modernized plants, a broader distribution network and, in Pucusana, a long-promised water and sewage system delivered through the works-for-taxes route.

Whether the pledged US$1 billion translates into the promised infrastructure will play out over the five-year horizon, but the scale of the commitment underscores the weight of the Coca-Cola system in Peru’s consumer economy.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much are Coca-Cola and Arca Continental Lindley investing in Peru?

The companies announced a US$1 billion investment in Peru over the next five years to expand and modernize production, distribution and cold-chain infrastructure and to promote returnable packaging. It was unveiled at Arca Continental Lindley’s Pucusana plant.

Who announced the Coca-Cola Peru investment?

President Keiko Fujimori announced the plan on 4 August 2026 during a visit to the Pucusana plant. Arca Continental Lindley’s chief executive, Enrique Pérez Barba, said the investment reaffirms the company’s long-term confidence in Peru.

What is the Pucusana water project?

Separately, the companies will invest about US$90 million through Peru’s ‘obras por impuestos’ scheme, a S/291 million (about US$81 million) project to bring drinking water and sewerage to more than 31,000 residents of Pucusana, later transferred to the utility Sedapal.

World.title: Illegal Gold in Colombia Now Rivals Coffee at US$3.5 Billion
World.content:
Economy: Bogotá

Key Facts —Scale. A Universidad EAFIT study estimates Colombia’s illegal gold economy moves about US$3.5 billion a year and generates roughly US$3 billion in added value, about 0.8% of GDP. —Comparison. That size is comparable to Colombia’s coffee exports and equal to about a third of the cocaine economy, the researchers say. —Laundering. The study finds around 72% of Colombia’s ‘legal’ gold exports are actually illegally sourced metal that gains legal paperwork before shipping. —Footprint. In 2023 about 105,060 hectares were under alluvial gold mining, 76% of it unlicensed, concentrated in Bajo Cauca, Antioquia, Chocó and southern Bolívar. —Money stays home. Unlike cocaine, whose profits accrue abroad, almost all the value of illegal gold stays inside Colombia, funding armed groups, according to the study.

Illegal gold has become one of Colombia’s most lucrative criminal economies, moving an estimated US$3.5 billion a year — a haul that a new Universidad EAFIT study says now rivals the country’s coffee exports.

An artisanal gold-mining site in Colombia, where illegal gold moves an estimated US$3.5 billion a year. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons). (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

A Criminal Economy the Size of Coffee

A study by Valor Público, the research center at Medellín’s Universidad EAFIT, estimates that illegal gold in Colombia moves about US$3.5 billion a year, generates roughly US$3 billion in added value and now accounts for about 0.8% of gross domestic product.

That scale, the researchers say, is comparable to Colombia’s coffee exports and equal to roughly a third of the cocaine economy. The weight of illegal gold in GDP has nearly doubled over the past decade, from about 0.4% in 2014 to 0.8% in 2023.

Colombia keeps no official estimate of the activity, so the team built its figure from public data, combining mining-production records, foreign-trade statistics and satellite imagery to size the illegal metal’s economic footprint.

Most ‘Legal’ Gold Exports Trace Back to Illegal Mines

One of the study’s central findings is that about 72% of Colombia’s legally exported gold actually corresponds to illegally mined metal that acquires legal documentation somewhere along the supply chain. Only about 28% has a fully verifiable origin.

In 2023 Colombia formally exported roughly US$3.4 billion in gold. On top of that, the researchers estimate an additional US$600 million to US$1.6 billion left the country through smuggling.

The laundering typically happens, the study says, when traders, processing plants and smelters fold gold of uncertain origin into the formal chain, turning it into an exportable product with legal paperwork.

Where the Mining Happens

The estimate draws on the EVOA program run by the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) and Colombia’s mines ministry, which tracks alluvial gold mining by satellite. In 2023 it identified 105,060 hectares under alluvial gold extraction.

Of that area, 76% was unlicensed or illegal, while only about 20% held environmental and technical permits. The main clusters sit in the Bajo Cauca and northeast of Antioquia, the lowlands of the Pacific coast in Chocó, and southern Bolívar.

Scaling productivity from legal mines, researchers estimate illegal operations produced around 40 tonnes of alluvial gold; adding underground extraction and smuggled metal, total illegal gold traded in 2023 reached about 55 tonnes.

Why Gold Is Different From Cocaine

The study highlights a key contrast with the drug trade: where the money ends up. Cocaine earns much of its value during international transport and distribution, so a large share of the profit is generated abroad.

Gold, by contrast, sells at the international price the moment it leaves the country, so almost all of the economic value stays in Colombia and benefits those who control extraction and illegal trade. The Organization of American States has identified gold as the top financing source for several armed groups, above drug trafficking.

The researchers note that although illegal gold represents about 0.8% of GDP against an estimated 2.5% for cocaine, the cash reaching criminal groups may be far closer than those headline shares suggest.

Buriticá, Smuggling and the Role of Panama

The study devotes a section to Buriticá, in Antioquia, where it says the Clan del Golfo controls roughly 60% of the illegal tunnels operating within the concession of Chinese miner Zijin. In 2023, illegal miners there are estimated to have extracted about three tonnes of gold, worth around US$200 million.

The criminal organization is thought to take about 10% of that output as payment for allowing access to tunnels under its control. Beyond Buriticá, the report identifies Panama as a main route for smuggled Colombian gold, sometimes disguised as jewelry to evade controls.

Record gold prices, which have pushed toward US$5,000 an ounce, have made the business more profitable and helped drive its expansion, with new mining fronts appearing especially after 2019.

What Colombia Could Do About It

The researchers argue that fighting illegal mining only at extraction sites is insufficient, because those operations can relocate quickly. Instead, they say the state should focus on traders, processing plants and smelters, the points where illegal gold takes on a legal appearance before export.

Strengthening traceability at those chokepoints, they contend, would curb the laundering of illegal metal and squeeze one of the main financing streams for armed groups, particularly while international prices remain high.

The findings land amid a broader surge in Colombian gold exports, which official figures show jumped sharply in early 2026, intensifying scrutiny of how much of that flow is genuinely legal.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much money does illegal gold move in Colombia?

A Universidad EAFIT study estimates illegal gold moves about US$3.5 billion a year and generates roughly US$3 billion in added value, equal to about 0.8% of GDP. Researchers say that scale is comparable to Colombia’s coffee exports.

How does illegal gold become a legal export?

The study says about 72% of Colombia’s legally exported gold is actually illegally mined metal. It gains legal paperwork when traders, processing plants and smelters mix gold of uncertain origin into the formal supply chain before it is shipped abroad.

How does illegal gold compare with cocaine in Colombia?

The study puts illegal gold at about 0.8% of GDP versus an estimated 2.5% for cocaine, or roughly a third of the cocaine economy. Crucially, almost all gold revenue stays in Colombia, and the OAS ranks gold as the top financing source for several armed groups.

World.title: Mexico’s 98M Prepaid Lines Face CURP ID Cutoff Starting Aug 15
World.content:
Telecom: Mexico City

Key Facts —Scale. Mexico’s telecom regulator, the CRT, says about 98 million mobile lines — roughly 61% of the market — are still not linked to a CURP national ID, against some 63 million already registered. —Deadline. The first hard cutoff falls on 15 August 2026 for numbers ending in 0; the rest follow a staggered calendar by last digit through 31 December 2026. —Who. Only prepaid lines must act; postpaid and monthly-plan users are already registered, and data-only and emergency numbers are exempt. —Penalty. After each deadline, carriers Telcel, AT&T and Movistar have up to 72 hours to suspend unlinked lines, leaving only emergency calls and official alerts. —Legal. The 2026 CURP registry is not the biometric PANAUT struck down by the Supreme Court; the Court barred fingerprint and facial data but let ID-based line linking stand.

Mexico’s CURP phone registration reaches its first hard cutoff on 15 August, when carriers may begin suspending prepaid mobile lines that are not linked to a national ID under a rule covering some 98 million unregistered numbers.

A pedestrian uses a mobile phone in Mexico City as the CURP line-registration deadline nears. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons). (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

What Changes on 15 August

The CRT (Comisión Reguladora de Telecomunicaciones), Mexico’s telecom regulator, has set 15 August 2026 as the first firm deadline in a program requiring every mobile line to be linked to the holder’s CURP, the country’s unique population registry code. Numbers ending in 0 must be registered by that date.

The regulator says roughly 98 million lines, about 61% of the market, are still unregistered, against some 63 million already linked. Headlines describing 98 million people losing service on a single day overstate the mechanics: only lines ending in 0 face the 15 August cutoff.

The remaining digits follow a staggered calendar. Numbers ending in 1 have until 31 August, and the sequence continues roughly every two weeks until numbers ending in 9 reach their deadline on 31 December 2026.

Who Has to Register — and Who Does Not

The obligation applies only to prepaid lines, the pay-as-you-go plans historically sold without tying a number to a named holder. The CRT frames the drive as a way to attach each line to an identifiable person.

Postpaid and monthly-plan customers are exempt because their details were captured when they signed contracts. Lines used only for data transmission, and numbers reserved for emergency services, also fall outside the rule.

For the roughly 98 million unregistered lines, the great majority of them prepaid, the practical task is to link the number to a CURP before that number’s calendar date, or risk having service cut off.

How the Registration Works

The CRT says the process is free and must be completed with the mobile carrier, not with the federal government. Users can register through their operator’s website or app, or in person at a customer-service center.

Applicants provide their CURP and a valid official ID, such as a voter credential or passport. Some online flows add an identity check using photos of the document and a ‘liveness’ test through the phone’s camera; the regulator says verification images must be deleted once the process ends.

If a line is not linked by its deadline, carriers Telcel, AT&T and Movistar have up to 72 hours to suspend it. A suspended line can still reach emergency numbers, contact the operator and receive official alerts such as earthquake warnings, and full service returns once registration is completed.

The Legal Backdrop: This Is Not PANAUT

The initiative revives a politically sensitive idea. In 2021 Mexico created PANAUT, the Padrón Nacional de Usuarios de Telefonía Móvil, a centralized registry that would have collected biometric data. The Supreme Court (SCJN) struck it down in April 2022, ruling it disproportionate and a risk to privacy.

Officials and fact-checkers stress that the 2026 scheme is not PANAUT. It does not gather fingerprints or facial recognition and does not build a single state-held biometric database; instead it links a line to an existing CURP and an official ID held by the carrier.

The distinction has still drawn legal challenges. In early 2026 the SCJN again rejected any requirement to hand over biometric data to register a line, while allowing ID-based linking to proceed. Courts have continued to weigh injunctions over the broader CURP debate, and the outcome remains contested.

Why Mexico Says It Is Doing This

The CRT presents the registry as a tool against fraud and extortion, crimes frequently carried out from anonymous prepaid lines. It says the measure aligns Mexico with a practice used in more than 160 countries.

Carriers have felt the impact. Reports indicate AT&T alone lost more than 600,000 prepaid users tied to the registration push, as some customers abandoned lines rather than register.

Critics counter that the earlier PANAUT experience produced little evidence that such registries reduce crime, and civil-society groups have raised data-protection concerns. The government maintains that the lighter, CURP-based model addresses those objections.

What Expats in Mexico Should Do

Foreign residents are covered like anyone else if they hold a Mexican prepaid line. The CURP is now issued to foreigners with legal residence, so expats can obtain one and use it to register their number.

Those on postpaid or monthly plans generally do not need to act, since their details were recorded at signup. Prepaid users, common among new arrivals and short-term visitors, should check their number’s last digit against the CRT calendar and register before that date.

A practical warning: a suspended line can disrupt more than calls. Many banks send verification codes by SMS and use the mobile number to confirm transfers or recover passwords, so a lapsed registration could temporarily complicate access to digital banking.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many phone lines could be cut in Mexico, and when?

The CRT says about 98 million mobile lines, roughly 61% of the market, are still not linked to a CURP. Suspensions are staggered by the number’s last digit: those ending in 0 face a 15 August 2026 cutoff, with the rest running through 31 December 2026.

Do I have to register my Mexican phone line?

Only prepaid lines must be linked to a CURP and an official ID. Postpaid and plan customers were registered at signup, and data-only and emergency numbers are exempt. The process is free and is done with your carrier, not the government.

Is this the same as PANAUT, the registry the Supreme Court struck down?

No. Officials and fact-checkers say the 2026 CURP registration does not collect biometric data or build a central state database. The Supreme Court barred fingerprint and facial-data requirements but allowed carriers to link lines to a CURP and official ID.

World.title: PRIO Q2 Profit Jumps 169% to US$413 Million on Record Output
World.content:
Energy: Rio de Janeiro

Key Facts —Profit. PRIO reported second-quarter 2026 net profit of US$413.3 million, up 169% from a year earlier. —EBITDA. Adjusted EBITDA hit a record; outlets cited figures from about US$847 million to roughly US$879 million, driven by higher output and lower costs. —Production. Average output reached a company record of about 172,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day, up roughly 72% year-on-year. —July surge. Production rose further in July 2026 to about 196,000 boepd, as the Wahoo field continued to ramp up. —Costs. PRIO cut its lifting (extraction) cost to about US$8.9 per barrel, among the lowest for a Brazilian independent.

Brazilian oil independent PRIO posted record second-quarter output near 172,000 barrels a day and a 169% jump in net profit to US$413.3 million, as its Wahoo field and Peregrino stake drove growth.

An offshore production platform of the type used in Brazil's offshore basins. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons). (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

A Record Quarter

PRIO, Brazil’s largest independent oil producer, reported net profit of US$413.3 million for the second quarter of 2026, a 169% increase from the same period of 2025, according to results carried by Money Times, InfoMoney and other outlets.

Adjusted EBITDA reached a record. PRIO reports in US dollars, and outlets put the figure between about US$847 million (Money Times) and roughly US$879 million (BPMoney), with the company crediting higher production, firm oil prices and lower unit costs.

Average production of about 172,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day set a company record, up roughly 71.9% year-on-year and about 10.7% from the first quarter.

What Drove the Jump: Wahoo and Peregrino

The gains stem largely from two moves: the completion and ramp-up of the Wahoo field development in the Campos Basin, and PRIO’s expanded stake in the Peregrino field.

Wahoo added significant new barrels, while Peregrino, a heavy-oil field, boosted volumes after PRIO increased its interest. Together they lifted output to record levels.

Spreading fixed costs over more barrels also helped margins, reinforcing the profit and cash-flow gains PRIO reported for the quarter.

Low Costs, High Margins

PRIO’s model centres on buying and revitalising mature offshore fields, then squeezing costs. In the second quarter of 2026 it reported a lifting cost of about US$8.9 per barrel, among the lowest for a Brazilian producer.

Low extraction costs give PRIO resilience when oil prices swing, protecting cash flow even if benchmark crude weakens.

The combination of record volumes and low unit costs is what powered the record EBITDA and the sharp rise in profit.

July’s Even Higher Output

Momentum carried into July 2026, when PRIO’s total exported oil-and-gas production reached about 196,260 boepd, according to the company’s monthly figures, a fresh high above the second-quarter average.

The July level suggests Wahoo continued to ramp, pointing to a strong start to the third quarter.

Sustained output near 196,000 boepd, if maintained, would keep PRIO on a steep growth path for full-year 2026.

Context: From 2025 to a Bigger PRIO

The 2026 numbers mark a step change. For full-year 2025, PRIO averaged about 106,000 barrels a day and reported adjusted EBITDA of about US$1.4 billion.

In the first quarter of 2026, production hit a then-record of about 155,400 boepd and EBITDA rose about 91% year-on-year, figures the second quarter has now surpassed.

The trajectory reflects PRIO’s strategy of scaling through acquisitions and field redevelopment rather than frontier exploration.

Why It Matters for Brazil

PRIO is a bellwether for Brazil’s independent oil sector, which operates alongside state-controlled Petrobras in the offshore basins that make Brazil a top-tier global crude producer.

Strong results from independents underscore investor appetite for Brazilian oil assets even amid the global energy-transition debate.

For Rio de Janeiro, home to much of Brazil’s offshore industry, PRIO’s expansion supports service-sector activity and tax revenue, though output remains exposed to oil-price cycles.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much did PRIO earn in the second quarter of 2026?

PRIO reported net profit of US$413.3 million for the second quarter of 2026, up 169% from a year earlier, alongside record adjusted EBITDA and record production.

How much oil is PRIO producing?

PRIO averaged about 172,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day in the second quarter of 2026, a company record, and output rose further to about 196,000 boepd in July 2026.

What drove PRIO’s record results?

The ramp-up of the Wahoo field and an enlarged stake in the Peregrino field lifted volumes, while a lifting cost near US$8.9 per barrel kept margins high.

World.title: Compass IPO Ends Brazil’s 5-Year IPO Drought, Raises up to US$630M
World.content:
Markets: São Paulo

Key Facts —Pricing. Compass, the natural-gas holding controlled by Cosan, priced its IPO at R$28.00 (about US$5.51) per share, the bottom of the R$28–R$35 (about US$5.51–US$6.89) range. —Size. The sale of about 89.3 million shares raised roughly R$2.5 billion (about US$492 million), rising to as much as R$3.2 billion (about US$630 million) with the over-allotment. —Listing. Shares began trading on the B3 exchange in São Paulo on 11 May 2026 under the ticker PASS3, in the Novo Mercado segment. —Drought. The deal was Brazil’s first IPO since 2021, ending a near five-year drought — the country’s longest such gap in decades. —Structure. The offering was entirely secondary, so proceeds went to selling shareholders, chiefly Cosan, rather than into Compass itself.

Compass, the natural-gas arm of Brazilian conglomerate Cosan, priced its B3 initial public offering at R$28.00 (about US$5.51) a share, ending a near five-year IPO drought in Latin America’s largest economy.

The B3 stock exchange in São Paulo, where Compass listed under the ticker PASS3. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons). (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

A Long-Awaited Return to the IPO Market

Compass, the natural-gas distribution and trading arm of the Cosan group, priced its IPO at R$28.00 (about US$5.51) per share and began trading on São Paulo’s B3 exchange on Monday 11 May 2026 under the ticker PASS3.

The pricing landed at the bottom of the indicated R$28–R$35 (about US$5.51–US$6.89) band. The base offering of about 89.3 million shares raised roughly R$2.5 billion (about US$492 million); with the supplementary over-allotment lot, the total could reach as much as R$3.2 billion (about US$630 million), according to figures reported by Bloomberg and InfoMoney.

The listing valued Compass at around R$20 billion (about US$3.9 billion).

Ending Brazil’s IPO Drought

The deal is significant less for its size than its symbolism: it was the first IPO on B3 since 2021, ending a drought of nearly five years that several outlets called the longest such gap in Brazil in decades.

Brazil’s new-listings market froze after 2021 as high domestic interest rates, currency swings and political uncertainty pushed investors toward fixed income and kept would-be issuers on the sidelines.

A successful debut by a large, established company like Compass was watched as a test of whether the window for Brazilian equity offerings had reopened.

A Fully Secondary Deal, No New Cash for Compass

The offering was entirely secondary. That means Compass issued no new shares and received none of the proceeds; instead, existing shareholders sold down their stakes.

The main seller was Cosan, Compass’s controlling shareholder, which sold about 76.78 million shares for roughly R$2.15 billion (about US$423 million). The structure gave Cosan, which has carried substantial debt, a way to raise cash and cut leverage.

For new investors, the secondary format means the money raised does not fund expansion, debt reduction or investment at Compass itself, a point analysts flagged when the price landed at the low end of the range.

What Compass Does

Compass is one of Brazil’s largest natural-gas players. It is built around gas distribution, including Comgás, the country’s biggest piped-gas distributor, which serves São Paulo state, alongside gas marketing and infrastructure assets.

Natural gas sits at the centre of Brazil’s energy-transition debate, and Compass has expanded through distribution networks and regasification capacity.

The company had first tried to list around 2020, when Cosan filed and then shelved the plan amid unfavourable market conditions; the 2026 deal revived that long-delayed ambition.

Why the Price Landed Low

Pricing at R$28 (about US$5.51), the floor of the range, signalled that investors demanded a discount to commit to Brazil’s first big equity offering in years.

Brazil Stock Guide and others framed the outcome as an issuer discount: the deal got done, reopening the market, but on terms more favourable to buyers than to sellers.

Even so, completing a multibillion-real offering after such a long freeze was widely read as a modest vote of confidence in Brazilian equities.

What It Signals for B3 and Cosan

A completed IPO can encourage other Brazilian companies that had delayed listings to test the market, though bankers cautioned that one deal does not make a trend.

For Cosan, a conglomerate spanning fuel distribution, lubricants, logistics and land, the sale helps address a stretched balance sheet.

The broader question is whether Brazil’s macro backdrop, from interest rates to the real and the electoral calendar, will stay supportive enough for a sustained revival in new listings.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much did the Compass IPO raise?

The base offering of about 89.3 million shares at R$28.00 (about US$5.51) each raised roughly R$2.5 billion (about US$492 million), rising to as much as R$3.2 billion (about US$630 million) with the over-allotment tranche.

Why is the Compass IPO important?

It was Brazil’s first IPO since 2021, ending a near five-year drought on the B3 exchange and testing whether the country’s equity-offering market had reopened.

Did Compass receive the money from the IPO?

No. The offering was entirely secondary, so the proceeds went to selling shareholders, chiefly Cosan, and not to Compass itself.

World.title: Codelco Suspends El Teniente ‘Andes Norte’ Over Seismic Risk
World.content:
Mining: Rancagua

Key Facts —Decision. On 4 August 2026, Codelco temporarily suspended development and construction of the Andes Norte project at its El Teniente mine in central Chile. —Reason. The state miner cited an emerging deep-seismicity phenomenon at the mine’s lowest levels, which it says behaves differently from risks it has historically managed. —Scale. The measure affects four contractor companies, more than 20 contracts and about 3,000 workers, according to Chilean media, and pauses a flagship expansion. —Context. It comes about a year after a fatal collapse at El Teniente on 31 July 2025 that killed six workers; the new step is preventive, with no injuries reported. —Andes Norte. The sector is the deepest part of the New Mine Level works, at roughly 1,880 metres, holding some 375 million tonnes of copper reserves.

Chile’s state copper giant Codelco has suspended work on the Andes Norte sector of its El Teniente mine after detecting a new deep-seismic risk, pausing a flagship expansion and idling four contractors.

Codelco's El Teniente, the world's largest underground copper mine, in central Chile near Rancagua. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons). (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)
