El Teniente suspension. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

What Codelco Suspended and Why

On Monday 4 August 2026, Corporación Nacional del Cobre (Codelco) said it had temporarily halted development and construction at the Andes Norte project, part of its El Teniente division near Rancagua, about 85 kilometres south of Santiago.

The company described the move as a preventive safety measure taken after identifying an emerging seismic phenomenon at the mine’s greatest depths, with characteristics it said differ from the seismic risks it has historically managed. Recent episodes of deep seismicity, it said, occurred spontaneously and were hard to anticipate.

Codelco said the decision followed technical analyses carried out over the previous six months, and that it would reinforce instrumentation, monitoring and study before defining measures to resume work.

The Contractors and Workers Affected

The suspension directly affects at least four contractor companies engaged in development and construction at Andes Norte, covering more than 20 contracts, according to Diario Financiero.

Chilean outlet Emol reported that roughly 3,000 workers are involved. Codelco said it would carry out an orderly halt covering administrative, contractual and labour matters as it paralyses contractor activity.

Andes Norte is one of the structural projects meant to extend the life of El Teniente, the world’s largest underground copper mine, so a prolonged pause carries implications for Codelco’s long-term output plans.

A Mine Still Marked by the 2025 Collapse

The suspension comes almost exactly a year after a deadly accident at El Teniente. On 31 July 2025, a seismic event triggered a collapse in the mine’s Andesita sector, killing six workers and injuring several others.

Chile’s National Seismological Center measured that 2025 event at magnitude 4.2, while the USGS put it near 5.0. Subsequent expert reviews indicated the tremor was probably induced by mining activity rather than natural tectonic movement.

The 2025 collapse and the 2026 suspension are separate events and should not be conflated: the earlier incident was fatal, while the current measure is precautionary, with no casualties reported. Codelco has framed the new step as acting before, rather than after, a failure.

Why Seismicity Haunts Deep Copper Mining

El Teniente extracts ore at increasing depth, and Andes Norte sits at roughly 1,880 metres, the deepest level of the expansion. As mines go deeper, surrounding rock comes under greater stress, and extraction can release that energy suddenly as rock bursts, or mining-induced earthquakes.

Managing this risk is central to Chilean underground mining, which relies heavily on block-caving methods. Codelco said the newly detected phenomenon behaves differently from the patterns its control systems were built to handle, which is why it chose to stop rather than continue under existing protocols.

What It Means for Codelco and Copper

Codelco is the world’s largest copper producer and a major contributor to Chile’s public finances, so setbacks at its flagship division draw close scrutiny from investors and the government.

The company has been through a difficult stretch: it lost its El Teniente mine manager in August 2025, and three senior executives departed in February 2026 amid internal-audit findings tied to earlier rock-burst incidents. In April 2026, regulators fined Codelco and contractors over the fatal collapse.

El Teniente remains one of Codelco’s biggest divisions, and Andes Norte is central to plans to sustain its output as older ore bodies are depleted, which is why the pause matters beyond the immediate work stoppage.

What Happens Next

Codelco said it will strengthen monitoring, instrumentation and technical analysis before deciding how and when to restart Andes Norte, without giving a firm timeline.

The company stressed that the rest of the El Teniente division and its wider operations continue as normal, limiting the immediate production hit to the paused expansion works.

For the affected contractors and their workers, the coming weeks will hinge on how quickly Codelco can characterise the new seismic risk and design controls that satisfy its safety standards.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Codelco suspend at El Teniente?

On 4 August 2026 Codelco temporarily halted development and construction at the Andes Norte project, one of the deepest sectors of its El Teniente mine in central Chile, as a preventive safety measure.

Why was Andes Norte suspended?

Codelco cited an emerging deep-seismicity risk detected at the mine’s lowest levels, which it says behaves differently from previously managed seismic patterns. The pause affects four contractors, more than 20 contracts and about 3,000 workers.

Is this the same as the 2025 El Teniente accident?

No. A seismic collapse on 31 July 2025 killed six workers at the Andesita sector. The 2026 suspension is a precautionary pause with no injuries reported, though it stems from the same broader concern about deep-mining seismicity.

World.title: Guatemala’s Fuego Volcano Eruption Forces 1,700 Evacuations
World.content:
A powerful eruption of Guatemala’s Fuego Volcano has forced authorities to evacuate at least 1,700 residents from areas near the crater and declare the highest alert level Tuesday in zones exposed to falling ash. Fuego, considered the most active volcano in Central America and located near the capital, entered an eruptive phase Monday morning.

Its activity intensified overnight into Tuesday, with streams of lava flowing down its slopes and enormous columns of gas and ash rising into the sky. “The volcano is going through one of its most critical explosive phases,” producing mudflows, incandescent rocks, gases and ash, said Edwin Rojas, director of the Institute of Volcanology, known as Insivumeh.

Guatemala’s National Coordinator for Disaster Reduction, Conred, began evacuating communities near the volcano Monday evening and declared an orange danger alert nationwide. On Tuesday, the agency raised the alert to red in the departments of Sacatepéquez, Chimaltenango and Escuintla, which are home to 1.6 million people.

According to Conred Executive Secretary Claudinne Ogaldes, about 29,000 people are directly exposed to ashfall, making evacuations from the area essential. Ogaldes urged residents of nearby communities to wear masks and cover their water and food supplies. Conred said more than 1,700 people had been evacuated.

“We have become accustomed to living with a volcano that is always active, but this time it was simply too much,” said Sonia Vasquez, a 50-year-old resident of El Porvenir who spent the night in a shelter. Alejandro Garcia, another resident, also evacuated Monday evening after the alert was issued.

“We ran out, terrified,” he said, after seeing lava flowing down the volcano’s slopes. Despite the higher alert level, authorities reopened a road leading to the colonial city of Antigua, a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of Guatemala’s main tourist destinations. Operations at Guatemala City’s international airport have not been affected so far.

Lava Fountain

The Ministry of Education suspended in-person classes at schools in three communities near the volcano. “It would be better if we could move somewhere else because we live with this fear, since the volcano gives no warning,” said Lidia Ortiz, another evacuee. According to Insivumeh experts, a lava fountain reaching between 200 and 300 meters above the crater formed Monday, while the ash column rose to more than 7,000 meters.

As the ash dispersed at altitudes between 5,000 and 6,000 meters, it traveled as far as 130 kilometers westward. The institute said 34 earthquakes were recorded in Guatemala during the previous 24 hours, most with epicenters in the Pacific Ocean. Guatemala is located along the Pacific Ring of Fire and experiences significant seismic and volcanic activity.

Several mass evacuations have taken place in recent years because of eruptions at Fuego, which rises 3,763 meters above sea level and is located about 35 kilometers from Guatemala City in a straight line. In June 2025, around 800 people were evacuated because of eruptions at Fuego.

In 2018, 215 people were killed and about 200 others were reported missing after volcanic flows devastated a village on the slopes of the volcano.

World.title: Renting Versus Buying in Costa Rica and How to Decide
World.content:
One longtime foreign resident of Costa Rica could buy a house or a condominium outright tomorrow. He has the cash, he has been here for decades, and he still rents the same apartment he has rented for years and he has no plans to change that. His reasoning is worth hearing before you sign anything, because the instinct most newcomers arrive with — buy early, buy fast, get it settled — is the expensive instinct if you turn out to be wrong about where you want to live.

He gives three reasons. The first is that Costa Rica is not one place. The dry heat of Guanacaste, the green wall of the South Pacific around Uvita and Ojochal, the Caribbean side, the Central Valley — these are different countries as far as your daily life is concerned, and the region that suits you in year one may not suit you in year five.

He spends the low season at the beach, when the crowds are gone and prices drop, and returns to the Central Valley for the high season, when the weather is better and the airport, the hospitals and the shopping are close. Owning a house in either place would end that arrangement.

The second is cost. The third, and the one he considers most important, is the exit. If he ever decides to leave the country for health, for family, or simply because he wants to, he wants that to be his decision and not a function of how fast he can move a piece of real estate. Here is what those arguments look like with numbers attached, and where they break down.

Renting here protects you more than you probably expect

Costa Rican rental law is unusually favorable to tenants, and most foreigners do not know it before they sign. Residential leases fall under the General Law of Urban and Suburban Leases, Ley 7527. Article 70 sets a three-year minimum. If your contract says one year, or says nothing about duration, the law treats it as three.

Your landlord cannot decide in month eight that they would rather list the place on a short-term rental site. And under Article 71, if the landlord fails to tell you at least three months before the term expires that they will not renew, the lease renews automatically for another three years on the same terms.

The rent rules matter just as much. Article 67 is explicit: when a residential rent is agreed in foreign currency, the amount stays fixed for the entire term of the contract, with no right to adjustment. If your lease is in dollars, your rent cannot go up for three years. If it is in colones, the landlord may raise it once a year by no more than accumulated inflation. Separately, Article 57 lets you pay in colones at the Central Bank selling rate even when the lease is written in dollars.

Two more provisions worth knowing. Article 58 bars a landlord from demanding more than one month of rent in advance on a home. And Article 72 says that unless your contract states otherwise in writing, you end the lease by giving the landlord three months’ notice. That is the mechanism behind the “just give notice and go” argument — three months, not thirty days, and check what your contract says, because this one can be modified by agreement.

These rights are non-waivable. Article 3 voids any clause in which a tenant signs them away. There is one exclusion that matters enormously to anyone planning a beach stay. Article 7 puts hotels and guesthouses outside the law entirely, and it also excludes homes and premises in tourism zones designated by the Costa Rican Tourism Board when they are rented by season.

A furnished place taken for the green season in a beach town may fall outside every protection described above. The three-year term, the frozen rent, the notice rules — none of it necessarily applies. If you want those protections, you need a residential lease, not a seasonal one.

What ownership actually costs you every year

The annual carrying costs of a Costa Rican property are lower than most North Americans expect in one respect and higher in several others. Property tax is the pleasant surprise. It runs 0.25 percent of the registered value, paid to your municipality, with a discount for settling the full year in January. On a home registered at $400,000 that is about $1,000 a year, and registered values often sit below what you actually paid. If you are coming from New Jersey or Ontario, this line item will not be your problem.

The luxury home tax might be. Formally the solidarity tax, it applies when the construction value of a residence — the building and fixed installations, not the land — exceeds a threshold Hacienda updates each year for inflation. For 2026, Decreto 45358-H set that threshold at ₡143 million, roughly $315,000 at the Central Bank reference rate in late July 2026.

Above it, rates run from 0.25 to 0.55 percent on a progressive scale. You declare it every three years on form D-174 and pay every January, through Hacienda’s TRIBU-CR system. Plenty of the properties marketed to foreign buyers cross that line. Note how the two halves work, because it catches people out. Only the construction value decides whether you owe the tax at all. Once you cross the threshold, the land goes into the base you are taxed on, valued from Hacienda’s zone maps, and in a condominium you pick up a share of the common areas as well. A modest house on an expensive lot can trip the threshold and then be assessed on a far larger figure than the building alone.

Condominium fees are where the real money goes. In the gated developments popular with foreign buyers, monthly fees covering security, landscaping, pool and building maintenance commonly run from a couple of hundred dollars to well over a thousand. You owe them whether or not you are in the country. They rise over time. And the owners’ assembly can vote extraordinary assessments for a new roof or a failed pump, which arrive as a bill you did not budget for.

Then there is the structure. Many foreign buyers hold property through a corporation, which brings an annual corporate tax, a resident agent and legal fees every year for as long as you own.

What it costs to get in and out

This is the part that decides whether buying makes sense for you, and the part listings never mention. Going in, expect roughly 3.5 to 4 percent of the purchase price in transaction costs. The transfer tax alone is 1.5 percent of the registered value, with notary fees, registry stamps and legal work on top. Buyer and seller often split some of it, but that is negotiated, not automatic.

Coming out is worse, and it is worse specifically for people who have already left. Agent commission typically runs 5 to 6 percent, with value-added tax on the commission. On the gain itself, the standard rate is 15 percent. If you bought before July 1, 2019, you may instead elect a flat 2.25 percent of the total sale price, which usually wins for long-held property. If the home was your primary residence, the gain is generally exempt.

The rule that catches foreign sellers is the withholding. Hacienda spent 2025 revising this: a September resolution created withholding obligations for both resident and non-resident sellers, then a second resolution published in early October repealed it and kept only one. What survives is a 2.5 percent withholding on the sale price when the seller is not domiciled in Costa Rica, under Article 28 ter of the Income Tax Law, declared on form 129 in TRIBU-CR.

Whether that 2.5 percent settles your liability outright or counts as a payment on account you can reconcile later is read differently by different tax practices here, so establish which treatment applies to you before you close rather than after. Domiciled sellers face no equivalent withholding. A 2 percent version was written into the September resolution but was repealed before it ever took effect.

Read that again if you are planning an eventual exit, because the definition is what matters. A foreign individual who spends fewer than 183 days a year in Costa Rica is not domiciled here. If you sell after you have already moved home, you are almost certainly the non-domiciled seller, and 2.5 percent of the gross price comes off the top regardless of whether you made money.

Add it up. A round trip on a Costa Rican property costs somewhere near ten percent of its value before a single month of fees or a single dollar of price movement. You need to hold long enough, or gain enough, to clear that. If there is a real chance you will want out inside five years, the arithmetic is not on your side.

The currency question cuts both ways

The colón has strengthened sharply against the dollar. It traded near ₡700 in mid-2022 and sat around ₡450 at the Central Bank reference rate in late July 2026. If your income arrives in dollars, your local purchasing power has fallen by roughly a third in four years. That is an argument for owning, but only a partial one. A colón-denominated rent rises in dollar terms every time the colón strengthens, while a paid-off house has no housing exposure at all.

A dollar-denominated lease, frozen for its term by Article 67, gives you close to the same protection for three years at a stretch without the purchase — and it is the reason the currency of your lease deserves more thought than most renters give it. Your groceries, your utilities and your medical care are priced in colones either way. Buying a house does not hedge your life, only your rent.

At the beach, you may not be buying ownership at all

Along the coast, Ley 6043 sets aside a 200-meter (656-foot) strip measured inland from the ordinary high tide line. The first 50 meters (164 feet) is public zone that nobody can own or fence, and mangroves and estuaries are public regardless of how far they extend. The next 150 meters (492 feet) is the restricted zone, where what changes hands is a municipal concession — a right to use the land for a term of five to twenty years, not title to it.

Foreigners face specific limits here. Article 47 bars concessions to foreigners who have not lived in the country for at least five years, and to companies whose shares or capital are more than half foreign-held. Existing concessions granted lawfully remain valid, but renewal and transfer are governed by those same rules.

Inland and outside that strip, the picture is simpler than most newcomers assume. Foreigners can hold titled property in their own name with the same rights as Costa Rican citizens. There is no foreign-buyer surcharge and no restriction on selling. The complication is coastal, not national — which is precisely where most people picture themselves living.

When buying is the right call

None of this makes ownership a mistake. If your horizon is long, the round-trip costs stop mattering. If the home is your primary residence and you are a tax resident here, the capital gains exemption removes the largest exit cost and the withholding does not apply. If you want to renovate, keep animals, plant something that takes years, or simply stop asking permission, owning is the only route.

There is also a supply problem renting does not solve. In several beach towns, long-term rental stock has been thinned by short-term vacation conversions, and what remains is expensive or poor quality. The flexibility argument works best where there is something to be flexible about, which in practice means the Central Valley and the larger coastal towns.

How to decide

Rent first, for at least a year, in the region you think you want. Green season is the honest test. If you still like a place in October, you like the place. Check the currency your lease is written in and whether it is a residential lease or a seasonal one. Those two details determine which protections you actually have.

Before you buy in a condominium, ask for the last two years of assembly minutes and the reserve fund balance. That tells you what is coming. Run your realistic holding period against the round-trip cost. If you cannot see yourself there in eight years, rent. And hire your own Costa Rican attorney, with no relationship to the seller or the agent, to run the title study and hold the funds.

Renting for years is not a failure to commit. It is a strategy built around keeping options open rather than accumulating equity, and in a market where the exit is slow and expensive and the law protects tenants better than most people realize, it is a defensible one. Buying is defensible too. What is hard to defend is deciding before you know which coast you want to wake up on.

This article is general information, not legal or tax advice. Tax thresholds and withholding rules change, sometimes within a single year. Consult a Costa Rican attorney and tax adviser before buying, selling or signing a long-term lease.

World.title: Fisherman fined for possession of crack pipe, denies resisting arrest
World.content:
Fisherman fined for possession of crack pipe, denies resisting arrest

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City fisherman was fined after pleading guilty to possession of a utensil used for smoking a controlled drug but denied a separate charge of resisting lawful arrest.

Richard Slusher, 35, of West Canal, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Monday on charges stemming from an incident on Sunday, August 2.

Police allege that officers stopped Slusher at the corner of West and Basra streets and found a metal pipe, believed to be used for smoking crack cocaine, concealed in the waist of his pants.

Slusher initially pleaded guilty to both charges. However, after the prosecution’s facts were read, he disputed the allegation that he resisted arrest and a not-guilty plea was entered on his behalf.

He was fined $150 plus $5 court costs for possession of the pipe and was given until September 30, 2026, to pay. Failure to pay will result in one week’s imprisonment.

Slusher was offered bail of $300 with one surety for the resisting-arrest charge, which he met after settling an outstanding court fine.

He is scheduled to return to court on September 7, 2026.

World.title: Mediation set for ‘Trinibad’ man accused of leaving Golden Bay Hotel with unpaid $11,000 bill
World.content:
Mediation set for ‘Trinibad’ man accused of leaving Golden Bay Hotel with unpaid $11,000 bill

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A mediation session has been scheduled for a Trinidadian national accused of leaving the Golden Bay Hotel without paying a bill of more than $11,000.

Rubindra Rampersad, 46, remains at the Belize Central Prison after being unable to satisfy his bail conditions, which reportedly include providing proof of a residence in Belize and securing a Belizean surety.

Rampersad’s attorney, Darrell Bradley, informed the court that mediation is scheduled for Thursday, August 13, 2026. The criminal matter is expected to return before the Chief Magistrate on August 20.

A successful mediation could lead to a resolution of the dispute and the eventual withdrawal of the criminal charge. However, the outcome will depend on whether an agreement can be reached with the hotel.

Rampersad is charged with making off without payment. He has pleaded not guilty to allegations that he left the Golden Bay Hotel on May 29 without settling an outstanding bill of $11,470.24.

Police allege that Rampersad stayed at the Belize City hotel from May 1 to May 29 after booking a double room with a credit card. The card was reportedly declined several times, while Rampersad allegedly requested extensions to his stay without making payment.

Hotel management allegedly discovered at around 6:00 a.m. on May 29 that Rampersad had left the property. Police subsequently detained him at the Philip Goldson International Airport as he was preparing to leave Belize.

Rampersad was initially denied bail because he was considered a flight risk due to his foreign nationality and lack of ties to Belize. Earlier reports said the court later indicated that bail could be considered once suitable accommodation and other assurances were provided.

He was escorted back to the Belize Central Prison on Tuesday after again being unable to meet the requirements for his release.

World.title: Two police officers convicted of manslaughter in death of Andrew Dougal
World.content:
Two police officers convicted of manslaughter in death of Andrew Dougal

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Two police officers have been convicted of manslaughter in connection with the 2022 death of 25-year-old Santa Cruz resident Andrew Dougal.

Justice Antoinette Moore delivered the guilty verdicts against officers John Lucas and Jaleel Lewis at around 12:30 p.m. on Tuesday, following their trial in the Belmopan High Court.

Both men were remanded pending sentencing, which has been scheduled for Tuesday, August 11, 2026.

Lucas was represented by attorney Audrey Matura, while attorney Hurl Hamilton represented Lewis. Crown Counsel Javier Chan prosecuted the case on behalf of the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions. Both officers exercised their right to remain silent during the trial.

The case arose after Dougal was allegedly beaten and forcefully placed into the back of a police pickup truck during an encounter with the officers in Santa Cruz. Cellphone footage later emerged showing portions of the incident.

Dougal subsequently died at the hospital after reportedly suffering internal bleeding and other complications from his injuries.

Matura said a central issue during the trial was Dougal’s haemophilia, an inherited condition that prevents the blood from clotting normally. The court considered whether injuries sustained during the encounter were worsened by the condition and ultimately led to his death.

World.title: 24-year-old Lennox Gentle charged with murder of Kiffer McKenzie
World.content:
24-year-old Lennox Gentle charged with murder of Kiffer McKenzie

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have formally arrested and charged 24-year-old Lennox Linford Gentle, a Belizean labourer of Belize City, with the murder of Kiffer Alexander McKenzie.

Gentle was charged on Tuesday, August 4, following an investigation into McKenzie’s killing, which occurred on June 13, 2026.

McKenzie, 29, was shot shortly after 10:00 a.m. while inside his vehicle on Albert Street in downtown Belize City. Children were reportedly inside the vehicle when the gunman opened fire. After being wounded, McKenzie lost control of the vehicle and crashed near the former Scotiabank building.

He was transported to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, where he succumbed to his injuries.

Police have not released further details regarding the evidence that led to Gentle’s arrest. He is expected to be arraigned in court on the murder charge.

World.title: One week after being busted in tourist’s stolen clothes, Collin Ramclam arrested for boisterous behavior over losing money in casino – Told police he was protected by God
World.content:
One week after being busted in tourist’s stolen clothes, Collin Ramclam arrested for boisterous behavior over losing money in casino – Told police he was protected by God

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A self-described Jehovah’s Witness who was convicted of theft last week returned to court on Tuesday, this time accused of behaving boisterously on Orange Street after allegedly losing his money gambling.

Collin Burton Ramclam, 37, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he pleaded not guilty to one count of boisterous behaviour. With no objection from the prosecution, he was offered bail of $200 plus one surety of the same amount. His next court appearance is scheduled for September 2, 2026.

Police allege that at around 2:30 a.m. on Tuesday, officers conducting foot patrols saw Ramclam walking from the direction of Albert Street toward the Pound Yard Bridge while shouting about money he had lost gambling at the Princess Casino on his birthday.

According to police, Ramclam continued shouting, used obscene language and refused instructions to leave the area quietly. He allegedly told officers that he was protected by God and could do whatever he wanted before he was detained and taken to the Precinct One Police Station.

Ramclam also allegedly confronted and threatened a court reporter while being escorted to court, accusing her of making him look foolish in a recent Breaking Belize News report.

His latest court appearance came one week after he pleaded guilty to stealing a suitcase belonging to 20-year-old French national Ange Cesar Cirnevin. Breaking Belize News previously reported that Ramclam admitted taking the unattended suitcase from a bus travelling from Belmopan to Belize City and was found wearing some of the tourist’s belongings.

Ramclam was subsequently fined $1,000 plus $5 cost of court, payable by October 30, 2026, or he will serve five months in prison in default.

World.title: Three men remanded after police find ammunition near abandoned vehicle
World.content:
Three men remanded after police find ammunition near abandoned vehicle

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Three Belize City men have been remanded to the Belize Central Prison after police allegedly found three live 9mm rounds in and around a vehicle abandoned on the Yabra Bridge.

Esmond Austin, 19, Devon Garcia, 21, and Isani Conorquie, 19, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where they were jointly charged with keeping ammunition without a gun licence. Garcia was additionally charged with obstruction.

Police say officers responded to the bridge at about 4:30 a.m. on Sunday, August 2, after receiving reports that a damaged black Ford Escape had been abandoned and several men were seen running from the area.

The three men were later detained and taken back to the scene. During a search, officers allegedly found one live round near the vehicle’s rear door, another inside the rear passenger area and a third inside a white cloth bag.

Police further allege that Garcia grabbed one of the rounds while officers were processing the vehicle and attempted to throw it into a nearby canal. The ammunition instead landed in an adjoining yard and was recovered.

Garcia initially pleaded guilty to obstruction but later disputed the facts presented by the prosecution. Austin and Conorquie also indicated that they wanted to plead guilty to the ammunition charge, but the Magistrate advised the men to seek legal advice before entering pleas.

Due to the nature of the ammunition charge, bail was denied and all three men were remanded until October 5, 2026.

World.title: Hold It In: Police alleged that man possessed firearm under the influence of alcohol but because he refused to give urine sample Court threw out the case
World.content:
Hold It In: Police alleged that man possessed firearm under the influence of alcohol but because he refused to give urine sample Court threw out the case

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City man walked free on Monday after the Chief Magistrate ruled that the facts presented by police did not support charges of possessing a firearm while under the influence of alcohol or drugs and failing to provide a specimen.

Dijon Jamaal Smith, 32, of Flamboyant Street, was initially remanded to the Belize Central Prison after pleading not guilty to the firearm-related offences. He was later returned to court after indicating that he wished to change his plea to guilty.

However, the Chief Magistrate declined to accept the guilty plea, finding that the prosecution’s account did not contain sufficient facts to establish the offences. The court noted that no urine or blood test had been obtained to prove that Smith was under the influence.

Police alleged that at approximately 1:26 a.m. on Monday, August 3, officers pursued a white Chevrolet Equinox that was reportedly travelling at high speed in Belize City. The vehicle was eventually stopped on Heart Street.

During a search, officers found a licensed firearm fitted with a drum magazine. Smith subsequently produced a valid firearm licence, but officers alleged that his speech was slurred and that they detected a strong smell of alcohol on his breath.

He was taken to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, where police said he refused to provide a urine or blood specimen. Officers later removed and counted 43 live 9mm rounds from the firearm’s magazine.

The court raised several procedural concerns, including whether Smith was provided with a suitable private facility to give a urine sample and whether he had been clearly informed that refusing to provide a specimen constituted an offence.

The Chief Magistrate ruled that a guilty plea could not be accepted where the underlying facts failed to establish the essential elements of the charges. Both matters were consequently dismissed and Smith was released.

World.title: UDP raises concerns over BTL’s reported acquisition of SMART
World.content:
UDP raises concerns over BTL’s reported acquisition of SMART

By Zoila Palma: The United Democratic Party (UDP) has criticized the decision by Belize Telemedia Limited (BTL) to proceed with the reported BZ$80 million acquisition of Speednet/SMART, saying the move lacks sufficient transparency and due diligence.

In a statement, the party said, “The acquisition of a strategic national asset using public resources should never proceed under a cloud of uncertainty,” adding that “Belizeans deserve to know whether this transaction represents value for money.” The UDP also argued that the Board ignored concerns raised by the Belize Chamber of Commerce and Industry, the National Trade Union Congress of Belize, and other stakeholders.

The UDP announced it will hold an urgent meeting with the NTUCB and called on the Public Utilities Commission to ensure a transparent review of the proposed acquisition. The party added it “will continue to hold the Government and all public officials accountable” over the transaction.

World.title: UHWI at fault
World.content:
A view of the University Hospital of the West Indies

The University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI) has been ordered to pay millions in damages after the Supreme Court found that the facility “fell below the standard of care” expected of it and also “breached the duty of care” provided to a 16-year-old girl, who died six days after being admitted to the hospital in March 2018.

The girl’s parents later sued the hospital’s board of management for failing to “use all proper professional skill, care, competence, and diligence during their investigation, diagnosis, management, and treatment of their only child”.

The court on Friday awarded $1,687,380.19 “for pain and suffering” endured by the child prior to her death. For loss of life/loss of expectation of life, the court awarded $344,127.70 with interest at three per cent per annum from April 15, 2021 to July 31 this year. In assessing how much the child, who was described as “a perennial high achiever” and a “polyglot” (a person who knows, speaks, or writes several different languages) would have lost in terms of earnings from before the trial to the last hearing date the court awarded $6 million. In satisfying the parent’s claims for special damages, the court awarded $975,573.41 plus interest of three per cent per annum, from the date she died to the date the judgement was handed down. It also awarded US$8,000 in respect of the report prepared by the expert witness relied on in the case.

The teenager who was described as “an accomplished and promising fifth-form student at Campion College, St Andrew” was preparing to sit the May/June sitting of the Caribbean Secondary Examination Council (CSEC) examinations at the time of her passing. She was said to have “entrepreneurial dreams and aspirations to become a scientist or a medical researcher”.

According to the civil negligence and estate lawsuit filed by her parents in the civil division of the Supreme Court in 2021, the young girl, on or around March 30, 2018 was admitted by the UHWI for treatment at its medical facility. Her mother said the ordeal began on March 27, 2018 when her daughter complained of what had become a persistent headache. She said after being examined by the family doctor, her daughter — who had also been warm to the touch — was prescribed medication. When that headache persisted three days later, along with weakness the parents — who said they began to “suspect that their daughter was suffering from another bout of meningitis, an illness with which she had been diagnosed at the age of eight years” — decided to take her to the UHWI.

Once there, they said they informed medical staff of her symptoms and history of meningitis as well as their suspicions. The parents said on March 31 after blood samples, a CT scan and an unsuccessful lumbar puncture procedure (which was to be done over), they were informed that their daughter was suffering from hemiplegic migraine. After some 18 seizures and two heart attacks, the teen who had also been placed on life support was pronounced dead on April 5, 2018.

Unmoored and set adrift by the loss of their child, the parents asserted that they suffered emotional and psychiatric distress. The father alleged that he became unable to focus, depressed and angry, making it difficult for him to hold onto a job. His wife maintained that, as a sales manager, the mental distress caused by, and the toll of, her daughter’s death affected her so drastically that she could not do her job as well as she did before.

According to court documents two medical professionals who gave evidence on behalf of the hospital maintained that the UHWI and its medical teams acted in accordance with standard practices and that there were no actions of negligence in the diagnosis, treatment and/or management of the teen.

However the court, in choosing to rely on the evidence of an expert witness called by the parents, said there were “aspects of negligence on the part of the UHWI, which are of great concern”.

“The documentary evidence discloses that, during the course of [her] admission to the UHWI, it was noted on three separate occasions that a diagnosis of meningitis was to be ruled out… in fact, it is readily apparent from the medical docket that no further attempt was made to rule out or to exclude the differential diagnosis of meningitis. This court is of the view that there is an absolute need for a physician to ensure that sufficient tests and detailed investigations are conducted before ruling out one disease over another. Negligence must be ascribed to the UHWI, by its servants and/or agents, for its failure to properly employ all usual diagnostic aids in ruling out the possibility of meningitis, including a lumbar puncture test,” the court said.

“The court finds that the UHWI was negligent in the failure on the part of its servants and/or agents to recognise that [name withheld] was brain-dead on 1 April 2018 at 11:00 pm. The evidence of the rapid deterioration in [the child’s] condition in the five days following her admission to the UHWI is concerning,” said the ruling handed down by Supreme Court Justice Anne-Marie Nembhard.

“The court finds that there was no clear plan of treatment, on the part of the servants and/or agents of the UHWI, to treat [her] in the face of her rapid deterioration, whilst being admitted as a patient to the UHWI. Nor does there seem to have been a corresponding, commensurate escalation in the UHWI’s plan of treatment or course of treatment in the face of her rapid deterioration,” the justice added.

In additional findings, the court said based on the evidence of the expert witness, an accurate diagnosis could have been arrived at, had a lumbar puncture been performed.

World.title: Daydreams shows up white-hot before YUSH nostalgia
World.content:
Dexta Daps holds a vibe onstage at Daydreams on Saturday at the Montego Bay Convention Centre.

MONTEGO BAY, St James — Dream Wknd transformed the Montego Bay Convention Centre into two completely different worlds on Saturday. From the elegance and romance of Daydreams to the nostalgic throwback energy of YUSH, patrons experienced a seamless journey through two distinct eras of music and celebration.

The afternoon belonged to Daydreams, where thousands dressed in all white filled the venue for one of the festival’s most-anticipated events. Against a backdrop of premium décor, unlimited drinks, and an atmosphere that balanced sophistication with celebration, patrons eagerly awaited dancehall’s leading man, Dexta Daps. And the singer delivered exactly what fans had come for.

Opening to deafening screams, Dexta Daps commanded the stage with a performance that blended passion, charisma, and crowd interaction. Couples embraced, friends sang ‘at the top of their lungs’, and phones lit up the venue as fans captured every moment.

His catalogue of hits, including WIFI, Owner, Call Me If, and Breaking News, had the ladies in the audience swooning and singing every word.

For nearly an hour the space became less of a concert venue and more of a shared celebration of music, romance, and dancehall culture, led by Dexta Daps.

For Sophia Khan, who flew in from Birmingham, Daydreams stood out as one of the highlights of Dream Wknd.

“This is my first-ever Dream Wknd, and Daydreams has definitely lived up to the hype. The vibe was amazing, the all-white theme looked so good, and Dexta Daps gave us everything we wanted. It’s one of those events you don’t want to leave,” she said.

As the sun went down, the atmosphere shifted from polished and elegant to playful and nostalgic as YUSH took over.

Presented by Casamigos, the throwback event invited patrons to relive their school days with a uniform dress code that saw party-goers arriving in creative takes on the classic classroom looks. This set the tone for an evening dedicated to celebrating the unforgettable sounds, style, and spirit of the late 1990s and early 2000s.

The nostalgia only intensified once the music started. Dancehall star Tifa took to the stage first, delivering a high-energy performance from the opening song. She set the tone for the night with a string of crowd-favourites before passing the baton to dancehall veteran Elephant Man, who raised the energy even further with his trademark infectious hits and signature dance moves. Together, the performances perfectly complemented the event’s retro concept, transporting the audience back to one of dancehall’s most celebrated eras.

The seamless transition highlighted the festival’s ability to deliver distinctly different experiences, each with its own unique personality while maintaining the premium standard patrons have come to expect.

Scott Dunn, group managing director of Dream Entertainment, expressed that, “Saturday really showcased what Dream Wknd is all about, offering completely different experiences within the same festival while maintaining the same level of quality. Daydreams delivered the premium, feel-good atmosphere we envisioned, and then YUSH allowed patrons to relive the music and culture that defined an era. Watching thousands of people fully embrace both concepts is incredibly rewarding and reinforces why Dream continues to evolve year after year.”

World.title: CREDIT CARD BALANCES HIT RECORD $94B
World.content:
Commercial banks are being urged to tighten their credit card lending practices after outstanding balances climbed to a record $94 billion, with one economist warning that the trend could push more households into financial distress.

Bank of Jamaica (BOJ) data show that commercial banks’ credit card receivables more than doubled in nominal terms, rising from $40.2 billion in 2017 to $94 billion as at April 2026. The central bank’s record shows 435,883 credit cards were in circulation at the end of 2025.

Economist and researcher Janiel McEwan in an interview with the Jamaica Observer said that while consumers must take responsibility for managing their finances, financial institutions should also shoulder some of the blame for encouraging borrowing through aggressive marketing and automatic credit-limit increases, while charging what he described as some of the highest credit card interest rates in the region.

“Banks have made borrowing much easier to say yes to, which from a marketing perspective is not inherently harmful, but they also have a fiduciary responsibility to ensure that they are lending responsibly. If they know someone is consistently struggling to meet repayments, there should be programmes to restructure those obligations before the debt spirals out of control,” he told the Business Observer.

“Credit by itself is not the enemy. Used wisely, it can open doors to opportunity. But without proper understanding, it can become a burden,” he added.

McEwan said the persistent rise in credit card balances could not be attributed solely to reckless spending, pointing to a combination of stagnant wage growth, persistent inflation, high transportation and living costs, and elevated borrowing costs as contributing factors.

“Wage growth is not keeping pace with the cost of living for many people. As such credit cards have increasingly become a backup plan or a social safety net for many households that are trying to manage everyday expenses,” he said, adding that credit card debt in Jamaica has not spiked overnight but has climbed steadily for about a decade, interrupted only briefly by the pandemic, with growth accelerating since 2023.

McEwan said annual credit card interest rates in Jamaica typically range from 35 and 40 per cent, which he contrasted with average rates of about 20 per cent in the United States.

“These interest rates are among the highest consumers will encounter in the financial system. Once people are unable to pay the balance in full, the debt accumulates very quickly,” McEwan noted.

Criticising what he described as aggressive marketing practices by some financial institutions, he said consumers are routinely encouraged to take up new credit cards or accept higher credit limits while receiving little guidance on responsible borrowing.

“They tell you that you can get the card without paying anything upfront and encourage you to spend beyond your income. But many people do not fully understand how interest compounds once the payment period expires,” he said.

Stressing the need for lenders to undertake more robust affordability assessments before issuing cards or increasing credit limits, McEwan deemed this a more worthwhile strategy than relying primarily on customers’ banking relationships.

“They should not simply look at someone’s salary and decide they qualify for a larger limit. Banks need to determine whether that person can realistically service the debt,” he said.

While acknowledging that lenders face genuine risks from loan defaults, he argued that profitability should not come at the expense of responsible lending.

As he called on the central bank to strengthen oversight of consumer lending, he said there is an immediate need for the BOJ as regulator to require that financial institutions adopt stricter affordability standards and more responsible credit practices.

Beyond regulation, McEwan also said Jamaica urgently needs financial literacy programmes that focus specifically on the responsible use of credit rather than general savings education.

“We have spent years promoting saving, but we also need to teach people how credit works, how interest accumulates and the long-term consequences of carrying balances month after month,” he said.

He argued that financial education should begin at an early age and become a core part of the local school curriculum, while public awareness campaigns should also be rolled out to target existing credit card users.

McEwan suggested that while higher-income earners may use credit cards strategically to earn rewards while investing their cash elsewhere, much of the country’s growing credit card debt is likely concentrated among middle- and lower-income households struggling with rising living costs.

“The people who understand credit tend to use it as a financial tool. The concern, however, is with those who are relying on it simply to make ends meet,” he said.

While stopping short of declaring that Jamaica has entered a full-scale debt crisis, McEwan warned that current trends suggest the country is moving in that direction if borrowing continues to outpace repayment.

“When one looks at the size of the outstanding balance, the number of repossessions by banks now taking place and the financial pressures households are facing… we are moving dangerously close to a debt crisis,” he said.

To this end, he urged banks to adopt more responsible lending practices and to tailor credit limits that are in line with the customers’ ability to repay and where possible to offer debt restructuring options for those borrowers showing signs of financial distress.

“Financial institutions should also be more considerate in deciding who gets a credit card and also what limit they receive. Better guardrails now could help to prevent much bigger problems later,” McEwan concluded.

World.title: ON THE ROPES
World.content:
Bowler Ali Usman (right) of Pakistan celebrates after he caught and bowled batter Roston Chase (unseen) of West Indies as non-striking batter Justin Greaves (left) looks on during the third day of their second Test match at Queen’s Park Oval in Port of Spain, Trinidad and Tobago, on Tuesday. (Photo: AFP)

PORT OF SPAIN, Trinidad (CMC) — Jomel Warrican continued his love affair with Pakistan’s batters, but the visitors’ spinning duo of Sajid Khan and Ali Usman grabbed six wickets in the final session to leave West Indies on the brink of defeat in the second and final Test here on Tuesday.

On a pitch offering significant assistance to the spinners, Khan and Usman bemused the Windies’ batters to leave them reeling on 103 for six at the end of day three at the Queen’s Park Oval — an overall lead of only 60 runs.

Those late strikes overshadowed an earlier impressive bowling spell by Warrican, that saw him record his second-best figures of 6-112 and claim his third five-wicket haul in Tests — all of them against Pakistan.

His efforts helped the home side fight their way back into the match after Pakistan, who resumed the day comfortably placed at 266 for two, were bowled out for 387 in reply to the Windies’ 344.

West Indies reaped success early on when Pakistan captain Babar Azam, who failed to add to his overnight score of 88, was run out by a direct throw from Brandon King at cover, following a mix up with Abdullah Shafique.

That proved to be a bittersweet moment for the Windies, as King was injured in the process and had to be stretchered off the field.

An update from Cricket West Indies (CWI) revealed that the opener was experiencing lower back spasms and he did not return to the field for the remainder of the day.

Warrican then bowled Awais Zafar and Mohammad Rizwan, while pacer Shamar Joseph trapped Salman Agha lbw for a duck to see Pakistan slip to 311 for six.

However, Shafique continued to defy the Windies’ bowlers and he reached 150 during a 59-run partnership with Khan that gave them the lead.

But once Jayden Seales had Khan caught behind for 30, Warrican cleaned up the tail by dismissing Usman, Ubaid Shah and Mohammad Ali in the space of four deliveries.

Shafique remained unbeaten on 160 off 323 balls and hit 15 fours and three sixes.

Faced with a slender deficit of 43 runs, West Indies made a positive start with Tagenarine Chanderpaul and makeshift opener Kavem Hodge all but erasing it during a stand of 40 runs for the first wicket.

However, the introduction of Khan in the 10th over changed the complexion of the match as he had Chanderpaul lbw with his second ball.

Amir Jangoo and Hodge ensured the Windies wiped away the deficit, but shortly after Khan struck again by bowling Jangoo for 13 with a delivery that straightened to leave them 62 for two.

Usman then got the key wicket of Hodge for 34. A voracious appeal for lbw was turned down by the umpire, but the review showed the ball crashing into the stumps to make it 74 for three.

Shai Hope was then undone by a delivery from Khan that kept low to be lbw for 15 and two runs later Khan also accounted for the wicket of nightwatchman Jayden Seales for a duck.

With the close of play in sight, Roston Chase drove a delivery straight back into the hands of Usman in what turned out to be the last ball of the day, with the Windies essentially 60 for six heading into the penultimate day of play.

Khan has so far taken 4-32, while Usman has grabbed 2-29.

World.title: Paramount pursues international lubricant deal
World.content:
Lubricant being poured from a container. Paramount Trading (Jamaica) Limited is negotiating to manufacture lubricant brands for an international marketer serving local and export markets. .

PARAMOUNT Trading (Jamaica) Limited is negotiating with an unnamed international lubricant marketer to manufacture its brands in Jamaica for local and export markets, a prospective arrangement that could reshape the company’s lubricant operation, although there is no timetable for concluding the negotiations.

Chief Executive Officer Hugh Graham said Paramount deliberately reduced some existing lubricant production to preserve blending capacity for the prospective customer.

“We have a big player at the table that would take up all the capacity that we have,” Graham told the Jamaica Observer on Tuesday.

If an agreement is reached, he said, Paramount may eventually have to expand its plant.

Graham did not identify the customer or disclose the proposed contract’s value, duration, production volumes or export markets. He also did not say whether the parties had signed a preliminary agreement.

He said Paramount had obtained certification to standards developed by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) as part of its preparations. Graham described the prospective customer as “one of the biggest marketers in the world”.

Graham said he hoped the negotiations would conclude soon but could not provide a timetable, citing the war in West Asia and volatility in the global oil industry.

His explanation provides context for the 43.1 per cent decline in lubricant revenue during the year ended May 31, 2026. Sales from the division fell to $60.6 million from $106.4 million a year earlier. Paramount has not quantified how much of that decline resulted from the production cut or disclosed when the reduction began.

The discussions form part of Paramount’s plan to shift towards contract manufacturing. Under that model, the company blends and packages lubricants for customers that already have established brands and distribution networks.

“We prefer to produce and have someone else market it,” Graham told the Business Observer.

Paramount already manufactures Futrol lubricants for Future Energy Source Company Limited (Fesco) and the ALTRA brand for Allegheny Petroleum Products Company. Based on Graham’s description, the proposed international arrangement would apply that model on a much larger scale, with production intended for Jamaica and export markets.

The negotiations come after a financial year in which Paramount’s profit recovered but revenue declined.

Total revenue fell 2.1 per cent to $1.69 billion. Chemicals, the company’s largest division, declined 6.9 per cent to $1.13 billion, while lubricants recorded the steepest contraction.

Growth in smaller divisions partly offset those declines. Revenue from construction products and adhesives increased 26.7 per cent to $251.3 million, while manufacturing revenue rose 16.8 per cent to $228.2 million.

Graham expects sales of construction chemicals to benefit from high-rise developments, underground parking facilities, water-storage projects and hotel renovations. Paramount distributes Sika-branded construction products.

He also expects demand to recover among hotels and industrial and water-treatment customers affected by Hurricane Melissa. Paramount, however, has not issued a formal revenue or profit forecast for the new financial year.

Net profit increased to $99.1 million from $26.1 million, although the improvement was supported substantially by $138.1 million in other operating income rather than higher sales.

The largest disclosed item was the write-off of a vendor liability of approximately $54 million after Paramount was informed that the obligation had been settled by the vendor’s parent company. Other operating income included a $33-million unrealised foreign-exchange gain, $33.9 million from services and $10.5 million arising from the termination of a lease.

All were reflected in Paramount’s audited profit, but some may not recur at the same level. A calculation using the audited figures shows that before other operating income and expenses were taken into account, gross profit after administrative, selling and distribution expenses fell to approximately $77.8 million from $153.2 million a year earlier.

Paramount also increased its provision for customer debts that may not be collected to $96.2 million from $50.4 million. At the end of May, approximately $215.9 million — nearly half of gross trade receivables — had been outstanding for more than 90 days.

World.title: Honours Overdue: The music icons Jamaica still hasn’t recognised
World.content:
Recipients of the National Honours and Awards will be announced this week by the government of Jamaica. Today, we look at stalwarts of the country’s music industry whose contributions have never been recognised.

Earl “Chinna” Smith

Arguably the most prolific session musician in the history of reggae, Smith has played on classic songs by Dennis Brown (Westbound Train, Cassandra), Bob Marley (Rastaman Vibration), and Burning Spear (Marcus Garvey). His licks can also be heard on Grammy-winning albums by Ziggy Marley and The Melody Makers and Lauryn Hill, as well as Amy Winehouse’s first album. In October 2023, Rolling Stone Magazine named Smith at #182 on its 250 Greatest Guitarists of All Time.

Lynn Taitt

The Trinidadian guitarist is credited with starting rocksteady. He reportedly directed the 1966 recording session that resulted in Take it Easy by Hopeton Lewis, the song many musicologists believe launched that genre. Taitt played on numerous hit songs including the Shank I Sheck rhythm; (007) Shantytown and Israelites by Desmond Dekker and The Aces; Stop That Train by Keith and Tex; and Walk The Street at Night by Derrick Harriott. Lynn Taitt — who was named at #204 on Rolling Stone Magazine’s 250 Greatest Guitarists of All Time in 2023 — died in 2010.

The Abyssinians

The legendary roots trio are best known for the seminal Sata Masa Gana, the 1971 song considered by many to be reggae’s official anthem. Bernard Collins, Donald Manning and Lynford Manning comprised the most famous version of the group, which still tours with Donald in its lineup. Declaration of Rights and Forward On To Zion are other famous songs by The Abyssinians.

Tenor Saw

Maybe the most original dancehall singer. His unique yodel made songs like Pumpkin Belly, Golden Hen and Ring The Alarm standards. That sound influenced singers such as Anthony Redrose and King Kong. Tenor Saw died in 1985.

Sister Nancy

A pioneer female deejay who made her name on sound systems before rocking the mic for producer Winston Riley in the early 1980s. It was Riley who produced Bam Bam, the 1983 song that remains her signature. Bam Bam has been used in ads by major companies such as Reebok, and sampled by heavyweight rappers including Jay Z.

Stanley Beckford

The four-star general of mento! Stanley was not only a fixture of the Festival Song Competition (which he won three times), but he had hit songs during the 1970s when mento was shunned as ‘old people music’. Soldering (recorded with The Starlights), Broom Weed and Brown Gal were some of his popular songs. He died in 2007.

Sanchez

The dancehall Sinatra, Sanchez ruled the roost during the 1980s and 1990s with a series of hit songs. They include Loneliness, Baby Can I Hold You, I Can’t Wait, Here I Am and Brown Eye Girl.

Flabba Holt

Bassist and founder of The Roots Radics Band, he is a ‘foundation’ of contemporary dancehall. Gunman (Michael Palmer), Big Ship (Freddie McGregor), Night Nurse (Gregory Isaacs), Police In Helicopter (John Holt) and Wa Do Dem by Eek A Mouse are some of the songs he played on. He can also be heard on albums by Bunny Wailer and Israel Vibration.

The first winner of the Best Reggae Album (then known as Best Reggae Recording) Grammy, this group earned their stripes with edgy Sly and Robbie-produced songs like Plastic Smile, Abortion, General Penitentiary and Guess Who’s Coming to Dinner. Mykal Rose, Duckie Simpson and Puma Jones (who died in 1990) comprised the most successful version of the group.

Wycliffe “Steely” Johnson

One of the godfathers of digital dancehall, this talented keyboardist was a member of The Roots Radics Band before forming a mega partnership with drummer Cleveland Browne, known as Steely and Clevie. They played on and produced countless hit songs including No, No, No by Dawn Penn; Love Is The Answer by Garnet Silk; Fast Car by Foxy Brown and Trailer Load A Girls by Shabba Ranks. Steely died in 2009.

The Grace Thrillers

Formed in the early 1970s by Noel Willis, this group were the first successful exponents of what became gospel-reggae. Spiritual songs like Can’t Even Walk, Jesus and He’s Alive were played in dancehalls and drew ‘forwards’ from the most hardened ‘rude bwoys’.

Winston Wallace

This former educator and trade unionist wrote Land of My Birth, the unofficial national anthem of Jamaica. That song, by Eric Donaldson, won the Festival Song Competition in 1978. The previous year, they won that contest with Sweet Jamaica. Land of My Birth transcends ‘Festival’, and is played at national events in Jamaica and its Diaspora.

World.title: CLA weeds out high fees
World.content:
From left: Walter Melbourne, Cannabis Licensing Authority’s (CLA) director of licensing and applications; CLA board chair Dr Nadeen Spence; Chief Executive Officer Farrah Blake; and Simoy Brown, director of public relations and communications, address journalists at yesterday’s Jamaica Observer Monday Exchange.(Photo: Joseph Wellington)

A craving for traditional marijuana farmers to be included in the regulated industry locally has prompted the Cannabis Licensing Authority (CLA) to relax and reduce some entry requirements, including the cost of registration, for easier access to the system.

The registration fee for ganja farmers, which was US$3,000, has been slashed to US$150 under a Cultivator’s Transitional Special Permit Programme introduced by the CLA.

This provides a phased pathway for traditional cannabis farmers to transition into the regulated industry while working toward full licensing compliance.

Addressing this week’s Jamaica Observer Monday Exchange at the newspaper’s head office in St Andrew, senior members of the CLA, including board chair Dr Nadeen Spence and Chief Executive Officer Farrah Blake, were adamant that the new moves are intended to open the doors to the regulated industry for traditional ganja farmers, and were in no way an attempt to shut them down.

Spence told Observer editors and reporters that there are many traditional ganja farmers who yearn to be a part of the regulated industry and the CLA is ready and willing to assist them in doing so.

“Those who want to do business in the medical cannabis industry, we will give them the information to do so if they want,” Spence said.

“The CLA processes licences for those who would like to conduct business, conduct operations [under the Dangerous Drugs Act]. For those who want to be involved, we want to provide as much information and guidance as possible,” added Spence.

She pointed to an ongoing roadshow which forms part of the initiatives that the CLA has embarked on to attract small farmers.

This is designed to expand participation in the sector as well as to guide applicants and promote the medical cannabis special permit programmes, such as the community and transitional cultivators’ permit.

Meanwhile, Blake said the roadshows are a source of education for the public and an opportunity for officials of the CLA to meet face-to-face with people who want to enter the regulated industry.

“There is going to be, maybe, some apprehension about engaging us through these programmes. The islandwide road tour is to ensure that we have that face-to-face interaction. If there’s assistance needed to complete the forms, we’re there to do that. If there’s assistance needed to determine whether or not these farming programmes are for you, we can give that advice. We can also give advice about the existing licensing products that we have,” said Blake as she underscored that farmers who are not currently regulated will not be reported to law enforcement agencies.

“You have to understand that me asking you to come into the legal space is not to try to burn down your farms or anything like that. The law of the amended Dangerous Drugs Act provides for the religious side and it provides for the commercial side. That is where the CLA operates, within the commercial space. So we try to encourage the public to stay on the right side of the law, come into the legal framework, and operate there. These farming programmes are created to further engage traditional farmers who might not have wanted to participate as of 2015 to now. We’re not planning to report you. We’re not calling the police on you,” insisted Blake.

She was supported by Walter Melbourne, the CLA’s director of licensing and applications, who scoffed at claims that there is no room for small ganja farmers in the regulated industry.

“That is why we have the cultivators’ permit. Those persons who would not have the necessary skills and requirements, moneywise as well, you could come in, and we’ll accept you into the programme. There’s a US$150 application fee and there are no more [fees] once you’re qualified,” said Melbourne.

“It is actually creating a pathway for the small man,” added Melbourne as he indicated that the CLA is prepared to hold the hands of people who want to enter the formal system and guide them through the entire process.

For the people concerned about whether they will be able to continue to operate their farms while they transition through the programme, Melbourne said they would be given special permits once they meet the requirements, which, he pointed out, are no longer very strict.

“You would have to make an application to come into the system and [the programme] is for two years. It is meant to allow you to transition. We’ll hold your hand, show you what to do. We have a Cannabis Specialisation Unit within the CLA that will assist you in terms of growing techniques, everything that you need to assist you to ensure that it’s viable. We have the requisite resources within the authority to assist you. You just have to make the application. We will assist you in guiding you in setting up your home, to set up your farm, and all of that, and you make the transition.

“We’ll go through line by line with you. I’ve seen situations in which a person cannot read or write, and I’m not mentioning this to be discriminatory or anything, but to show that we are very inclusive, in the sense that if persons cannot read or write, we’ll hold your hand. People will actually fill out the form and show you where to sign. So you take in stuff to us, like what area of land are you going to use… do you have a lease agreement? Do you have a title? Land is not a sore issue, in the sense that if you don’t even have title to it, we will say, if you have been farming the land for some time, occupying the land, we’ll take declarations from persons who have known the land for several years, just to verify and just to authenticate the fact that you have been occupying the land,” added Melbourne, as he explained that the process to become registered could take up to five months.

World.title: Gateway to Africa
World.content:
Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama (left) shakes hands with Prime Minister of Jamaica Dr Andrew Holness following their media briefing at the Office of the Prime Minister on Monday. (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

JAMAICAN manufacturers and exporters could soon gain easier access to a market of 1.4 billion people worth nearly US$3 trillion after Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama announced on Monday that he intends to push for the Caribbean’s inclusion in Africa’s free trade area next year.

Mahama also said Ghana would fast-track parliamentary approval of the air services agreement to allow direct flights between its capital, Accra, and Montego Bay, a move expected to strengthen trade, tourism and investment between the two countries.

Speaking during a media briefing with Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness as part of his four-day state visit to Jamaica, Mahama said discussions between the two leaders had focused on moving the long-standing historical relationship between Ghana and Jamaica beyond shared heritage and towards deeper economic cooperation.

He said Ghana intends to use its chairmanship of the African Union (AU) next year to pursue closer trade ties between Africa and the Caribbean, arguing that stronger commercial partnerships must become the next phase of Pan-African cooperation.

“When I was speaking with Mr Prime Minister, I said that one of the things that I would champion when I become AU chair next year… is to expand the remit of the African continental free trade area to include the Caribbean. We set up the African continental free trade area that allows us to export goods duty-free and tariff-free into each other’s markets. That’s a 1.4 billion population market, and that also is a 1.3 trillion GDP economy, and so we can plug the Caribbean in so that we can exchange goods between Africa and the Caribbean duty-free, tariff-free,” he announced.

The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), which came into force in 2021, is the world’s largest free trade area by the number of participating countries and is designed to boost trade by reducing tariffs and other barriers among African nations. Mahama suggested extending that framework to the Caribbean would significantly broaden opportunities for businesses on both sides of the Atlantic.

He added that improved transport links would be critical to making those ambitions a reality, revealing that Ghana intends to move quickly to activate the air services agreement negotiated between the two countries.

“We have to activate the bilateral air services agreement between us, and it’s currently before our Parliament, and we’ll fast-track it so that it becomes operational, so that either national carriers between Jamaica and Ghana or third-party carriers can fly direct flights from Accra to Montego Bay,” he said.

Holness welcomed the commitment, saying direct air links would represent one of the most tangible outcomes of the state visit and could help unlock greater tourism, trade and investment between the two countries.

“Africa is the fastest-growing continent both in terms of demographics and in terms of their economies. It is an area which we have paid as a people great rhetoric, we’ve always been speaking about south-south cooperation. What I try to do is to find meaningful, tangible ways in which we can bring this cooperation to fulfilment. Clearly, Marcus Garvey set the foundation, connecting us intellectually, connecting us as a people. We now must take that and create… the economic emancipation of our people,” he said.

Holness noted that the state visit should not be viewed as merely symbolic, stressing that both governments are seeking practical outcomes capable of generating jobs, investment and long-term economic growth.

“We have focused primarily on, from a tourism perspective, trade and services, heavily on North American and European markets of late South American markets. But now we have to turn our attention to the African continent where there is a growing middle class who wants to travel, who wants to experience the world and who could be right at home and comfortable right here in Jamaica. So we see these visits as not just courtesies; these visits are important to set the foundation for the trade in goods and services that will come,” he said.

Beyond aviation, both leaders outlined plans to strengthen logistics and maritime cooperation, viewing their countries as strategic gateways to their respective regions.

Holness pointed to Jamaica’s continued investment in expanding the Port of Kingston, while noting Ghana is pursuing similar ambitions in West Africa. He said connecting the two logistics hubs could create more efficient trade routes for exporters and investors.

Mahama echoed that view, saying the Atlantic should become a conduit for commerce rather than a barrier separating the two regions.

World.title: Europe’s Palantir problem
World.content:
Europe wants to kick its U.S. tech habit, but it’s struggling to detangle itself from American data analytics firm Palantir.

The problem is, the company’s tools are already deeply embedded in critical sectors across the bloc like policing, national defense and health systems. A report released today also shows that the tech firm has found ways to pay minimal taxes in Europe. On the show, hosts Zoya Sheftalovich and Ian Wishart discuss European alternatives and why detaching is easier said than done.

Next, our colleague Seb Starcevic has interviewed Mediterranean Commissioner Dubravka Šuica. The role that was originally thought to be low profile has instead thrust the Croatian official into the limelight as various crises hit the Middle East and the Mediterranean.

Plus: Three new foods are being added to the EU’s list of products with geographic indicators. These are the labels given to products that can only be made in a specific region, like Champagne or … yes, you guessed it, halloumi.

World.title: Electricité : à gauche, Bernard Cazeneuve joue sa propre partition
World.content:
En 2011, il n’avait rejoint l’équipe de François Hollande pendant sa campagne victorieuse qu’à la condition que le candidat retire de son programme l’arrêt annoncé de la production de combustible MOX en France — suivant une recommandation d’Areva, son producteur.

Dans la Sarthe fin juin, invité par son ancien collègue de gouvernement Stéphane Le Foll, actuel maire du Mans, à s’exprimer sur son programme en matière de nucléaire, l’ancien Premier ministre n’hésitait pas à critiquer La France insoumise et les Ecologistes qui se “trompent” en ne voulant pas faire comme lui. Surtout qu’il peut se prévaloir de sa constance sur la question, quand d’autres membres de son camp ont viré de bord.

Lorsqu’il quittait le pouvoir en 2017, en même temps que François Hollande, la France était engagée dans une trajectoire de réduction de sa production d’électricité nucléaire (une décision qu’il ne cautionne pas), avec une planification à mettre en œuvre pour fermer des réacteurs. Mais depuis, l’heure est à la relance : le prolongement de la quasi-totalité des réacteurs est examiné par le gouvernement, et de nouveaux doivent voir le jour dans une dizaine d’années.

Des conseillers pronucléaires

Pour élaborer son programme, Bernard Cazeneuve peut compter sur les éclairages de Marc Fontecave, chimiste et professeur au Collège de France, ou de Louis Gallois, ancien dirigeant de plusieurs entreprises publiques, ont confirmé les intéressés à POLITICO — le second n’a pas souhaité entrer dans le détail “d’échanges privés”.

Marc Fontecave, qui préside également le conseil scientifique d’EDF, se penche depuis plusieurs mois sur la stratégie énergétique du pays dans ses cours ouverts à tous au Collège de France. Le scientifique est un opposant aux “catastrophistes” du climat, le surnom qu’il donne aux militants Cyril Dion, Greta Thunberg ou Aurélien Barrau, auxquels il a consacré un livre.

Il siège également à l’Académie des sciences, qui a rendu un avis assez sévère — mais “équilibré”, selon Marc Fontecave — sur la feuille de route du gouvernement, notamment sur le soutien au développement des énergies renouvelables.
