Another key asset, which has remained almost entirely outside our foreign policy efforts, is the Circassian diaspora. Four million people spread across 50 countries represent a powerful resource we can genuinely rely on. More importantly, we should offer them the prospect of political cooperation.

Abkhazia can and should become the centre of the Circassian world as the only independent state of this sub-ethnic group. Our country can become the same kind of homeland for Circassians worldwide that Israel has become for Jews. If every Circassian, wherever they live, knows they will find protection and support for their interests in Abkhazia, it will create a strong foundation for advancing our shared interests.”

Bzhania concluded: “It will probably not happen tomorrow, no matter how much effort we put in. But it can happen within a foreseeable future if those efforts remain consistent and systematic.

In 2017, I had the honour of welcoming a delegation from Nauru’s parliament to Abkhazia on behalf of the Abkhaz parliament. They were wonderful, warm people. Unfortunately, ships at sea do not only meet – they also part ways. Today, Nauru has set a course away from Abkhazia, apparently believing it to be the safer option. I wish them well. As for us, we will continue on our own course.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Nauru’s withdrawal of recognition of Abkhazia

World.title: “For safe and strong Georgia”: Saturday march in Tbilisi. Georgia protests video blog
World.content:
612th day of protests in Tbilisi

“For a Safe and Strong Georgia” was the main slogan of the traditional pro-European Saturday march held in Tbilisi on 1 August 2026.

Before the march began, participants observed a minute’s silence in memory of a teenager who was recently killed in central Tbilisi and who would have turned 18 today.

Hundreds of people gathered once again in Avlabari Square for the 612th consecutive day of protests. With construction work continuing on Rustaveli Avenue, the march followed an alternative route for the second Saturday in a row, starting at Avlabari metro station and ending outside the parliament building.

For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms. For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners, new parliamentary elections – as they do not recognize the results of the 2024 vote – and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years. To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

612th day of protests in Tbilisi

World.title: Hawks' Wizard looking to pull off Coleman medal shock
World.content:
Hawthorn coach Sam Mitchell has sung the praises of Nick Watson as the 170cm "Wizard" attempts to snare what would be one of the most unlikely and magical Coleman medals in VFL/AFL history.

Watson's five-goal haul in last week's 16-point win over North Melbourne lifted his season tally to 52 goals.

It means Watson became the first player since Syd Dyer and Lou Richards in 1946 to kick 50-plus goals in a season despite being 170cm or shorter.

Sydney's 194cm forward Charlie Curnow leads this year's Coleman medal count with 57 goals, with Gold Coast's 202cm spearhead Ben King (53 goals) in second and Watson lurking in third.

AFL round 21 Saturday live updates Josh Fraser's bid to become Carlton's next full-time coach receives a massive boost as the Blues record a thumping win over the Brisbane Lions.

Hawthorn face Brisbane at the Gabba on Friday night before rounding out their home-and-away campaign against Collingwood and West Coast.

A big finish from Watson could be enough to snare him the Coleman, and although Mitchell says the Hawks won't go out of their way to target him in the next three weeks, they would celebrate his achievement if he gets there.

"It'd be great if it happened," Mitchell said.

"But he's young and he's got plenty of opportunities in front of him.

"I certainly hope that's not the focus of the lads going into a game like this. But I won't be shying away from it if he gets that opportunity, of course."

Watson, fondly dubbed "The Wizard", is already a superstar of the competition despite being just 21 years old and 61 games into his AFL career.

"The level of consistency is probably the best thing that we've got from Wizard this year," Mitchell said.

"And it's probably one season earlier than most. He's certainly maturing. Like, he's 21 years old and he's quite popular, and how he handles that is really impressive."

Third-placed Hawthorn (14-5-1) haven't won at the Gabba since 2016, but they have only played three games at the venue since then.

Mitchell wants his team to use Friday's blockbuster against two-time defending premiers Brisbane (13-7) as an interstate finals rehearsal.

"I think if you look at the ladder most Victorian teams are going to have to win interstate at some point, and this is a start for us," said Mitchell, who earlier this week re-signed with Hawthorn until the end of 2030.

The Hawks have a number of selection queries heading into the crunch clash with Ned Reeves (knee), Karl Amon (knee), Mitch Lewis (concussion) and Henry Hustwaite (face) all under injury clouds.

Meanwhile, an American court has formally dismissed charges against Hawthorn player Connor Macdonald for his off-season misadventure.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Macdonald and teammate Dylan Moore spent a night in a US jail after being charged with trespassing for climbing onto a cherry picker.

Moore's case was wrapped up last month, while Macdonald's case has also now been concluded with the pair having previously agreed to complete a substance abuse counselling program.

"It's probably nice for them to have it off their back," Mitchell said.

"They're both having really good seasons and really pleased with their performances. Sometimes dealing with adversity can make you grow, and I think they've both done that this year."

AAP

World.title: Gold Coast pub assault victim in coma as accused refused bail
World.content:
A man charged over an alleged assault at a Gold Coast pub that left another man fighting for life has been denied bail.

Police allege 27-year-old Haami Makiroa Burns Prescott approached 36-year-old Ross Burckhardt in the car park of the Coomera Boathouse Tavern at about 1am on Sunday and punched him in the face.

Mr Burckhardt allegedly fell and suffered serious head injuries.

He was taken to Gold Coast University Hospital, where he remains in a critical condition.

Police further allege Mr Prescott fled the scene in a rideshare vehicle.

He was arrested at Ormeau on Monday and charged with one count of grievous bodily harm.

The alleged incident happened at the Boathouse Tavern in Coomera. (Supplied)

Mr Prescott appeared in Southport Magistrates Court on Wednesday, wearing a singlet and track pants, for a bail application.

His solicitor, Torik Dib, told the court his client had planned to surrender himself on Tuesday after receiving legal advice, but was arrested the day before.

"There was no information that was provided to him or myself in relation to any warrants that were outstanding," Mr Dib said.

Mr Dib also submitted that his client was acting in self-defence of another patron at the venue.

"At the time that they're leaving the venue, the complainant had a pool cue in his hand," Mr Dib said.

"He's arguing with the security guard while he's leaving the venue.

"There was a dispute between one of the other patrons, and that patron was with a female that was much smaller in size to the alleged complainant … he's being aggressive to two other people; that's the point where he allegedly assaults him."

Mr Prescott (pictured) was arrested on Monday. (Supplied: Queensland Police Service)

Police prosecutor Ricky Tsoi opposed bail, telling the court CCTV footage captured the alleged incident, and witnesses had "failed to identify mitigating circumstances in relation to the defendant's actions."

The court also heard Mr Prescott has a criminal history in New South Wales and is subject to a two-year community corrections order from Newcastle, which expires on December 28, 2027.

Acting Magistrate Gary Finger refused Mr Prescott bail, finding he was an "unacceptable risk of reoffending".

Mr Prescott was remanded in custody and will return to court next month.

Mr Prescott was refused bail. (ABC News: Kimberley Bernard)

Victim's family 'devastated'

Mr Burckhardt's brother, Paul Burckhardt, told the ABC his family were "devastated" by what had happened.

"Ross is a disability support worker who has dedicated his career to helping others," he said.

"He is a kind, compassionate person who is passionate about supporting people's mental health and wellbeing.

"Outside of work, he enjoys spending time with family and friends and loves playing pool."

Paul said his brother was in an induced coma in the intensive care unit.

"While we are incredibly grateful that his condition has remained stable, there is still significant swelling on his brain, and doctors continue to monitor him closely," he said.

World.title: Labor MP Luke Gosling set to be prosecuted for assault by Commonwealth DPP
World.content:
The Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions (Commonwealth DPP) is set to take over the case against Federal Labor MP Luke Gosling, to avoid a perceived conflict of interest within the Northern Territory Director of Public Prosecutions (NT DPP).

Mr Gosling, who has served as the Member for Solomon since 2016, was last week charged with two counts of allegedly assaulting Northern Territory Administrator David Connolly.

The NT administrator is the territory's equivalent of a state governor.

David Connolly was allegedly assaulted by Luke Gosling at a Thai festival in Darwin. (ABC News: Sam Parry)

According to a hearing in the Darwin Local Court on Friday, the charges relate to two separate incidents that occurred at the NT Thailand Grand Festival on July 18, including one in which Mr Gosling allegedly elbowed Mr Connolly.

At Friday's hearing, which led to changes to the terms of Mr Gosling's bail, the matter was prosecuted by a senior lawyer from the NT Police Force.

Luke Gosling banned from approaching NT Government House Federal Labor MP Luke Gosling has been banned from approaching Government House in Darwin after facing court for the first time since being charged with assaulting NT Administrator David Connolly.

However, the NT DPP today said in a statement it would not be taking carriage of the matter.

"The NT Director of Public Prosecutions received a brief from NT Police in relation to the matter," the statement said.

" The DPP determined that it should not have conduct of the matter, and the matter should be referred to another jurisdiction to avoid any perceived conflict of interest. "

"The NT DPP and Commonwealth DPP are in the process of arranging for the CDPP to take over the prosecution."

The NT DPP did not elaborate on the nature of the perceived conflict of interest.

The matter is due to return to court on September 30.

World.title: Australia's largest contiguous sheep station sold to Adelaide businessman
World.content:
Australia's largest contiguous sheep station has been bought by billionaire Adelaide businessman Khalil (Charlie) Shahin, whose family founded the On The Run (OTR) petrol station and convenience store network.

The three South Australian stations — which have a combined total of nearly 1.3 million hectares — were purchased for an undisclosed sum after being on the market for around two months.

Mr Shahin and his family have a combined wealth of $1.93 billion, putting them in the top 95 of Australia's richest families or individuals, according to this year's Rich List.

The family, who came to Australia as Palestinian refugees in the 1980s, founded OTR; a company they sold for $1.2bn in 2023. The sale for which was finalised last year.

Charlie and Fred Shahin. Fred started the family company, now Peregrine Corporation, with the purchase of a single service station in 1984. (Supplied)

The stations — Commonwealth Hill, Mobella and Bulgunnia — were all sold by the family farming dynasty the MacLachlans under the company name Jumbuck Pastoral.

The nearly 140-year-old company is one of Australia's oldest and most powerful farming families with an empire that extended across South Australia, Western Australia and New South Wales.

Elders Real Estate chief executive Tom Russo, who oversaw the sale, would not comment on how much the three properties sold for.

Speaking with the SA's Country Hour, Mr Russo said the 1.29 million hectares in South Australia's far north-west was "some of the largest sheep productions ever offered to the market".

"We saw corporate investors, both domestic and international, have a good look at this asset. We also saw really strong incumbent local pastoral families participate in the process and run the ruler over the assets," he said.

The 310,000ha Bulgunnia sheep station in SA's outback is a two-hour drive from Coober Pedy. (Supplied: Elders)

Mr Russo said the sale was part of the multi-generation farming family's proactive succession planning process.

"Like all families, there comes a point in time where succession planning needs to be done and ... they've divested a few stations now," he said.

"We can see now that that's the end of that ... and the group [Jumbuck Pastoral] … is now divided up between the siblings and they'll continue to run individual assets themselves and get on with creating their own legacies."

Mr Russo added that the relatively quick sale of the 1.29m ha of traditional merino country, which was capable of running more than 83,300 sheep, was indicative of how Mr Shahin did business.

"He knows what he's looking for and he acts quickly and decisively," he said.

"Charlie actually has agriculture in his blood. He studied agronomy back in the day … Charlie intends to keep running it as a sheep station. I think we can probably see an enterprise change in terms of perhaps some dorpers into the production mix."

Since the sale of OTR in 2023, Mr Shahin and his family have been acquiring massive agricultural stations under the business group ATAYF, which is made of up Mr Shahin, his wife and his daughters.

In 2024, the family purchased the 408,000-hectare cattle station Aileron in the Northern Territory.

The Shahin family, including Charlie Shahin (far right), sold OTR to Viva Energy (CEO Scott Wyatt pictured second from left). (Supplied)

In a statement from Elders provided on Mr Shahin's behalf, the chairman of ATAYF said owning and working with agricultural assets had been "a lifelong ambition" of his.

"This acquisition is a long-term family investment. We intend to build on the foundations established by Jumbuck, support the existing operations and continue investing in the productivity and resilience of the enterprise for future generations," he said.

"We have great confidence in the future of the Australian sheep and wool industry. Demand for high-quality natural fibre and premium protein continues to grow globally and Australia remains uniquely positioned to meet that demand."

The ABC has sought direct comment from the Shahin family.

End to a family dynasty

According to Jumbuck Pastoral's website, the Jumbuck North West Pastoral Aggregation of Commonwealth Hill, Mobella and Bulgunnia consists of 23 staff.

While a fourth station Mulgathing, adjoins the properties recently sold off, it was not part of the sale.

In a company-wide newsletter released following the listing of the three sheep stations, Jumbuck Pastoral said the decision had "not been made lightly".

These words were reiterated in a statement from Elders on MacLachlan Pastoral Group executive director Callum MacLachlan's behalf, saying it was important to Jumbuck Pastoral the stations were passed to an owner "who understood the significance of the assets, respected the work of the people who have managed them and shared our belief in the future of Australian agriculture".

Jumbuck Pastoral has been selling off its agricultural assets. (Supplied: Sarah Bensen)

"We have come to know Charlie [Shahin] and his family through this process and believe they will be excellent custodians of the aggregation.

"Their commitment to long-term investment, family values and Australian agriculture gives us great confidence that these stations have a bright future ahead of them.

"While this transaction represents the end of one chapter, we are pleased that the next chapter will be written by another South Australian family with a genuine passion for the land and a multi-generational perspective."

The ABC has sought direct comment from Jumbuck Pastoral and the MacLachlan family.

Jumbuck Pastoral was established in South Australia in 1888 by HP MacLachlan at Paratoo Station near Yunta.

Charlie Shahin (second from right) with his late father Fred Shahin and brothers. (Supplied)

In more recent years, Jumbuck Pastoral announced it would start breaking up and selling off its massive agricultural assets as part of proactive succession planning.

Last year Jumbuck Pastoral sold the largest of its stations, which is also Australia's largest sheep station to a foreign buyer.

The million-hectare station Rawlinna in Western Australia's remote Nullarbor was sold by Jumbuck to UK-based Consolidated Pastoral Company (CPC) for an undisclosed sum.

The deal included a flock of about 30,000 sheep and was subject to several conditions, including approval by the Foreign Investment Review Board (FIRB) and the WA government, which needed to sign off on the transfer of the pastoral lease.

World.title: When this photo was posted online the racist commentary began
World.content:
After a hard day's work in the wet and cold Central Highlands, the Tebrakunna Rangers took a photo to capture their collaboration with members of Aboriginal Heritage Tasmania.

WARNING: This story contains racist and offensive language

But minutes after posting the image on social media there was a deluge of racist commentary.

"[There were] racial comments about the colour of their skin," said Tasmanian Regional Aboriginal Communities Alliance (TRACA) chairman Nick Cameron.

"[There were] racial comments about the percentage of Aboriginal blood they must have.

"Comments [saying] all the Tasmanian Aboriginal people died so who are these fake people pretending to be Aboriginal people?"

The Tebrakunna Rangers posted a site visit photo on Facebook, then was forced to disable comments. (Facebook: Tebrakunna Rangers)

Mr Cameron, a Pairrebeene/Trawlwoolway man, said the abuse was so offensive the ranger group was forced to disable comments on the post.

"That group of Aboriginal rangers is mostly made up of young Aboriginal men and women," he said.

"They are fine young people and they are our future leaders.

"What concerns me now, as an Aboriginal leader within our community, is this has got to the point since the Voice referendum where our young people have become fodder for political and commercial gain."

Mr Cameron shared the anecdote at a federal parliamentary inquiry examining racism, hate and violence directed at First Nations people.

The inquiry has held hearings across the country over the past few months, and today came to Hobart to hear from Aboriginal organisations and elders in Lutruwita/Tasmania.

Mr Cameron said his organisation had observed a significant escalation in racism since the Voice referendum.

"As we saw tragically recently in Sydney, hate and racism has severe impacts," he said.

"And just because it's not at the end of a gun, if it involves social media, if it's just words, it can be just as hurtful."

Hurtful comments of 'white fraud' aired

Peter Rowe, the chairman of the First Peoples Tasmania Aboriginal Corporation, told the inquiry he too had been subjected to racism after a photo was posted on social media.

The image featured himself and other Aboriginal elders at the Mannalargenna Day festival several months ago.

Soon after, he said an anonymous person posted a comment saying: "Pictured here is white man, Peter Rowe, who continues pretending to be Aboriginal. Many other white frauds attend this event."

Peter Rowe says some Aboriginal people in Tasmania are denied their identity by others. (Supplied)

Mr Rowe, a Trawlwoolway man, said some of the racism experienced by Aboriginal people in Tasmania was from other Aboriginal people.

"Some public voices and organisations have, in our view, contributed to a climate in which Aboriginal people are publicly labelled as fake Aboriginals, whities, or otherwise denied their identity," he said.

"These are not simply internal disagreements. They are forms of racialised gatekeeping that legitimise abuse and encourage others to question the identity of Aboriginal people who do not fit narrow stereotypes.

"This has contributed to significant lateral violence within our communities."

Mr Rowe was asked by the committee to identify the organisations he was referring to.

"The main group is the Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre (TAC)," he said.

"They seem to be the home of lateral violence in Tasmania."

The Joint Standing Committee on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Affairs held a hearing in Hobart on Wednesday. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

He said the TAC would not allow him to use its health service in Hobart even though his Aboriginality is accepted at other Aboriginal health services across the country.

"That's pretty disappointing to me," Mr Rowe said.

Mr Cameron said the TAC played an important role, but said the division was detrimental to the wider cause of improving Closing the Gap targets in Tasmania.

"We've got a significant issue where the peak partner body doesn't collaborate, doesn't speak with and talk with other Aboriginal regional organisations," Mr Cameron said.

"It doesn't collaborate at the moment with TRACA despite … the best way to actually achieve improvement in our lives, to improve the targets, reduce the suicides, reduce the deaths, improve our living age, is to collaborate and work together."

Racism 'about power and who holds it'

The Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre was not asked at the inquiry to respond the criticisms made against it.

The ABC contacted the TAC's campaign coordinator Nala Mansell for a right of reply.

Ms Mansell criticised the ABC for seeking comment from her rather than questioning the government about "racist laws" and said it showed racism was being "normalised in this state".

Mr Rowe had also been critical of the ABC during the inquiry.

"The government and media like ABC just look upon one group and rarely involve the whole Tasmanian Aboriginal community," he said.

Nala Mansell says racism is normalised in Tasmania and confirming a person's Aboriginality is controlled by the state. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Ms Mansell told the inquiry the state controlled the process of confirming Aboriginal identity.

"Here in Lutruwita we continue to see governments asserting authority over Aboriginal identity rather than recognising that we, as Aboriginal people, have the right to know and to determine who our community is and who gets to speak on our behalf," she said.

Plan to return Hobart land to Aboriginal group gets council support A proposal to return nearly 5 hectares of land at Hobart's Queens Domain to Aboriginal custodians passes its first hurdle after the city's council voted to provide in-principle support.

Ms Mansell said the government also controlled Aboriginal heritage.

"Here in Lutruwita, when white people create something that's seen as heritage, ownership remains with the people who created it or their descendants," she said.

"But when Aboriginal people create heritage, ownership and control over that heritage remains with the Crown.

"If it happened to anyone else's cultural property Australians would immediately recognise it as discriminatory."

She urged the committee to look at the wider picture and not focus solely on online abuse.

"Racism is not simply about words. It's about power and who holds it and who exercises it, as well as who is denied it," Ms Mansell said.

"Until we as Aboriginal people have the same right to determine our own identity, protect our own heritage, and make decisions affecting our own future just like every other Australian expects for themselves, racism will continue to be reproduced throughout institutions."

Uncle Jim Everett (left) spoke to the panel about the impact of "pretend Aboriginals". (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Palawa elder Jim Everett/Puralia Meenamatta accused the state and federal governments of allowing people to falsely claim Aboriginal identity.

"One of the major factors is their assimilation program which includes allowing the pretend Aboriginals to create organisations to attack other bona fide Aboriginal community-based organisations," Mr Everett said.

"And in this state here the government has basically run to these people and thrown money at them to [create] a divide and conquer strategy."

Aboriginal Affairs Minister Bridget Archer did not respond directly to the TAC's criticisms about Aboriginal identity and heritage.

She told the inquiry: "We acknowledge and recognises the role of governments in systemic racism experienced by Aboriginal people in Tasmania."

As examples, she pointed to the myth of extinction of Tasmanian Aboriginal people and their forced removal to Bass Strait islands.

Ms Archer said the over-representation of Aboriginal children in out-of-home care and youth justice facilities was an example of ongoing systemic racism linked to "structural factors".

"While Tasmanian government policies have improved over time they have caused intergenerational trauma that impacts Tasmanian Aboriginal people today," she said.

"We are working hard to build trust with Tasmanian Aboriginal people by partnering through genuine relationships."

World.title: 'Forever left wondering': Families of missing people struggle without answers
World.content:
For more than a decade, Cathy Wood has lived with a question she still can't answer: "What happened to Dad?"

"He'd gone out sailing and he just hadn't returned," she said.

"He'd sent me and my brother emails, nothing out of the ordinary, nothing that would make you think anything different."

An experienced sailor, Richard Wood had temporarily moved from Canberra to Brisbane for work when he disappeared.

" We spent a lot of the day waiting for phone calls from the police to give us an update. "

A senior Commonwealth Treasury official from the 1990s until 2001, Mr Wood represented Australia at the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and was promoted to assistant secretary of the department's special projects unit in mid-1997.

"He worked incredibly hard, always late at night, long days at the office, and very dedicated to his work," Ms Wood remembered.

Richard Wood was an experienced sailor who temporarily moved from Canberra to Brisbane for work when he disappeared. (Supplied)

'Forever left wondering'

Mr Wood resigned from the department in mid-2001 and was working as a private consultant and macro-economics lecturer at the time of his disappearance.

"It was up in Moreton Bay, in Queensland. [Police] travelled out and they found his boat moored in the water but no sign of anybody on board," Ms Wood said.

She said police had called off the search after eight days, and a coronial inquest was later held into her father's disappearance.

"My dad was a really gentle, kind, brilliant man. He was incredibly clever. Very much a family man."

"It's something that I think about every single day, just not having really a definitive answer," she said.

" You're left with questions about 'what ifs' that goes on, with no end date. "

That uncertainty has taken a significant toll.

"It will take your mind places that you know you don't want to go, definitely dark places," she said.

"Forever left wondering where somebody is or where they've gone; it's just continuous."

Cathy Wood says police called off the search for her father after eight days. (Supplied)

Psychologists call it "ambiguous loss" — a profound sense of grief without certainty or closure.

"Our brains are hardwired to try and fill gaps in knowledge, so you are constantly ruminating on every possible and impossible scenario as to the fate of your loved one," CEO of The Missed Foundation Lauren O'Keeffe said.

"That's why psychologists around the world consider ambiguous loss to be the most traumatic type of loss and the most unmanageable form of stress."

Police received 49,000 missing persons reports last year

Data from the AFP-led National Missing Persons Coordination Centre reveals more than 49,000 missing persons reports were made in Australia last year — an average of one every 11 minutes.

Crime Stoppers Australia defines a missing person as "anyone who is reported missing to police, whose whereabouts are unknown, and where there are fears for the safety or concern for the welfare of that person".

Richard Wood worked as a senior Commonwealth Treasury official. (Supplied)

While most people are found within a week, 2,827 people had been missing for more than three months by the end of 2025. Police classify these cases as 'long-term missing'.

For their loved ones, specialised support can be hard to find.

"We were offered the opportunity to go up to Queensland and get on a boat and be taken out to the site where the boat was found, if that would 'bring us some peace'," Ms Wood said.

"We haven't had any ongoing support after that.

" I thought I had exhausted all my resources … to find myself some help. "

Foundation offers support to affected families

A Google search directed Ms Wood to The Missed Foundation and Ms O'Keeffe, who has been working to lighten that burden since 2013.

"I started The Missed Foundation because it was the organisation that our family needed when my brother disappeared in 2011," Ms O'Keeffe said.

"I remember asking Geelong Police, the day that my brother disappeared, what to do and they just said, 'do whatever you feel like you need to do', which is not particularly helpful in a moment of distress."

Cathy Wood discovered The Missed Foundation after her father's disappearance. (Supplied)

The former communications advisor quit her job to launch 'Dan Come Home', encompassing "media coverage, nationwide billboards, T-shirts, celebrity shout-outs, bumper stickers, fun runs, and an unprecedented social media following".

That initiative became the Missing Persons Advocacy Network (MPAN), which rebranded as The Missed Foundation (Missed) in 2023 "to better reflect their work".

Now, 'Missed' provides everything from specialised counselling and legal advice, to billboards and educational resources.

"The sorts of things that help to humanise missing loved ones and alleviate the profound practical and emotional impact on families left behind," Ms O'Keeffe said.

Loren O'Keeffe says community support is important for families of missing people. (Supplied: Maricarmen Rubí Baeza)

Public resources for long-term support lacking

She said it operated specifically in the long-term space "because that's where there typically are no other support services".

"That's typically when the police resources, if there were any to begin with, have usually been exhausted," Ms O'Keeffe said.

"The media is no longer interested in the story and therefore the public has moved on.

"That's where our charity comes in to try and help families navigate what is their worst nightmare."

Ms Wood said when she talked to somebody who understood exactly what she was going through, "you have that sense of connection, but there's also some relief that you're not the only one going through this".

Ms O'Keeffe said Missed was working "with about 100 families all across Australia who have very different sets of circumstances and therefore very different needs".

"We are fielding inquiries from government agencies like DFAT and Services Australia and senior police, psychologists, GPs [and] social workers, who just don't know what to do and how to support families in this predicament because it is a very complex trauma and we have very few trained specialists to support people left behind."

World.title: 'Bitumen bandits' scam family out of almost $10k
World.content:
A family in South Australia's Riverland says it has been left almost $10,000 out of pocket and with nothing to show but a patch of shoddy bitumen after falling victim to a resurfacing scam.

A week ago Thuc Vu and his wife said they were working at their grocery shop when they were approached by a man who introduced himself as "Warren".

Warren told the couple he was with a road resurfacing group that had bitumen left over from a nearby job and that they did not want to transport the material back to Melbourne.

He offered to do any work that they might need done at a reduced rate, saying he would only charge for the cost of the product — just under $10,000.

The workers played on Thuc Vu's emotions and then tried to extort him for double what he had agreed to pay. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

"I [felt] very sorry for them," Mr Vu said.

His son, Vinnie, said the workers had a good "sob story".

"My dad agreed to it only if they had enough product to cover the area," he said.

"They used high pressure to get my dad to pay them."

Mr Vu agreed to proceed but noticed part-way through the job that the tools and equipment the group had were not appropriate for the work.

When he quizzed the workers on it he was told that it was the correct way to resurface the road.

Less than two hours later, what was left was a small patch of uneven and unfinished bitumen sitting on top of their gravel driveway.

The work was not done properly and will require repairs. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

"Then I realised that is their plan," Mr Vu said.

He was told that if he wanted the job finished he would need to pay an additional $21,000.

"It was like a heart-drop moment," Vinnie said.

The family turned the group away and will now have to fork out more money to get the driveway fixed.

The family will now to pay money to fix a job they did not want. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

'Bitumen bandits' on the road

Reports of the "bitumen bandits" scam operating in the Riverland, Barossa, O'Halloran Hill and the Yorke Peninsula were made to Consumer Business Services (CBS) in July.

Commissioner Brett Humphrey said six complaints were being "actively investigated".

"It's hard to confirm that it is actually the same business, but the timing of it and the areas involved would indicate that at least they're involved with each other," he said.

"These consumers have all been left with a hefty bill to fix the mess that has been left by this company."

The scam has been known to occur in South Australia and Western Australia for a number of years.

In 2023 the WA government said the organised operation was linked to scammers from overseas.

Brett Humphrey says tracking down the scammers is no easy task. (ABC News)

On its website, CBS said the "conmen" were known to use threatening or intimidating behaviour to close deals and sometimes used legitimate business names on flyers to trick customers.

It said the offenders breached consumer laws, such as coercing customers for payment, failing to observe the required 10 business day cooling-off period, unsolicited consumer agreements, providing false representations and wrongly claiming to be affiliated with reputable entities.

Mr Humphrey said he was concerned that the scam was still being run and encouraged people to do their homework on businesses they engage.

"A lot of these have previously been hard to follow up," he said.

"Make sure you're not paying for work until you're satisfied with the quality that's been done."

CBS said the offenders would need to be brought before the court for the victims to receive compensation.

The scam has been reported a number of times over the years. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

Mr Vu's family reported the incident to CBS and hope no-one else will fall victim to the scam.

"The best thing is to get the local to do the job for you," Mr Vu said.

"We paid close to $10,000 for a lesson."

World.title: Driver dies after crashing into truck in front of police cars
World.content:
A driver has died after veering into the path of a cement truck as police vehicles using lights and sirens approached from behind.

A critical incident investigation is underway into the fatal crash in Sydney's south-west.

Assistant Commissioner Brett McFadden said officers were responding to an urgent, unrelated incident near Appin, north-west of Wollongong, around 10am today.

"This was a job with a male armed with a knife in a domestic situation," he said.

A hatchback, driven by a 39-year-old man, was travelling about 50 metres in front of the two police vehicles on a flat stretch of Appin Road.

Assistant Commissioner McFadden said dash-cam vision showed the hatchback swerve onto the wrong side of the road and collide with an oncoming truck.

The driver of the car died at the scene and has yet to be formally identified.

The truck driver suffered only minor injuries, including shock, and was taken to Campbelltown Hospital for mandatory testing.

Appin Road is a busy thoroughfare connecting Wollongong to south-west Sydney. (ABC News)

"I have viewed the video footage from the cement truck which depicts the crash," Assistant Commissioner McFadden said.

"It clearly shows the proximity of police vehicles.

"It also clearly shows the path taken by the vehicle into the front of the cement truck."

Assistant Commissioner McFadden said there was "no indication" the hatchback driver panicked as the police cars approached.

"The circumstances as to why that path was taken is subject to our investigation," he said.

" Police had been operating with lights and sirens for some time. "

Brett McFadden says he is confident in the actions of police. (Supplied)

Assistant Commissioner McFadden said officers travelling behind the hatchback "pivoted" to render assistance to those involved in the crash.

"A tragic set of circumstances has unfolded immediately in front of them [police]," he said.

"I want to make it clear that the vehicle that crossed onto the incorrect side of the road was not subject to inquiry, investigation or any attempt by the police responding to the job at Appin.

"In the normal course of business, they would have safely negotiated around that vehicle and continued on their way to the priority job."

Appin Road remains closed in both directions and is due to reopen later today.

World.title: ‘Felt pressure to make people proud’: Why Jean-Claude Perrottet paid for Liberal memberships
World.content:
NSW Liberal apparatchik and key Reformer Jean-Claude Perrottet has told a corruption inquiry he felt so pressured to stack branches in the Hills Shire he resorted to paying for party memberships. The youngest brother of former premier Dominic Perrottet is a person of interest in an Independent Commission Against Corruption inquiry investigating whether Jean-Claude Perrottet, and several others, played a role in soliciting unlawful donations from prohibited donors. Jean-Claude Perrottet leaving the ICAC after giving evidence. Dominic Lorrimer When asked on Wednesday whether he felt he was being pushed to boost recruitment numbers, Jean-Claude Perrottet told the commission: “I felt pressured to make people proud, to do a good job.” Counsel assisting Juliet Curtin referred to earlier evidence given to the commission by another Reformer, Robert Assaf, who claimed Perrottet paid fees for new members to join Liberal Party branches.



“Maybe I was pressured to deliver, or someone had been a member of the party for 25 years, and they were saying, ‘I’m fed up’. And yeah, maybe Rob’s right … in the sense of pressure built up and, you know, I just needed to get it over the line,” Perrottet told the commission. He also told the commission on Wednesday he was “let go” from his job at Catholic Schools NSW in June, just one month after being promoted. Loading Catholic Schools NSW chief executive Dallas McInerney is also a person of interest to the ICAC. Curtin said to Perrottet: “I want to suggest to you, Mr Perrottet, that the reason you were made redundant only a month after you’ve been promoted to this new role was because of your involvement in this inquiry. Is that right?”



“That wasn’t what was communicated to me from the office and the emails that I received. But I mean, obviously, I’ve thought about the timing of it,” Perrottet responded. The inquiry also heard Reformer co-founder Christian Ellis prepared a “staff report” to plant allies of the right-wing Catholic group in ministerial offices to spread the load of factional work after the 2019 election win. The inquiry was told the staff report was sent to Perrottet and another of his brothers, Charles, on March 25, 2019 – just two days after the election. Charles Perrottet is also a person of interest in the inquiry. Jean-Claude Perrottet was asked about the staff report on Wednesday.



Curtin said Ellis was “conducting some kind of tally or assessment of each of these proposed staffers in terms of their attributes and qualities as a staffer”. Related Article Updated

Operation Rosny Tudehope concedes leaking confidential report to Liberal operative on the run The staff report had letters next to proposed staffers’ names denoting each characteristic. “R” meant recruiter, Curtin said. “Does that mean someone who is willing to engage in the factional work of recruiting new members of the Liberal Party?” she asked. Perrottet said he would not characterise it like that. Meanwhile, John Ruddick, a Libertarian Party member of the NSW upper house, has called for the ICAC’s examination of illegal donations to be paused pending an inquiry into whether the watchdog has been leaking information to the media.



Ruddick claimed in parliament on Wednesday that Operation Rosny “appears to be tainted” because the Herald has revealed several details about the key players targeted by the ICAC over recent weeks. The former Liberal Party member wants the inspector-general of the ICAC, Gail Furness, SC, to investigate whether ICAC staff had disclosed information in a potential breach of the law, and also demanded parliament order an independent inquiry into his claims. He offered no evidence to support his allegations, other than that the Herald’s coverage has referenced sources who are unauthorised to speak publicly. The ICAC began its investigation in mid-2022 into the links between NSW Liberal figures, fugitive Sydney developer Jean Nassif, Catholic Schools NSW and several other figures, including from the Labor Party. Operation Rosny is due to hold eight weeks of public hearings. Ruddick is particularly focused on a story by the Herald late last month that revealed names on the witness list for the first week of hearings. Ruddick has repeatedly suggested on social media platform X that the ICAC staff leaked the document.



However, the witness list was widely circulated to parties involved in Operation Rosny before the Herald obtained and published the document. Ruddick told parliament it should condemn “any attempt by a financially desperate, taxpayer-supported media organisation to weaponise confidential ICAC processes or interfere with the integrity of public hearings for its own commercial or political ends”. On Tuesday the commission heard that senior NSW Liberal MP Damien Tudehope conceded he had leaked a confidential draft report from a parliamentary inquiry to a key witness who deliberately avoided providing evidence. Tudehope, then the Coalition government’s most senior member of the upper house, sent the 2023 confidential report into illegal donations and the Hills Shire Council to lobbyist and Liberal Party operative Jeremy Greenwood, the ICAC heard on Tuesday. Greenwood was one of four Liberal apparatchiks who hid or fled overseas to avoid being handed a summons to appear before the parliamentary inquiry, which was one of the catalysts for the broader ICAC probe.



Liberal leader Kellie Sloane on Wednesday said the Tudehope revelation was not acceptable. But she left open the possibility he could return to her frontbench after the inquiry, saying his evidence had “not changed my position about keeping Damien on the backbench for the short term”. The Herald revealed last week that Liberal MP Chris Rath was captured by a wiretap helping party apparatchiks evade the statewide manhunt to force them before the parliamentary probe. World.title: Labor’s news bargaining plan faces Senate block after US anger
World.content:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s plan to force digital platforms could be killed in the Senate by the Greens and Coalition, casting doubt on a scheme condemned by the US as extortion despite changes made to satisfy tech giants’ demands. Days after big Australian news outlets claimed Labor had weakened the news bargaining incentive, Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young said she feared Labor was letting tech firms off the hook. Anthony Albanese is bound for the US in September facing strong pushback to his News Bargaining Incentive legislation. Alex Ellinghausen One of her chief concerns was a move to increase a levy on tech firms – designed to push Google, Microsoft and Meta to pay for news articles in their platforms – but restrict the charge to their revenue made from advertising. Previously, the law applied to their total revenue. Nine, owner of this masthead, and News Corp have described this change as a gift to the big tech companies that protested against the draft policy.



“Why would the government want to reduce the baseline to deliver even less for Australian news?” Hanson-Young said. “Once we get the detail of the legislation, I’ll be kicking the tyres hard. I’m concerned the government is squibbing this opportunity.” If the Greens and Coalition oppose the change, Labor will need to go back to the drawing board. Nine’s chief executive Matt Stanton urged a rethink on Tuesday in a sharply worded statement which said that Nine felt “deeply misled” by Labor’s last-minute change. The Trump administration has attacked the legislation as “extortion”. AP Coalition communications spokeswoman Sarah Henderson said media companies had warned the new code could mean fewer journalists, jeopardising political support for a policy that began as a bipartisan project under the Morrison government. “The changes around the calculation of the penalty if tech giants refuse to play ball potentially excludes billions of dollars in revenue and weakens the incentive for digital platforms to strike fair commercial deals with Australian news outlet,” Henderson said.



“While we will consider the details of this scheme, Labor cannot claim to support Australian journalism while overseeing changes which media companies say will mean fewer journalists and less investment.” Another change alarming media firms is one that caps at 16.7 per cent, rather than 25 per cent, the amount any one company can pay to a single firm out of its total liability. Larger media firms such as Nine argue privately that they contribute more than 16.7 per cent of a digital giant’s news content. Companies such as News Corp and Nine now expect the total value of their deals with Google and Meta to be smaller than previously expected, though smaller media companies of the likes of SBS and Australian Community Media are believed to have lobbied for this change, having feared they may be left out of any deals at all. The government’s view is that the amount of money that would flow to media firms will not be much less under the changes, and that any difference may be made up by the inclusion of LinkedIn and Tiktok. The feud between media firms and the federal government demonstrates the difficulty of landing a deal for local media while managing the Trump administration’s concerns about punitive taxes on US firms.



Several sources in Labor said its change to how revenue would be collected, revealed on Monday, was driven partly by anxiety about the US response. The news levy has not attracted as much attention from US officials as Australia’s under-16 social media ban, according to government sources, but Albanese did hear concerns about the scheme on his trip to Washington last year. Tech companies can offset the charge by striking individual, tax-deductible deals. The Trump administration has strongly condemned digital services taxes – mostly in Europe. “President Trump is committed to defending America’s leading technology sector from digital services taxes and other forms of foreign extortion,” the US State Department said on Wednesday. “The Trump administration will continue to address these issues with our trading partners.” Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, and Google have so far declined to comment on the latest version of the policy. But their representatives in Washington signalled that the companies were prepared to fight it using the Trump administration.



The Computer & Communications Industry Association, which counts Meta and Google among its members, said the changes to the tax were “for the most part cosmetic” and “critically, do not alter the discriminatory nature of the proposal”. Related Article Publishing ‘Deeply misled’: Nine says news bargaining plan could cost jobs “Targeting a select few foreign firms, mainly American, to fund Australian news businesses, remains a bad policy that is inconsistent with the Australia-US free trade agreement,” said the organisation’s vice president for digital trade, Jonathan McHale. “Australia should abandon this misguided approach and if it chooses not to, US authorities should respond vigorously.” The National Foreign Trade Council (NFTC), a US industry group with Meta, Google and Microsoft in its membership, said it was disappointed that Australia was sticking with the policy and that it now covered a broader spectrum of US companies.



Tiffany Smith, the group’s vice president for global trade, said the Trump administration was “committed to the fair treatment of American companies abroad”. “We call on the Australian government to reconsider this measure, which adds to a broader deteriorating trend in the tax and investment climate in Australia,” she said. Related Article Media & marketing News Corp says plan to make tech giants pay for news has been ‘gutted’ Australia was also hit with a new 12.5 per cent tariff due to Canberra’s alleged failure to deal with imports produced with forced labour. The jousting comes ahead of US visits by Albanese, who is expected to go to New York in September and attend the G20 in Miami in December, and Foreign Minister Penny Wong, who is due to attend a G20 meeting in Atlanta in October.



Albanese previously suggested he wouldn’t be swayed by pushback from the White House. “We’re a sovereign nation, and my government will make decisions based upon the Australian national interest,” he said in April. “We do that right across the board.” Microsoft, which owns LinkedIn, said it shared the government’s objective of promoting a sustainable news ecosystem and appreciated the consultation. World.title: Trolls take their toll as online abuse turns women off politics
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership Editorial Trolls take their toll as online abuse turns women off politics The Herald's View Editorial August 5, 2026 — 5:52pm

August 5, 2026 — 5:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In 1984, under the guiding hand of the late senator Susan Ryan, the first female Labor federal cabinet member, the federal parliament passed the Sex Discrimination Act, a largely successful attempt to ensure that women had the same access to jobs, services and accommodation as men. It also made sexual harassment illegal in Australia. New research found almost 90 per cent of the female politicians surveyed had experienced gendered online abuse. Glen McCurtayne Some believed the legislation helped redefine the role of women in Australian society. But five decades later, the abuse remains subliminal, surfacing mainly when politics, gender and power intersect and provoke out-of-touch and mostly anonymous Australians to denigrate women and put them down. New research from nonpartisan not-for-profit organisation Women for Election found almost 90 per cent of the female politicians surveyed had experienced gendered online abuse, with more than half reconsidering their positions in public office. The national research draws upon the experiences of 110 current and aspiring women politicians across all three levels of government.



Three-quarters believed online abuse of women in politics had increased in the past two years. About 65 per cent had personally experienced or witnessed AI-generated abuse, including deepfakes or manipulated content, and 98 per cent believed it would get worse. Half said online abuse had made them question whether they would run for office again. Of course, male politicians receive threats too, but the abuse targeted at female politicians is often more personal, gendered and sexualised. Women for Election CEO Licia Heath said the abuse was worse for politicians from multicultural backgrounds, LGBTQ+ women and young women. AI was scaling up harmful abuse at a rate faster than governments could respond to it. “All of these new ways to dehumanise women in politics, with the ultimate aim to try to silence their voices ... is when democracy suffers,” she said. “I don’t want to wait for a woman MP to be killed in office before we start making some changes.” Stories of abuse are many. Last week, NSW Agriculture Minister Tara Moriarty said threats of violence towards her following a feral pig program announcement she made had been reported to NSW Police. State Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane deactivated her X account after receiving violent threats when she criticised a neo-Nazi protest outside NSW Parliament House last November.



Snowy Monaro councillor Tanya Higgins has been labelled a “fat dumb blonde” by serial pest and fellow councillor Andrew Thaler. Her children have heard men call their mother a “stupid fat bitch” and “fat liar” online and last Boxing Day a trespasser repeatedly drove up and down the driveway of their home. “My children don’t deserve to be anxious about whether certain people come to our house,” she said. In the social media age, such harassment must deter many current and future generations of women remaining in or entering politics. Australia has a long way to go in terms of true equality and representation. While the number of women in parliament has risen, we can no longer accept that enduring abuse and harassment is the cost of doing politics. World.title: Revealed: The radical overhaul of cancer screening to detect most at risk
World.content:
NationalCancer Revealed: The radical overhaul of cancer screening to detect most at risk Kate Aubusson and Henrietta Cook August 5, 2026 — 5:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A radical overhaul of Australia’s breast cancer screening will implement a risk-based approach to detect cancers earlier with new technologies beyond mammograms, replacing the current one-size-fits-all, age-based model. Australia’s federal, state and territory governments on Wednesday endorsed a new national strategic framework for BreastScreen Australia, based on the latest evidence of risk assessment and new technologies. Breast screening is free for Australian women once they reach 40. Getty Images A high-priority action is establishing nationally consistent two-tiered risk-based screening pathways based on women’s risk factors for developing breast cancer – including breast density – that deploys a range of screening techniques, including contrast-based imaging and AI prediction models. Breast cancer is the most common cancer diagnosed in females in Australia. More than 20,000 people are diagnosed, and about 3000 women die of breast cancer every year.



Related Article Healthcare Beyond the mammogram: How AI is spotting hidden breast cancer risks Breast screening prevents up to half of breast cancer deaths among Australian women aged 50 to 74, but take-up remains low at 52 per cent, well below the 70 per cent target. Associate Professor Carolyn Nickson at the University of Sydney’s Cancer Elimination Collaboration group said the best available evidence showed a risk-stratified approach for women aged 50 to 74 could lead to some breast cancers being detected earlier, save lives and reduce the intensity of treatment. “We know that we can identify groups of women who may benefit from having some more intensive screening protocol than what’s standard for this screen,” said Nickson, who was part of an expert group tasked by the federal government to explore risk-adjusted breast screening program options. One such group was women with higher breast density, who have a higher risk of breast cancer, and whose tumours can be harder to see on mammograms.



Risk-stratified screening could also help determine which women in their 40s may benefit from starting screening sooner and with screening technologies better suited to younger women. “That could be contrast-based imaging or a change to their time between screenings,” Nickson said. A revamped BreastScreen Australia could also include a risk assessment questionnaire that considers family history and lifestyle factors, as well as AI mammogram image processing. “If we can combine all of that information, we know that we can identify groups of women who may benefit from having some more intensive screening protocol than what is standard,” she said. Australian research published in the prestigious Lancet medical journal in March showed an AI tool known as BRAIx could help predict which women were at high risk of developing breast cancer after receiving a mammogram all clear.



Related Article Science The five everyday products linked to nearly one-third of all deaths globally One in 10 women with the highest BRAIx risk scores developed cancer within four years – even after receiving an “all-clear” breast screen. The AI tool searched for patterns in mammograms to pick up signals for risk invisible to the human eye, making it easier to detect signs of cancer in dense breasts. Associate Professor Davis McCarthy, whose team at St Vincent’s Institute of Medical Research led the development of BRAIx, said the Australian government’s new risk-based strategy would do a much better job at identifying women at higher risk of developing breast cancer than the current protocol. “It’s a very successful program, but it’s a one-size-fits-all program, and what we have in the population are many people at many, many different levels of risk for breast cancer individually,” he said of the existing BreastScreen Australia program.



“If we can get it right in terms of allocating the right people to each pathway, then we have a huge opportunity here to do a much better job of keeping high-risk women safe while keeping lower-risk women equally safe.” The overhaul may also encourage more women to take part in screening, McCarthy said. “Hopefully, when people see these efforts to make positive changes with good evidence behind them, they see that this is a service that’s not stuck in the past, but is looking to the future.” The federal government will invest $1.3 million to implement the plan and help BreastScreen Australia keep pace with new technologies. The road to Australia’s risk-based breast screening program: Develop a national annual screening eligibility policy

Pilot approaches for women aged 45 to 49

Develop a risk assessment tool

Research alternative screening pathways for women with high breast density.



BreastScreen Australia would operate as normal while the reforms are implemented in phases over the next 10 years. Federal Assistant Health Minister Rebecca White said regular breast screening remains one of the most effective ways to detect cancer early, preventing more challenging treatment and poorer outcomes for women. “Early detection saves lives, and these reforms will help ensure even more women can access the care and support they need for years to come,” White said. Since 1991, BreastScreen Australia has detected more than 140,000 invasive breast cancers in women who had no symptoms. Breast Cancer Network Australia welcomed the announcement and urged the Federal government to publish a fully costed, 10-year implementation plan, which government modelling suggested could be $2 billion.
