World.title: Secret missions and staged meetings: How a backroom deal led to IBAC probe
World.content:
Updated PoliticsVictoriaIBAC Secret missions and staged meetings: How a backroom deal led to IBAC probe Kieran Rooney Updated August 5, 2026 — 5:49pm ,first published August 5, 2026 — 9:46am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Daniel Andrews’ decision to sideline a senior minister and strike a secret pay deal with firefighters gave a union boss “extraordinary influence” over one of the government’s most contentious reforms and exposed the state to the risk of corruption, an IBAC investigation found. At the height of a pay dispute with the state’s firefighters in 2016, Andrews as premier tasked key allies and senior public servants with a “secret mission” to reach agreement with United Firefighters boss Peter Marshall without the knowledge of the Country Fire Authority and then-emergency services minister Jane Garrett. Operation Richmond centred on dealings between Daniel Andrews’ government and the United Firefighters Union under Peter Marshall. Marija Ercegovac Tabled in parliament on Wednesday, the Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission’s findings into an eight-year-long investigation found “serious and concerning conduct” by Victorian ministers, MPs and public servants that included a text message to the premier about a secret handshake and a minister laughing about phone taps. Known as Operation Richmond, the investigation, which began in 2018 but was suppressed for years by legal challenges, found that hotel-room negotiations were hidden through a staged meeting with the premier that paved the way for Marshall to exert “extraordinary influence” and receive privileged access to senior members of the state government.



While the long-awaited report stopped short of finding corrupt conduct – for which Victoria has a higher threshold than any other state, IBAC identified serious issues in the way pay deals with the Country Fire Authority (CFA) and the Metropolitan Fire Brigade (MFB) were negotiated alongside the establishment of Fire Rescue Victoria. Related Article IBAC Five things to know about Operation Richmond In a statement, Andrews said the report showed no evidence “to support the false and completely outrageous claims that I had been blackmailed to force a favourable outcome for the United Firefighters Union”. “For the record and the avoidance of any doubt, there are no findings in relation to corrupt conduct made about me, any other member of the government, or the public service,” he added. In a video posted to the UFU Victoria website, Marshall slammed both IBAC and the Operation Richmond investigation, saying, “This is an organisation that has spent many millions of dollars of public money using coercive powers to go on a witch hunt.”



On Wednesday morning, Premier Ben Carroll said he had not yet read the report in full, but had received some “high-level advice” and that his government would accept IBAC’s recommendations. Asked whether the conduct of Andrews and others in the report would be considered corrupt under the expanded definition of corruption which Carroll pledged to adopt after being appointed premier last week, he said he would first read the IBAC report carefully. “I am going to study it and give Victorians the actions and answers they deserve,” he said. In the report’s opening, Commissioner Victoria Elliott said, “IBAC found that senior members of government acted contrary to established policies, procedures, codes of conduct and conventions in negotiating a deal with the secretary of the United Firefighters Union (UFU), Mr Peter Marshall, for the CFA Enterprise Bargaining Agreement (EBA) without the knowledge and involvement of the responsible minister, agencies and department. “By doing so, the government placed itself in a position where Mr Marshall was able to exert extraordinary influence over the negotiations for both the CFA EBA and the MFB EBA,” the report said, noting that, “Mr Marshall was afforded privileged access to senior members of government which, in many cases, were not disclosed and were to the exclusion of other key stakeholders”.



“The government placed itself in a position where Mr Marshall was able to exert extraordinary influence.” Delayed Operation Richmond report At the time, the CFA pay deal became a political flashpoint for the Andrews government. In June 2016, Garrett resigned as emergency services minister and quit the cabinet because she disagreed with her government’s moves to accept UFU demands. She died in 2022. “Operation Richmond highlights how government leaders, including ministers and the premier, can undermine established checks and balances when they fail to model high integrity standards and act as stewards of good governance,” the report found. The report was originally scheduled for release by the end of June, but was delayed by an unsuccessful legal challenge from Marshall. Operation Richmond began after IBAC received allegations that Marshall had blackmailed or compromised the premier to change his position on the 2016 CFA pay deal. The blackmail claim was never substantiated.



The investigation was then widened to include negotiations for a pay deal with the Metropolitan Fire Brigade and the creation of its replacement, Fire Rescue Victoria. Related Article IBAC Firefighters’ union boss loses court battle to bury corruption investigation, but appeal possible Negotiations on the CFA deal began in 2015, but had broken down by the end of the year. The UFU’s log of claims was 400 pages long and the agency was concerned some of its key requests were unlawful. Andrews and then-special minister of state Gavin Jennings both told IBAC that by March 2016, the dispute had reached a crisis point, with the former premier describing the situation as “completely intractable”, with both sides miles apart. IBAC found Andrews authorised Jennings, with the assistance of Tony Bates – a deputy secretary at the Department of Premier and Cabinet – to negotiate the CFA deal directly without the knowledge of the CFA themselves.



“While in negotiations on 11 April 2016, Minister Jennings referred to being ‘off doing my secret mission’ and ‘secret business’ in text messages to staff in his office and the PPO [Premier’s Private Office],” the report said. “Private meetings were held with the UFU in rented meeting spaces and a hotel. Those involved were instructed to keep the meetings confidential.” After four days of negotiations, the two sides agreed to terms and Jennings texted Andrews: “Handshake has occurred – it’s done!” Once negotiations were finished, IBAC found, a document outlining the terms was presented to cabinet as a proposal from the union, with ministers – including Garrett – unaware they had been negotiated with people inside the government. In an intercepted phone call from 2019, Marshall summarised the meetings, telling a ministerial adviser the pay deal “was negotiated with f---in’ Jennings in a back room. It was endorsed by f---in’ Andrews and cabinet.”



On April 13, 2016, Marshall met with Andrews and a staffer for what IBAC viewed as a staged event so that there could be a witness to the agreement being presented to the government as a “proposal” from the union. Evidence from Bates appeared to support this assessment. The senior public servant told investigators he led the development of the deal and “if there was a presentation of the agreement to the premier’s office, I would categorise it as ceremonial”. Even after cabinet’s expenditure committee signed off on the deal on April 19, however, Jane Garrett and the CFA remained opposed to it. A key concern among those who did not support the deal were clauses that required the CFA to “consult and agree” with the UFU on decisions before they could be made.



They became known as “veto clauses”, which effectively allowed the union to increase its control of the CFA by blocking policies it did not agree with. Before her death, Garrett told IBAC she was contacted by a federal Labor senator to persuade her to progress the deal with the Fair Work Commission. The CFA agreed to return to the commission in May and resume conciliation, but Marshall resisted any attempts to compromise on the EBA and would not budge on the veto clauses. On May 23, 2016, the premier sent a text message to Jennings asking how mediation was progressing. Jennings responded: “At 11am, he [Marshall] was convinced you were a treacherous c--- and I was a f---ing idiot ... By lunchtime he was giving me the benefit of the doubt.” The IBAC report said evidence gathered through Operation Richmond showed Andrews wanted to end the pay dispute in a way that excluded Garrett, then emergency services minister, whom he didn’t believe could resolve the matter.



Firefighters’ union chief Peter Marshall on the steps of Victoria’s Parliament House in 2022. Chris Hopkins “At the time of the decision, the premier was facing internal political pressure, negative media attention and industrial unrest,” the report said. But IBAC found that in secretly excluding Garrett, the CFA and other key parts of government from the process, the premier, Jennings and Bates behaved contrary to “government policy, procedures, convention and their respective codes of conduct”. It also found the undisclosed negotiations limited the state’s bargaining position and their ability to resist Marshall’s demands. Garrett quit cabinet in June 2016 because she considered the pay deal unacceptable, and when the CFA board refused to endorse the agreement, they were stood down and replaced. Their successors signed off on the arrangement.



At the same time, Marshall expected the terms of the CFA deal to be replicated in a pay deal with the Metropolitan Fire Brigade. One former MFB chief executive told IBAC that they had concerns similar to the CFA’s, including that some elements of the deal were unlawful or undermined safety obligations. “Ultimately, to resolve the dispute, the government appointed new members to the MFB board who understood the government’s preferred position on the MFB EBA,” the report said. During his examination by IBAC, Bates said that on April 17, 2016 he received a call from an MFB executive who asked the government employee, “What the f--- do you think you’re playing at?” in relation to concerns the department had been negotiating with the UFU without the knowledge of the fire services. The executive told IBAC they found Bates’ behaviour deeply concerning, and said, “the path that it was heading down was disastrous for the organisation”.



IBAC also raised concerns about the way a 2019 bill that reformed the fire services was passed – which ultimately turned the MFB and the paid parts of the CFA into a new body named Fire Rescue Victoria. The corruption watchdog found Marshall had sought to secure the support of a crossbench MP by hiring their relative days before it was due for a vote in the upper house. In an intercepted phone call from June 2019, Marshall told a friend the MP was “100 per cent behind us … just to make sure we just employed [their relative].” The investigation also found Marshall had privileged access to Lisa Neville, who served as emergency services minister from 2018 to 2019, and sought to influence her decision on who should be appointed commissioner of the new agency.



“While IBAC makes no findings as to whether Mr Marshall did influence the minister on the appointment of the FRV commissioner, IBAC found that the minister’s stakeholder management of Mr Marshall created significant opportunities for him to do so,” the report said. “Finally, during this period, IBAC also found evidence that an MFB board member, Mr Greg Sword, shared confidential information with Mr Marshall in 2019 in breach of his professional obligations.” In a statement, Daniel Andrews said the report showed “no evidence whatsoever to support the false and completely outrageous claims that I had been blackmailed to force a favourable outcome for the United Firefighters Union and its thousands of career firefighter members”. “For the record and the avoidance of any doubt, there are no findings in relation to corrupt conduct made about me, any other member of the government, or the public service. That is a fact,” Andrews said. “By 2016, the relationship between the Country Fire Authority and the UFU had completely broken down, and a spiteful and dysfunctional enterprise bargaining dispute had dragged on for years. Fire chiefs were spending more time in the Fair Work Commission than running their organisations.



“That was not acceptable to me or to the government when community safety was on the line. The dispute needed to be resolved in the public interest, and it was.” Opposition Leader Jess Wilson said on Wednesday that the report showed the state was being run by a “gangster government”. “This government, time and time again, has not acted with integrity,” she said. Read more on Operation Richmond: How we got here: 5 things to know about Operation Richmond.

World.title: Union seizes on viral video of violent patient to renew security calls
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland Health Union seizes on viral video of violent patient to renew security calls Dominique Tassell August 5, 2026 — 5:16pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Queensland Nurses and Midwives’ Union has called for better working conditions and increased health funding, days after the Queensland government celebrated additional frontline staff, and a video of a nurse taking down an aggressive patient went viral. Of 8000 QNMU members recently surveyed, 82 per cent reported experiencing violence at work. Exposure to racism had also increased since their last survey. Kat, a senior nurse who spoke to the media outside the QNMU annual conference but asked for her surname not to be used, said she was punched in the face by a patient about a year ago. Secretary of the Queensland Nurses and Midwives’ Union Sarah Beaman (centre) with members of its council. Dominique Tassell Initially, she thought her jaw was broken, and she was left with a large, almost black, bruise for some time afterwards.



Working in the emergency department, Kat said she constantly witnessed violence against her staff. “It’s devastating. Every time I go to employment, the possibility of one of my staff members getting assaulted is quite high,” she said. The union said staff often blamed themselves, or worried they had initiated the incident. “I can tell you, in my case, I did not [initiate it],” Kat said. “I experienced that flight or fight. Because I’m quite stubborn, I fought.” At the press conference, every member of the QNMU Council raised a hand when asked if they had experienced violence at work.



Union secretary Sarah Beaman said Kat’s experience was a good example of nurses and midwives putting others first. Related Article Queensland Health Shocking video of patient assaulting nurse prompts union call for safer conditions “No nurse or midwife should ever be put in a position that they are punched in the jaw or feel a sense of obligation to come back and continue to provide care,” she said. “I think it’s incredible that we have nurses and midwives and carers that do this. But the focus for governments should not be on having amazingly resilient nurses and midwives; it should be on ensuring there are programs in place to prevent this from ever occurring.” On Monday, Health Minister Tim Nicholls released figures showing 10,000 new health workers had been hired since the LNP was elected, including 7200 frontline doctors, nurses and allied health workers.



But Beaman said that while frontline numbers were increasing, staff were burning out. Related Article Hospitals ‘Bashed, stabbed and spat at’: Violence in public hospitals on the rise “We are holding the government to account on their commitment to 18,700 more nurses and midwives by 2032, [but] we have to retain every nurse, midwife and carer we have,” she said. The QNMU urged the state government to put extra funding into the “highly successful” ambassador model, which uses specially trained, non-traditional security and support staff to de-escalate aggressive behaviour. “In the budget before last, it was expanded in number by about 10 by the LNP government,” Beaman said.



“However, this year there has been no additional funding and no further rollout, and the budget itself has very limited additional funding in relation to occupational violence prevention, which is deeply concerning. “There is some money there for security, but it’s a bit like the workforce recruitment plans, and the retention plans – there are words on paper, but there are no specifics to match this policy.” Daniel Nelson was working in the RBWH Emergency Department in October 2024 when the incident occurred at 2am. Facebook In the video showing the 2024 attack on nurse Daniel Nelson at the Royal Brisbane and Women’s Hospital, which was only recently shared on Facebook, it took almost a full minute for help to arrive. Beaman commended security guards at Queensland hospitals, but said there were not enough of them.



“Every time a security guard is called to a particular area of concern, it means they’re taken away from another area,” she said. “This is why we need better intervention in that space, and we need more staff, not just formal security but other models … like the ambassador model.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘I could eat baked goods all day’: The diners, cafes and bakeries Rachel Khoo loves most
World.content:
FoodThe dish ‘I could eat baked goods all day’: The diners, cafes and bakeries Rachel Khoo loves most The cooking star’s favourite food spots will make you feel like a local-in-the-know the next time you go to Paris, London, Sydney or Melbourne. Jane Rocca August 5, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When popular British cook and author Rachel Khoo swapped fashion PR life in London for Le Cordon Bleu culinary school in Paris, little did she know it would lead to a television career that would kick off in Australia – beginning with SBS’s The Little Paris Kitchen back in 2013. Since then, there have also been celebrity judging gigs at My Kitchen Rules and Zumbo’s Just Desserts, but it’s The Great Australian Bake Off, returning for season nine on August 11, that has her happily returning to Sydney each year. Rachel Khoo with the Kimchi Croque Madame from her new book, The Smallest Restaurant in Paris. Archie Thomas “I love coming to Australia, and even though it’s so far away, I pinch myself that I have my dream job. It’s what I love to do.” It is indeed a long way from home, which, since leaving Paris in 2016, is now a seaside Swedish village, where she has happily settled with her husband and three children.



There’s also a new book, The Smallest Restaurant in Paris, a memoir packed with recipes and her first foray into long-form storytelling. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Rachel on the upcoming Great Australian Bake Off with fellow judge Darren Purchese. Geoff Magee Photography “I’m no Pulitzer Prize writer, but I wanted there to be a real sense of connection between the stories and the recipes. I got myself a writing coach for the project,” says Khoo of the book, which took six years to write. “It’s not a blog or a Substack. This is a far more detailed journey about my life and love of food, and one I am proud of.” Khoo took some time out of her busy schedule to share some of her food favourites at home and away.



Customers line up outside Mamiche cafe in Paris. Getty Images Eating Out Favourite home town restaurant (and go-to dish) I live in a seaside village in Sweden, and there is really nothing there, dining-wise. I make up for it when I am visiting Paris, four times a year. A favourite place I go to is called Le Café du Coin. They offer a three-course meal during the week for less than €30 ($49). The ambience is wonderful. I recently ate beautiful white asparagus, which were kind of meaty and juicy, with a simple vinaigrette on top. I am also regularly at Mamiche bakery. They have two locations in Paris, in the 9th and 10th arrondissements, and they make a great rustic dark sourdough loaf, stuffed with dried fruit.



Favourite Parisian cafes and bars I like to order a latte at a great bakery called Ten Belles. They were one of the first new-wave bakeries that doubled as a cafe and coffee place. They also make amazing sandwiches. I love going to L’Avant Comptoir – a bistro with counter service with small tapas-style plates. The wine list is great. There are now five of them dotted around Paris to try. Rachel cooking in her Little Paris Kitchen in 2015. SBS



Brasserie Le Zinc is very French – the service is fast and it’s great for solo diners. I love to have a glass of bubbly there. Crémant is a very underrated quality French sparkling wine, and when I lived in Paris, I’d always order it because it was more accessible and affordable than champagne, and just as nice. Le Grain de Riz is run by a Vietnamese lady who cooks in the kitchen and has done so for the past 15 years. I love the bo bun with lemongrass pork. My favourite food city It has to be London. I love The Barbary in Covent Garden (and also now in Notting Hill). They have an open fire and grill right in front of you − it’s a very intimate space. They also make their own bread in the tandoor oven. I loved the chargrilled octopus with salad. The aubergine (eggplant) was also fab.



The Impala in Soho is another fire-focused restaurant that’s quite fancy. LMA is a little more refined and elevated. Watching the chefs cook is all part of the experience. I ate veal sweetbreads made in a very rich gravy sauce, deliciously tender with a shaved fennel salad on the side. I also loved the octopus. French-Asian artisan Arôme Bakery has two locations in London – one is behind Selfridges [department store], and the other in Covent Garden. There is always a queue. The pastry laminations are spot on, and they make an amazing egg custard. The savoury croissants are great, too. For a good coffee, I like to go to Oma Coffee Roaster. Brawn is a neighbourhood restaurant that has been around a long time and serves great natural wines. It’s seasonal British food, but with a Mediterranean touch. Roma will be Khoo’s first stop when she next visits Melbourne. Simon Schluter



In Melbourne I haven’t visited Melbourne for a few years, but when I do get back there my first stop will be Roma, where chef Matt Wilkinson is these days − it’s on my list to visit. Matt is so talented, and I absolutely love what he does with his cooking. Lune Croissanterie is always a regular stop when I am in town. Kate Reid is amazing. She has grown a croissant empire, which is brilliant to see. Khoo rates the bread and the coffee at The Bakery on Glenayr. Brook Mitchell In Sydney



I loved going to Saint Peter by Josh Niland for his brilliant take on seafood – his cooking is genius. I have Josh’s cookbooks at home, and find his techniques so interesting – nothing I’d ever do myself, but I have so much admiration for it. Ice-cream made with fish eyeballs! Like every Pom who comes to Sydney, I am always in Bondi. I have my ritual of going to Bakery on Glenayr – the coffee is good, and they make a great quinoa loaf and excellent seeded sourdough bread. For ice-cream, it’s Mapo, also in Bondi, where I love the Amarena sour cherry swirl. “Absolute winner”: The duck at King Clarence. Jennifer Soo I love trying Asian food when I am in Sydney. My co-hosts and friends Darren Purchese and Natalie Tran from the show took me to King Clarence for my birthday. The duck is an absolute winner. I took my kids to the Royal Palace Seafood Restaurant in Haymarket because the kids love the trolley service and it’s how I grew up as a kid in Chinatown in London. It’s a tradition that has died out there, and it was such a new experience for my kids.



The fairy bread popcorn lamington from Tokyo Lamington in Haymarket, Sydney. James Alcock I also love going to Tenacious Croissant for all the pastries. I could eat baked goods all day and love the sweet spicy pork snag. Tokyo Lamington takes lamingtons to another level. I always have to get a box when I’m in that part of town. I’m partial to the fairy bread one. On my days off from filming, I go for a Japanese breakfast at Cool Mac cafe for the onigiri set – Natalie Tran from Bake Off first took me here. Khoo’s go-to dish while she’s filming in Australia is a fruit-packed breakfast bowl. Rachel Khoo Eating in



Signature dish when cooking at home Chocolate mousse. I make this with my kids every Friday. The breakfast recipe I make when I’m filming in Australia is mango, papaya, passionfruit, fresh chilli, a squeeze of lime and my granola on top, with yoghurt hiding at the bottom. My guilty pleasure There’s no such thing as a guilty pleasure – just enjoy what you choose and make sure you go for the best. I do love Kettle salt and vinegar chips.



The kitchen wisdom I cling to It’s not really about the cooking. It’s about sitting down with a cup of tea, being present and taking a moment to share it with other people you love. The Smallest Restaurant in Paris by Rachel Khoo is published by Ultimo Press. RRP $36.99 The Great Australian Bake Off returns to Foxtel and Binge on August 11. Related Article ‘It’s a great time to be Greek’: Cooking star Conor Curran’s restaurant favourites

World.title: Alan Jones fusses and frowns as secrecy shrouds blockbuster trial
World.content:
Analysis NationalNSWAlan Jones trial Alan Jones fusses and frowns as secrecy shrouds blockbuster trial Harriet Alexander August 5, 2026 — 5:07pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Alan Belford Jones stares straight ahead as the man he might once have loved appears supersized on giant screens on either side of the courtroom. The former broadcaster is bright as a parrot in his sky-blue jacket, and his beady eyes are mutinous. For nearly two days he endured this man’s characterisation of their relationship as exploitative and predatory, including sordid allegations that he had made unwanted advances to the witness, “J”, when the young athlete was in his late teens. Alan Jones has appeared irritated, angry and resolute throughout complainant “J”’s evidence. Sam Mooy J has claimed that these advances rose to the level of unwelcome sloppy kisses planted on his lips, undesired groping and parallel masturbation under duress. Jones denies all of it. Now J is under cross-examination and it is Jones’ opportunity to flip the script.



None of the content can be reported. Half an hour after the day’s evidence begins, Judge Glenn Walsh makes a non-publication order that he will revisit at the end of the cross-examination. On the third day of his trial it was Jones’ opportunity to flip the script. Sam Mooy Related Article Alan Jones trial Alan Jones trial as it happened: Judge makes non-publication order as complainant’s cross-examination continues in alleged indecent assault, sexual touching trial Not known for his retiring opinions, Jones sits in the pincer grip of the two screens. His eyes flicker and widen and smoulder as his former protege’s testimony rolls into evidence. He is irritated, he is angry, he is resolute. J was a promising athlete when he first crossed paths with Jones in his mid-teens, and the court has heard that Jones later paid him hundreds of dollars a week to focus on his training and gave him a car and a mobile phone. He reported Jones to police decades later in 2024, after reading media reports that Jones had been charged with indecent assault.



The virtual line between J and Jones’ barrister, Gabrielle Bashir, SC, slackens and pulls taut as she advances towards each of the inconsistencies she seeks to prove in his evidence. J is tense, eager and blinks often under the bright lights of the room where he is annexed. In the back corner of his room a court officer scrolls on a laptop. Bashir and J run through numbers and dates and events. She questions him about incidents and what he has said about incidents. As each line of questioning leads to a crescendo, the tapping of keyboards becomes more frenzied. Jones pulls his notebook and phone towards his chest, fusses with the bottom of his jacket, frowns and runs a finger across his brow. He settles his hands on top of his walking stick. Jones departs the Downing Centre courts in Sydney. Nine News The Crown interjects. The screens are made mute. J disappears from view. The lawyers argue over the questions. They argue over the follow-up questions. They argue over which answer refers to which question. They argue over whether the questions are unfair and they argue over whether the objections to the questions are unfair. The judge demurs. “In any event …”



Related Article Graphic content

Alan Jones trial ‘I just want justice’: Complainant’s emotional testimony in Alan Jones trial It is no more arguing than usual. The trial is taking place in a small courtroom usually reserved for procedural matters where, in ordinary times, dozens of lawyers pile in and out to have their matters dealt with quickly, and more spill into the corridor. This trial is closed to all but accredited media organisations, and during the breaks the hall is only filled with journalists grumbling that they cannot report on the content of the day’s proceedings due to the non-publication order. As the evidence rolls into the afternoon, Jones settles back in his chair. He screws shut his eyes, grazes his hand over his pate and pauses to inspect his finger before returning it to his lap.



Perhaps he feels the day went well. After court he meets his legal team in the foyer, makes a remark and then rolls back on his heels in laughter. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘Felt pressure to make people proud’: Why Jean-Claude Perrottet paid for Liberal memberships
World.content:
NSW Liberal apparatchik and key Reformer Jean-Claude Perrottet has told a corruption inquiry he felt so pressured to stack branches in the Hills Shire he resorted to paying for party memberships. The youngest brother of former premier Dominic Perrottet is a person of interest in an Independent Commission Against Corruption inquiry investigating whether Jean-Claude Perrottet, and several others, played a role in soliciting unlawful donations from prohibited donors. Jean-Claude Perrottet leaving the ICAC after giving evidence. Dominic Lorrimer When asked on Wednesday whether he felt he was being pushed to boost recruitment numbers, Jean-Claude Perrottet told the commission: “I felt pressured to make people proud, to do a good job.” Counsel assisting Juliet Curtin referred to earlier evidence given to the commission by another Reformer, Robert Assaf, who claimed Perrottet paid fees for new members to join Liberal Party branches.



“Maybe I was pressured to deliver, or someone had been a member of the party for 25 years, and they were saying, ‘I’m fed up’. And yeah, maybe Rob’s right … in the sense of pressure built up and, you know, I just needed to get it over the line,” Perrottet told the commission. He also told the commission on Wednesday he was “let go” from his job at Catholic Schools NSW in June, just one month after being promoted. Loading Catholic Schools NSW chief executive Dallas McInerney is also a person of interest to the ICAC. Curtin said to Perrottet: “I want to suggest to you, Mr Perrottet, that the reason you were made redundant only a month after you’ve been promoted to this new role was because of your involvement in this inquiry. Is that right?”



“That wasn’t what was communicated to me from the office and the emails that I received. But I mean, obviously, I’ve thought about the timing of it,” Perrottet responded. The inquiry also heard Reformer co-founder Christian Ellis prepared a “staff report” to plant allies of the right-wing Catholic group in ministerial offices to spread the load of factional work after the 2019 election win. The inquiry was told the staff report was sent to Perrottet and another of his brothers, Charles, on March 25, 2019 – just two days after the election. Charles Perrottet is also a person of interest in the inquiry. Jean-Claude Perrottet was asked about the staff report on Wednesday.



Curtin said Ellis was “conducting some kind of tally or assessment of each of these proposed staffers in terms of their attributes and qualities as a staffer”. Related Article Updated

Operation Rosny Tudehope concedes leaking confidential report to Liberal operative on the run The staff report had letters next to proposed staffers’ names denoting each characteristic. “R” meant recruiter, Curtin said. “Does that mean someone who is willing to engage in the factional work of recruiting new members of the Liberal Party?” she asked. Perrottet said he would not characterise it like that. Meanwhile, John Ruddick, a Libertarian Party member of the NSW upper house, has called for the ICAC’s examination of illegal donations to be paused pending an inquiry into whether the watchdog has been leaking information to the media.



Ruddick claimed in parliament on Wednesday that Operation Rosny “appears to be tainted” because the Herald has revealed several details about the key players targeted by the ICAC over recent weeks. The former Liberal Party member wants the inspector-general of the ICAC, Gail Furness, SC, to investigate whether ICAC staff had disclosed information in a potential breach of the law, and also demanded parliament order an independent inquiry into his claims. He offered no evidence to support his allegations, other than that the Herald’s coverage has referenced sources who are unauthorised to speak publicly. The ICAC began its investigation in mid-2022 into the links between NSW Liberal figures, fugitive Sydney developer Jean Nassif, Catholic Schools NSW and several other figures, including from the Labor Party. Operation Rosny is due to hold eight weeks of public hearings. Ruddick is particularly focused on a story by the Herald late last month that revealed names on the witness list for the first week of hearings. Ruddick has repeatedly suggested on social media platform X that the ICAC staff leaked the document.



However, the witness list was widely circulated to parties involved in Operation Rosny before the Herald obtained and published the document. Ruddick told parliament it should condemn “any attempt by a financially desperate, taxpayer-supported media organisation to weaponise confidential ICAC processes or interfere with the integrity of public hearings for its own commercial or political ends”. On Tuesday the commission heard that senior NSW Liberal MP Damien Tudehope conceded he had leaked a confidential draft report from a parliamentary inquiry to a key witness who deliberately avoided providing evidence. Tudehope, then the Coalition government’s most senior member of the upper house, sent the 2023 confidential report into illegal donations and the Hills Shire Council to lobbyist and Liberal Party operative Jeremy Greenwood, the ICAC heard on Tuesday. Greenwood was one of four Liberal apparatchiks who hid or fled overseas to avoid being handed a summons to appear before the parliamentary inquiry, which was one of the catalysts for the broader ICAC probe.



Liberal leader Kellie Sloane on Wednesday said the Tudehope revelation was not acceptable. But she left open the possibility he could return to her frontbench after the inquiry, saying his evidence had “not changed my position about keeping Damien on the backbench for the short term”. The Herald revealed last week that Liberal MP Chris Rath was captured by a wiretap helping party apparatchiks evade the statewide manhunt to force them before the parliamentary probe. World.title: Labor’s news bargaining plan faces Senate block after US anger
World.content:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s plan to force digital platforms could be killed in the Senate by the Greens and Coalition, casting doubt on a scheme condemned by the US as extortion despite changes made to satisfy tech giants’ demands. Days after big Australian news outlets claimed Labor had weakened the news bargaining incentive, Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young said she feared Labor was letting tech firms off the hook. Anthony Albanese is bound for the US in September facing strong pushback to his News Bargaining Incentive legislation. Alex Ellinghausen One of her chief concerns was a move to increase a levy on tech firms – designed to push Google, Microsoft and Meta to pay for news articles in their platforms – but restrict the charge to their revenue made from advertising. Previously, the law applied to their total revenue. Nine, owner of this masthead, and News Corp have described this change as a gift to the big tech companies that protested against the draft policy.



“Why would the government want to reduce the baseline to deliver even less for Australian news?” Hanson-Young said. “Once we get the detail of the legislation, I’ll be kicking the tyres hard. I’m concerned the government is squibbing this opportunity.” If the Greens and Coalition oppose the change, Labor will need to go back to the drawing board. Nine’s chief executive Matt Stanton urged a rethink on Tuesday in a sharply worded statement which said that Nine felt “deeply misled” by Labor’s last-minute change. The Trump administration has attacked the legislation as “extortion”. AP Coalition communications spokeswoman Sarah Henderson said media companies had warned the new code could mean fewer journalists, jeopardising political support for a policy that began as a bipartisan project under the Morrison government. “The changes around the calculation of the penalty if tech giants refuse to play ball potentially excludes billions of dollars in revenue and weakens the incentive for digital platforms to strike fair commercial deals with Australian news outlet,” Henderson said.



“While we will consider the details of this scheme, Labor cannot claim to support Australian journalism while overseeing changes which media companies say will mean fewer journalists and less investment.” Another change alarming media firms is one that caps at 16.7 per cent, rather than 25 per cent, the amount any one company can pay to a single firm out of its total liability. Larger media firms such as Nine argue privately that they contribute more than 16.7 per cent of a digital giant’s news content. Companies such as News Corp and Nine now expect the total value of their deals with Google and Meta to be smaller than previously expected, though smaller media companies of the likes of SBS and Australian Community Media are believed to have lobbied for this change, having feared they may be left out of any deals at all. The government’s view is that the amount of money that would flow to media firms will not be much less under the changes, and that any difference may be made up by the inclusion of LinkedIn and Tiktok. The feud between media firms and the federal government demonstrates the difficulty of landing a deal for local media while managing the Trump administration’s concerns about punitive taxes on US firms.



Several sources in Labor said its change to how revenue would be collected, revealed on Monday, was driven partly by anxiety about the US response. The news levy has not attracted as much attention from US officials as Australia’s under-16 social media ban, according to government sources, but Albanese did hear concerns about the scheme on his trip to Washington last year. Tech companies can offset the charge by striking individual, tax-deductible deals. The Trump administration has strongly condemned digital services taxes – mostly in Europe. “President Trump is committed to defending America’s leading technology sector from digital services taxes and other forms of foreign extortion,” the US State Department said on Wednesday. “The Trump administration will continue to address these issues with our trading partners.” Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, and Google have so far declined to comment on the latest version of the policy. But their representatives in Washington signalled that the companies were prepared to fight it using the Trump administration.



The Computer & Communications Industry Association, which counts Meta and Google among its members, said the changes to the tax were “for the most part cosmetic” and “critically, do not alter the discriminatory nature of the proposal”. Related Article Publishing ‘Deeply misled’: Nine says news bargaining plan could cost jobs “Targeting a select few foreign firms, mainly American, to fund Australian news businesses, remains a bad policy that is inconsistent with the Australia-US free trade agreement,” said the organisation’s vice president for digital trade, Jonathan McHale. “Australia should abandon this misguided approach and if it chooses not to, US authorities should respond vigorously.” The National Foreign Trade Council (NFTC), a US industry group with Meta, Google and Microsoft in its membership, said it was disappointed that Australia was sticking with the policy and that it now covered a broader spectrum of US companies.



Tiffany Smith, the group’s vice president for global trade, said the Trump administration was “committed to the fair treatment of American companies abroad”. “We call on the Australian government to reconsider this measure, which adds to a broader deteriorating trend in the tax and investment climate in Australia,” she said. Related Article Media & marketing News Corp says plan to make tech giants pay for news has been ‘gutted’ Australia was also hit with a new 12.5 per cent tariff due to Canberra’s alleged failure to deal with imports produced with forced labour. The jousting comes ahead of US visits by Albanese, who is expected to go to New York in September and attend the G20 in Miami in December, and Foreign Minister Penny Wong, who is due to attend a G20 meeting in Atlanta in October.



Albanese previously suggested he wouldn’t be swayed by pushback from the White House. “We’re a sovereign nation, and my government will make decisions based upon the Australian national interest,” he said in April. “We do that right across the board.” Microsoft, which owns LinkedIn, said it shared the government’s objective of promoting a sustainable news ecosystem and appreciated the consultation. World.title: Revealed: The radical overhaul of cancer screening to detect most at risk
World.content:
NationalCancer Revealed: The radical overhaul of cancer screening to detect most at risk Kate Aubusson and Henrietta Cook August 5, 2026 — 5:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A radical overhaul of Australia’s breast cancer screening will implement a risk-based approach to detect cancers earlier with new technologies beyond mammograms, replacing the current one-size-fits-all, age-based model. Australia’s federal, state and territory governments on Wednesday endorsed a new national strategic framework for BreastScreen Australia, based on the latest evidence of risk assessment and new technologies. Breast screening is free for Australian women once they reach 40. Getty Images A high-priority action is establishing nationally consistent two-tiered risk-based screening pathways based on women’s risk factors for developing breast cancer – including breast density – that deploys a range of screening techniques, including contrast-based imaging and AI prediction models. Breast cancer is the most common cancer diagnosed in females in Australia. More than 20,000 people are diagnosed, and about 3000 women die of breast cancer every year.



Related Article Healthcare Beyond the mammogram: How AI is spotting hidden breast cancer risks Breast screening prevents up to half of breast cancer deaths among Australian women aged 50 to 74, but take-up remains low at 52 per cent, well below the 70 per cent target. Associate Professor Carolyn Nickson at the University of Sydney’s Cancer Elimination Collaboration group said the best available evidence showed a risk-stratified approach for women aged 50 to 74 could lead to some breast cancers being detected earlier, save lives and reduce the intensity of treatment. “We know that we can identify groups of women who may benefit from having some more intensive screening protocol than what’s standard for this screen,” said Nickson, who was part of an expert group tasked by the federal government to explore risk-adjusted breast screening program options. One such group was women with higher breast density, who have a higher risk of breast cancer, and whose tumours can be harder to see on mammograms.



Risk-stratified screening could also help determine which women in their 40s may benefit from starting screening sooner and with screening technologies better suited to younger women. “That could be contrast-based imaging or a change to their time between screenings,” Nickson said. A revamped BreastScreen Australia could also include a risk assessment questionnaire that considers family history and lifestyle factors, as well as AI mammogram image processing. “If we can combine all of that information, we know that we can identify groups of women who may benefit from having some more intensive screening protocol than what is standard,” she said. Australian research published in the prestigious Lancet medical journal in March showed an AI tool known as BRAIx could help predict which women were at high risk of developing breast cancer after receiving a mammogram all clear.



Related Article Science The five everyday products linked to nearly one-third of all deaths globally One in 10 women with the highest BRAIx risk scores developed cancer within four years – even after receiving an “all-clear” breast screen. The AI tool searched for patterns in mammograms to pick up signals for risk invisible to the human eye, making it easier to detect signs of cancer in dense breasts. Associate Professor Davis McCarthy, whose team at St Vincent’s Institute of Medical Research led the development of BRAIx, said the Australian government’s new risk-based strategy would do a much better job at identifying women at higher risk of developing breast cancer than the current protocol. “It’s a very successful program, but it’s a one-size-fits-all program, and what we have in the population are many people at many, many different levels of risk for breast cancer individually,” he said of the existing BreastScreen Australia program.



“If we can get it right in terms of allocating the right people to each pathway, then we have a huge opportunity here to do a much better job of keeping high-risk women safe while keeping lower-risk women equally safe.” The overhaul may also encourage more women to take part in screening, McCarthy said. “Hopefully, when people see these efforts to make positive changes with good evidence behind them, they see that this is a service that’s not stuck in the past, but is looking to the future.” The federal government will invest $1.3 million to implement the plan and help BreastScreen Australia keep pace with new technologies. The road to Australia’s risk-based breast screening program: Develop a national annual screening eligibility policy

Pilot approaches for women aged 45 to 49

Develop a risk assessment tool

Research alternative screening pathways for women with high breast density.



BreastScreen Australia would operate as normal while the reforms are implemented in phases over the next 10 years. Federal Assistant Health Minister Rebecca White said regular breast screening remains one of the most effective ways to detect cancer early, preventing more challenging treatment and poorer outcomes for women. “Early detection saves lives, and these reforms will help ensure even more women can access the care and support they need for years to come,” White said. Since 1991, BreastScreen Australia has detected more than 140,000 invasive breast cancers in women who had no symptoms. Breast Cancer Network Australia welcomed the announcement and urged the Federal government to publish a fully costed, 10-year implementation plan, which government modelling suggested could be $2 billion. World.title: Secret missions and staged meetings: How a backroom deal led to IBAC probe
World.content:
Updated PoliticsVictoriaIBAC Secret missions and staged meetings: How a backroom deal led to IBAC probe Kieran Rooney Updated August 5, 2026 — 5:49pm ,first published August 5, 2026 — 9:46am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Daniel Andrews’ decision to sideline a senior minister and strike a secret pay deal with firefighters gave a union boss “extraordinary influence” over one of the government’s most contentious reforms and exposed the state to the risk of corruption, an IBAC investigation found. At the height of a pay dispute with the state’s firefighters in 2016, Andrews as premier tasked key allies and senior public servants with a “secret mission” to reach agreement with United Firefighters boss Peter Marshall without the knowledge of the Country Fire Authority and then-emergency services minister Jane Garrett. Operation Richmond centred on dealings between Daniel Andrews’ government and the United Firefighters Union under Peter Marshall. Marija Ercegovac Tabled in parliament on Wednesday, the Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission’s findings into an eight-year-long investigation found “serious and concerning conduct” by Victorian ministers, MPs and public servants that included a text message to the premier about a secret handshake and a minister laughing about phone taps. Known as Operation Richmond, the investigation, which began in 2018 but was suppressed for years by legal challenges, found that hotel-room negotiations were hidden through a staged meeting with the premier that paved the way for Marshall to exert “extraordinary influence” and receive privileged access to senior members of the state government.



While the long-awaited report stopped short of finding corrupt conduct – for which Victoria has a higher threshold than any other state, IBAC identified serious issues in the way pay deals with the Country Fire Authority (CFA) and the Metropolitan Fire Brigade (MFB) were negotiated alongside the establishment of Fire Rescue Victoria. Related Article IBAC Five things to know about Operation Richmond In a statement, Andrews said the report showed no evidence “to support the false and completely outrageous claims that I had been blackmailed to force a favourable outcome for the United Firefighters Union”. “For the record and the avoidance of any doubt, there are no findings in relation to corrupt conduct made about me, any other member of the government, or the public service,” he added. In a video posted to the UFU Victoria website, Marshall slammed both IBAC and the Operation Richmond investigation, saying, “This is an organisation that has spent many millions of dollars of public money using coercive powers to go on a witch hunt.”



On Wednesday morning, Premier Ben Carroll said he had not yet read the report in full, but had received some “high-level advice” and that his government would accept IBAC’s recommendations. Asked whether the conduct of Andrews and others in the report would be considered corrupt under the expanded definition of corruption which Carroll pledged to adopt after being appointed premier last week, he said he would first read the IBAC report carefully. “I am going to study it and give Victorians the actions and answers they deserve,” he said. In the report’s opening, Commissioner Victoria Elliott said, “IBAC found that senior members of government acted contrary to established policies, procedures, codes of conduct and conventions in negotiating a deal with the secretary of the United Firefighters Union (UFU), Mr Peter Marshall, for the CFA Enterprise Bargaining Agreement (EBA) without the knowledge and involvement of the responsible minister, agencies and department. “By doing so, the government placed itself in a position where Mr Marshall was able to exert extraordinary influence over the negotiations for both the CFA EBA and the MFB EBA,” the report said, noting that, “Mr Marshall was afforded privileged access to senior members of government which, in many cases, were not disclosed and were to the exclusion of other key stakeholders”.



“The government placed itself in a position where Mr Marshall was able to exert extraordinary influence.” Delayed Operation Richmond report At the time, the CFA pay deal became a political flashpoint for the Andrews government. In June 2016, Garrett resigned as emergency services minister and quit the cabinet because she disagreed with her government’s moves to accept UFU demands. She died in 2022. “Operation Richmond highlights how government leaders, including ministers and the premier, can undermine established checks and balances when they fail to model high integrity standards and act as stewards of good governance,” the report found. The report was originally scheduled for release by the end of June, but was delayed by an unsuccessful legal challenge from Marshall. Operation Richmond began after IBAC received allegations that Marshall had blackmailed or compromised the premier to change his position on the 2016 CFA pay deal. The blackmail claim was never substantiated.



The investigation was then widened to include negotiations for a pay deal with the Metropolitan Fire Brigade and the creation of its replacement, Fire Rescue Victoria. Related Article IBAC Firefighters’ union boss loses court battle to bury corruption investigation, but appeal possible Negotiations on the CFA deal began in 2015, but had broken down by the end of the year. The UFU’s log of claims was 400 pages long and the agency was concerned some of its key requests were unlawful. Andrews and then-special minister of state Gavin Jennings both told IBAC that by March 2016, the dispute had reached a crisis point, with the former premier describing the situation as “completely intractable”, with both sides miles apart. IBAC found Andrews authorised Jennings, with the assistance of Tony Bates – a deputy secretary at the Department of Premier and Cabinet – to negotiate the CFA deal directly without the knowledge of the CFA themselves.



“While in negotiations on 11 April 2016, Minister Jennings referred to being ‘off doing my secret mission’ and ‘secret business’ in text messages to staff in his office and the PPO [Premier’s Private Office],” the report said. “Private meetings were held with the UFU in rented meeting spaces and a hotel. Those involved were instructed to keep the meetings confidential.” After four days of negotiations, the two sides agreed to terms and Jennings texted Andrews: “Handshake has occurred – it’s done!” Once negotiations were finished, IBAC found, a document outlining the terms was presented to cabinet as a proposal from the union, with ministers – including Garrett – unaware they had been negotiated with people inside the government. In an intercepted phone call from 2019, Marshall summarised the meetings, telling a ministerial adviser the pay deal “was negotiated with f---in’ Jennings in a back room. It was endorsed by f---in’ Andrews and cabinet.”



On April 13, 2016, Marshall met with Andrews and a staffer for what IBAC viewed as a staged event so that there could be a witness to the agreement being presented to the government as a “proposal” from the union. Evidence from Bates appeared to support this assessment. The senior public servant told investigators he led the development of the deal and “if there was a presentation of the agreement to the premier’s office, I would categorise it as ceremonial”. Even after cabinet’s expenditure committee signed off on the deal on April 19, however, Jane Garrett and the CFA remained opposed to it. A key concern among those who did not support the deal were clauses that required the CFA to “consult and agree” with the UFU on decisions before they could be made.



They became known as “veto clauses”, which effectively allowed the union to increase its control of the CFA by blocking policies it did not agree with. Before her death, Garrett told IBAC she was contacted by a federal Labor senator to persuade her to progress the deal with the Fair Work Commission. The CFA agreed to return to the commission in May and resume conciliation, but Marshall resisted any attempts to compromise on the EBA and would not budge on the veto clauses. On May 23, 2016, the premier sent a text message to Jennings asking how mediation was progressing. Jennings responded: “At 11am, he [Marshall] was convinced you were a treacherous c--- and I was a f---ing idiot ... By lunchtime he was giving me the benefit of the doubt.” The IBAC report said evidence gathered through Operation Richmond showed Andrews wanted to end the pay dispute in a way that excluded Garrett, then emergency services minister, whom he didn’t believe could resolve the matter.



Firefighters’ union chief Peter Marshall on the steps of Victoria’s Parliament House in 2022. Chris Hopkins “At the time of the decision, the premier was facing internal political pressure, negative media attention and industrial unrest,” the report said. But IBAC found that in secretly excluding Garrett, the CFA and other key parts of government from the process, the premier, Jennings and Bates behaved contrary to “government policy, procedures, convention and their respective codes of conduct”. It also found the undisclosed negotiations limited the state’s bargaining position and their ability to resist Marshall’s demands. Garrett quit cabinet in June 2016 because she considered the pay deal unacceptable, and when the CFA board refused to endorse the agreement, they were stood down and replaced. Their successors signed off on the arrangement.



At the same time, Marshall expected the terms of the CFA deal to be replicated in a pay deal with the Metropolitan Fire Brigade. One former MFB chief executive told IBAC that they had concerns similar to the CFA’s, including that some elements of the deal were unlawful or undermined safety obligations. “Ultimately, to resolve the dispute, the government appointed new members to the MFB board who understood the government’s preferred position on the MFB EBA,” the report said. During his examination by IBAC, Bates said that on April 17, 2016 he received a call from an MFB executive who asked the government employee, “What the f--- do you think you’re playing at?” in relation to concerns the department had been negotiating with the UFU without the knowledge of the fire services. The executive told IBAC they found Bates’ behaviour deeply concerning, and said, “the path that it was heading down was disastrous for the organisation”.



IBAC also raised concerns about the way a 2019 bill that reformed the fire services was passed – which ultimately turned the MFB and the paid parts of the CFA into a new body named Fire Rescue Victoria. The corruption watchdog found Marshall had sought to secure the support of a crossbench MP by hiring their relative days before it was due for a vote in the upper house. In an intercepted phone call from June 2019, Marshall told a friend the MP was “100 per cent behind us … just to make sure we just employed [their relative].” The investigation also found Marshall had privileged access to Lisa Neville, who served as emergency services minister from 2018 to 2019, and sought to influence her decision on who should be appointed commissioner of the new agency.



“While IBAC makes no findings as to whether Mr Marshall did influence the minister on the appointment of the FRV commissioner, IBAC found that the minister’s stakeholder management of Mr Marshall created significant opportunities for him to do so,” the report said. “Finally, during this period, IBAC also found evidence that an MFB board member, Mr Greg Sword, shared confidential information with Mr Marshall in 2019 in breach of his professional obligations.” In a statement, Daniel Andrews said the report showed “no evidence whatsoever to support the false and completely outrageous claims that I had been blackmailed to force a favourable outcome for the United Firefighters Union and its thousands of career firefighter members”. “For the record and the avoidance of any doubt, there are no findings in relation to corrupt conduct made about me, any other member of the government, or the public service. That is a fact,” Andrews said. “By 2016, the relationship between the Country Fire Authority and the UFU had completely broken down, and a spiteful and dysfunctional enterprise bargaining dispute had dragged on for years. Fire chiefs were spending more time in the Fair Work Commission than running their organisations.



“That was not acceptable to me or to the government when community safety was on the line. The dispute needed to be resolved in the public interest, and it was.” Opposition Leader Jess Wilson said on Wednesday that the report showed the state was being run by a “gangster government”. “This government, time and time again, has not acted with integrity,” she said. Read more on Operation Richmond: How we got here: 5 things to know about Operation Richmond.

World.title: Union seizes on viral video of violent patient to renew security calls
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland Health Union seizes on viral video of violent patient to renew security calls Dominique Tassell August 5, 2026 — 5:16pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Queensland Nurses and Midwives’ Union has called for better working conditions and increased health funding, days after the Queensland government celebrated additional frontline staff, and a video of a nurse taking down an aggressive patient went viral. Of 8000 QNMU members recently surveyed, 82 per cent reported experiencing violence at work. Exposure to racism had also increased since their last survey. Kat, a senior nurse who spoke to the media outside the QNMU annual conference but asked for her surname not to be used, said she was punched in the face by a patient about a year ago. Secretary of the Queensland Nurses and Midwives’ Union Sarah Beaman (centre) with members of its council. Dominique Tassell Initially, she thought her jaw was broken, and she was left with a large, almost black, bruise for some time afterwards.



Working in the emergency department, Kat said she constantly witnessed violence against her staff. “It’s devastating. Every time I go to employment, the possibility of one of my staff members getting assaulted is quite high,” she said. The union said staff often blamed themselves, or worried they had initiated the incident. “I can tell you, in my case, I did not [initiate it],” Kat said. “I experienced that flight or fight. Because I’m quite stubborn, I fought.” At the press conference, every member of the QNMU Council raised a hand when asked if they had experienced violence at work.



Union secretary Sarah Beaman said Kat’s experience was a good example of nurses and midwives putting others first. Related Article Queensland Health Shocking video of patient assaulting nurse prompts union call for safer conditions “No nurse or midwife should ever be put in a position that they are punched in the jaw or feel a sense of obligation to come back and continue to provide care,” she said. “I think it’s incredible that we have nurses and midwives and carers that do this. But the focus for governments should not be on having amazingly resilient nurses and midwives; it should be on ensuring there are programs in place to prevent this from ever occurring.” On Monday, Health Minister Tim Nicholls released figures showing 10,000 new health workers had been hired since the LNP was elected, including 7200 frontline doctors, nurses and allied health workers.



But Beaman said that while frontline numbers were increasing, staff were burning out. Related Article Hospitals ‘Bashed, stabbed and spat at’: Violence in public hospitals on the rise “We are holding the government to account on their commitment to 18,700 more nurses and midwives by 2032, [but] we have to retain every nurse, midwife and carer we have,” she said. The QNMU urged the state government to put extra funding into the “highly successful” ambassador model, which uses specially trained, non-traditional security and support staff to de-escalate aggressive behaviour. “In the budget before last, it was expanded in number by about 10 by the LNP government,” Beaman said.



“However, this year there has been no additional funding and no further rollout, and the budget itself has very limited additional funding in relation to occupational violence prevention, which is deeply concerning. “There is some money there for security, but it’s a bit like the workforce recruitment plans, and the retention plans – there are words on paper, but there are no specifics to match this policy.” Daniel Nelson was working in the RBWH Emergency Department in October 2024 when the incident occurred at 2am. Facebook In the video showing the 2024 attack on nurse Daniel Nelson at the Royal Brisbane and Women’s Hospital, which was only recently shared on Facebook, it took almost a full minute for help to arrive. Beaman commended security guards at Queensland hospitals, but said there were not enough of them.



“Every time a security guard is called to a particular area of concern, it means they’re taken away from another area,” she said. “This is why we need better intervention in that space, and we need more staff, not just formal security but other models … like the ambassador model.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘I could eat baked goods all day’: The diners, cafes and bakeries Rachel Khoo loves most
World.content:
FoodThe dish ‘I could eat baked goods all day’: The diners, cafes and bakeries Rachel Khoo loves most The cooking star’s favourite food spots will make you feel like a local-in-the-know the next time you go to Paris, London, Sydney or Melbourne. Jane Rocca August 5, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When popular British cook and author Rachel Khoo swapped fashion PR life in London for Le Cordon Bleu culinary school in Paris, little did she know it would lead to a television career that would kick off in Australia – beginning with SBS’s The Little Paris Kitchen back in 2013. Since then, there have also been celebrity judging gigs at My Kitchen Rules and Zumbo’s Just Desserts, but it’s The Great Australian Bake Off, returning for season nine on August 11, that has her happily returning to Sydney each year. Rachel Khoo with the Kimchi Croque Madame from her new book, The Smallest Restaurant in Paris. Archie Thomas “I love coming to Australia, and even though it’s so far away, I pinch myself that I have my dream job. It’s what I love to do.” It is indeed a long way from home, which, since leaving Paris in 2016, is now a seaside Swedish village, where she has happily settled with her husband and three children.



There’s also a new book, The Smallest Restaurant in Paris, a memoir packed with recipes and her first foray into long-form storytelling. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Rachel on the upcoming Great Australian Bake Off with fellow judge Darren Purchese. Geoff Magee Photography “I’m no Pulitzer Prize writer, but I wanted there to be a real sense of connection between the stories and the recipes. I got myself a writing coach for the project,” says Khoo of the book, which took six years to write. “It’s not a blog or a Substack. This is a far more detailed journey about my life and love of food, and one I am proud of.” Khoo took some time out of her busy schedule to share some of her food favourites at home and away.



Customers line up outside Mamiche cafe in Paris. Getty Images Eating Out Favourite home town restaurant (and go-to dish) I live in a seaside village in Sweden, and there is really nothing there, dining-wise. I make up for it when I am visiting Paris, four times a year. A favourite place I go to is called Le Café du Coin. They offer a three-course meal during the week for less than €30 ($49). The ambience is wonderful. I recently ate beautiful white asparagus, which were kind of meaty and juicy, with a simple vinaigrette on top. I am also regularly at Mamiche bakery. They have two locations in Paris, in the 9th and 10th arrondissements, and they make a great rustic dark sourdough loaf, stuffed with dried fruit.



Favourite Parisian cafes and bars I like to order a latte at a great bakery called Ten Belles. They were one of the first new-wave bakeries that doubled as a cafe and coffee place. They also make amazing sandwiches. I love going to L’Avant Comptoir – a bistro with counter service with small tapas-style plates. The wine list is great. There are now five of them dotted around Paris to try. Rachel cooking in her Little Paris Kitchen in 2015. SBS



Brasserie Le Zinc is very French – the service is fast and it’s great for solo diners. I love to have a glass of bubbly there. Crémant is a very underrated quality French sparkling wine, and when I lived in Paris, I’d always order it because it was more accessible and affordable than champagne, and just as nice. Le Grain de Riz is run by a Vietnamese lady who cooks in the kitchen and has done so for the past 15 years. I love the bo bun with lemongrass pork. My favourite food city It has to be London. I love The Barbary in Covent Garden (and also now in Notting Hill). They have an open fire and grill right in front of you − it’s a very intimate space. They also make their own bread in the tandoor oven. I loved the chargrilled octopus with salad. The aubergine (eggplant) was also fab.



The Impala in Soho is another fire-focused restaurant that’s quite fancy. LMA is a little more refined and elevated. Watching the chefs cook is all part of the experience. I ate veal sweetbreads made in a very rich gravy sauce, deliciously tender with a shaved fennel salad on the side. I also loved the octopus. French-Asian artisan Arôme Bakery has two locations in London – one is behind Selfridges [department store], and the other in Covent Garden. There is always a queue. The pastry laminations are spot on, and they make an amazing egg custard. The savoury croissants are great, too. For a good coffee, I like to go to Oma Coffee Roaster. Brawn is a neighbourhood restaurant that has been around a long time and serves great natural wines. It’s seasonal British food, but with a Mediterranean touch. Roma will be Khoo’s first stop when she next visits Melbourne. Simon Schluter



In Melbourne I haven’t visited Melbourne for a few years, but when I do get back there my first stop will be Roma, where chef Matt Wilkinson is these days − it’s on my list to visit. Matt is so talented, and I absolutely love what he does with his cooking. Lune Croissanterie is always a regular stop when I am in town. Kate Reid is amazing. She has grown a croissant empire, which is brilliant to see. Khoo rates the bread and the coffee at The Bakery on Glenayr. Brook Mitchell In Sydney



I loved going to Saint Peter by Josh Niland for his brilliant take on seafood – his cooking is genius. I have Josh’s cookbooks at home, and find his techniques so interesting – nothing I’d ever do myself, but I have so much admiration for it. Ice-cream made with fish eyeballs! Like every Pom who comes to Sydney, I am always in Bondi. I have my ritual of going to Bakery on Glenayr – the coffee is good, and they make a great quinoa loaf and excellent seeded sourdough bread. For ice-cream, it’s Mapo, also in Bondi, where I love the Amarena sour cherry swirl. “Absolute winner”: The duck at King Clarence. Jennifer Soo I love trying Asian food when I am in Sydney. My co-hosts and friends Darren Purchese and Natalie Tran from the show took me to King Clarence for my birthday. The duck is an absolute winner. I took my kids to the Royal Palace Seafood Restaurant in Haymarket because the kids love the trolley service and it’s how I grew up as a kid in Chinatown in London. It’s a tradition that has died out there, and it was such a new experience for my kids.



The fairy bread popcorn lamington from Tokyo Lamington in Haymarket, Sydney. James Alcock I also love going to Tenacious Croissant for all the pastries. I could eat baked goods all day and love the sweet spicy pork snag. Tokyo Lamington takes lamingtons to another level. I always have to get a box when I’m in that part of town. I’m partial to the fairy bread one. On my days off from filming, I go for a Japanese breakfast at Cool Mac cafe for the onigiri set – Natalie Tran from Bake Off first took me here. Khoo’s go-to dish while she’s filming in Australia is a fruit-packed breakfast bowl. Rachel Khoo Eating in



Signature dish when cooking at home Chocolate mousse. I make this with my kids every Friday. The breakfast recipe I make when I’m filming in Australia is mango, papaya, passionfruit, fresh chilli, a squeeze of lime and my granola on top, with yoghurt hiding at the bottom. My guilty pleasure There’s no such thing as a guilty pleasure – just enjoy what you choose and make sure you go for the best. I do love Kettle salt and vinegar chips.



The kitchen wisdom I cling to It’s not really about the cooking. It’s about sitting down with a cup of tea, being present and taking a moment to share it with other people you love. World.title: Alan Jones fusses and frowns as secrecy shrouds blockbuster trial
World.content:
Analysis NationalNSWAlan Jones trial Alan Jones fusses and frowns as secrecy shrouds blockbuster trial Harriet Alexander August 5, 2026 — 5:07pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Alan Belford Jones stares straight ahead as the man he might once have loved appears supersized on giant screens on either side of the courtroom. The former broadcaster is bright as a parrot in his sky-blue jacket, and his beady eyes are mutinous. For nearly two days he endured this man’s characterisation of their relationship as exploitative and predatory, including sordid allegations that he had made unwanted advances to the witness, “J”, when the young athlete was in his late teens. Alan Jones has appeared irritated, angry and resolute throughout complainant “J”’s evidence. Sam Mooy J has claimed that these advances rose to the level of unwelcome sloppy kisses planted on his lips, undesired groping and parallel masturbation under duress. Jones denies all of it. Now J is under cross-examination and it is Jones’ opportunity to flip the script.



None of the content can be reported. Half an hour after the day’s evidence begins, Judge Glenn Walsh makes a non-publication order that he will revisit at the end of the cross-examination. On the third day of his trial it was Jones’ opportunity to flip the script. Sam Mooy Related Article Alan Jones trial Alan Jones trial as it happened: Judge makes non-publication order as complainant’s cross-examination continues in alleged indecent assault, sexual touching trial Not known for his retiring opinions, Jones sits in the pincer grip of the two screens. His eyes flicker and widen and smoulder as his former protege’s testimony rolls into evidence. He is irritated, he is angry, he is resolute. J was a promising athlete when he first crossed paths with Jones in his mid-teens, and the court has heard that Jones later paid him hundreds of dollars a week to focus on his training and gave him a car and a mobile phone. He reported Jones to police decades later in 2024, after reading media reports that Jones had been charged with indecent assault.



The virtual line between J and Jones’ barrister, Gabrielle Bashir, SC, slackens and pulls taut as she advances towards each of the inconsistencies she seeks to prove in his evidence. J is tense, eager and blinks often under the bright lights of the room where he is annexed. In the back corner of his room a court officer scrolls on a laptop. Bashir and J run through numbers and dates and events. She questions him about incidents and what he has said about incidents. As each line of questioning leads to a crescendo, the tapping of keyboards becomes more frenzied. Jones pulls his notebook and phone towards his chest, fusses with the bottom of his jacket, frowns and runs a finger across his brow. He settles his hands on top of his walking stick. Jones departs the Downing Centre courts in Sydney. Nine News The Crown interjects. The screens are made mute. J disappears from view. The lawyers argue over the questions. They argue over the follow-up questions. They argue over which answer refers to which question. They argue over whether the questions are unfair and they argue over whether the objections to the questions are unfair. The judge demurs. “In any event …”



Related Article Graphic content

Alan Jones trial ‘I just want justice’: Complainant’s emotional testimony in Alan Jones trial It is no more arguing than usual. The trial is taking place in a small courtroom usually reserved for procedural matters where, in ordinary times, dozens of lawyers pile in and out to have their matters dealt with quickly, and more spill into the corridor. This trial is closed to all but accredited media organisations, and during the breaks the hall is only filled with journalists grumbling that they cannot report on the content of the day’s proceedings due to the non-publication order. As the evidence rolls into the afternoon, Jones settles back in his chair. He screws shut his eyes, grazes his hand over his pate and pauses to inspect his finger before returning it to his lap.



Perhaps he feels the day went well. After court he meets his legal team in the foyer, makes a remark and then rolls back on his heels in laughter. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.
